Terminology in this reader

Hakeda’s wording and his bracketed expansions are retained in the BDK text. Wŏnhyo’s quotations of the treatise are translated afresh so you can see how he construes them. The BDK references alongside those quotations identify the English passage under discussion. An arrow beside a later paragraph returns to the same passage.

相 · xiàng
Characteristic when it means the feature by which something is distinguished (the usual Sanskrit equivalent is lakṣaṇa). “Appearance” fits what manifests to mind, as in the birds’ tracks. In the discussion of the four alternatives, Wŏnhyo reads 非有相 and 非無相 as denying that suchness can be characterized as existent or nonexistent.
理 and 事
Reality as such and particular phenomena. In the discussion of language, 理 is the reality called suchness (tathatā). In a phrase explaining why something follows, 理 can simply mean the rationale.
本覺 and 始覺
Original awakening and inceptive awakening. The latter is awakening realized in the course of practice, from its inception through its culmination. Hakeda calls it “the process of actualization of enlightenment.”
分別念 and 熏習
Discriminative thought distinguishes and identifies. Perfuming (vāsanā) describes conditioning by impressions. The image helps explain how phenomena come to appear differently.
如來藏 and 阿梨耶識
Tathāgatagarbha is the concealed or indwelling tathāgata. Ālayavijñāna is storehouse consciousness. Wŏnhyo asks in precisely what sense the two can be identified.
法身 and 法界
Dharmakāya is the Dharma body. Dharmadhātu is the realm of dharmas. The treatise speaks of the “one dharmadhātu.”
受、想、行、識
In passages on the aggregates these are feeling, perception, fabrications (volitional formations), and consciousness. Wŏnhyo also uses 行 for practice or conduct elsewhere.
作有
Take the form of what exists. 作 supplies the dynamic sense. 有 can mean bhava, “becoming,” in dependent origination. Here it is paired with emptiness. Compare the later passage on karma’s results in the three realms of becoming (Separate Notes on the continuing mind).

First-use terminology notes appear separately in each commentary so either work can be read on its own. They compare the Chinese at that occurrence with the linked BDK passage. Where Wŏnhyo uses a shorter or different Chinese name for an aspect, the note also gives the treatise’s Chinese beside Hakeda’s wording.

BDK p. 11

One Mind and its two gateways

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 11 The revelation of the true meaning [of the principle of the Mahayana can be achieved] by [unfolding the doctrine] that the principle of One Mind has two aspects.⁕ One is the aspect of Mind in terms of the absolute (tathatā; suchness), and the other is the aspect of Mind in terms of phenomena (samsara; birth and death). Each of these two aspects embraces all states of existence. Why? Because these two aspects are mutually inclusive.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

1.1.1.1. The general statement
One Mind and its two gateways
BDK 11 ↗One Mind has two aspects

In the general explanation, the words “the one dharma of mind has two gateways” accord with the sūtra.ᵀ “Quiescence is called One Mind. One Mind is called tathāgatagarbha.”

one dharma of mind · 一心法 yī xīn fǎ · BDK p. 11 principle of One Mind
two gateways · 二種門 èr zhǒng mén · BDK p. 11 two aspects
BDK 11 ↗Mind in terms of the absolute; Mind in terms of phenomena

The gateway of mind as suchness explains the sūtra’s “quiescence is called One Mind.”ᵀ The gateway of mind as arising and ceasing explains its “One Mind is called tathāgatagarbha.”ᵀ Why? All dharmas are without cessation. Quiescent from the beginning,ᵀ they are simply One Mind. This is called the gateway of mind as suchness. Hence “quiescence is called One Mind.”

gateway of mind as suchness · 心真如門 xīn zhēn rú mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of the absolute
gateway of mind as arising and ceasing · 心生滅門 xīn shēng miè mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of phenomena
All dharmas · 一切法 yī qiè fǎ · BDK p. 11 all states of existence

↥ This One Mind also has original awakening as intrinsic to its very being.ᵀ Moved by ignorance, it arises and ceases.ᵀ In this gateway, the nature of the Tathāgata lies hidden. Hence the name tathāgatagarbha. As the sūtra says, “The tathāgatagarbha is the cause of what is wholesome and unwholesome. It brings forth every kind of birth in every destiny, like an actor appearing by turns in the guise of beings in the various destinies.” Such meanings belong to the gateway of arising and ceasing. Thus “One Mind is called tathāgatagarbha” discloses this gateway of the One Mind.ᵀ

original awakening · 本覺 běn jué · BDK p. 17 original enlightenment
arises and ceases · 生滅 shēng miè · BDK p. 16 birth and death (samsara) Hakeda adds “(samsara)” when translating this passage.
gateway of arising and ceasing · 生滅門 shēng miè mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of phenomena

↥ The treatise says below, “As for mind’s arising and ceasing, it is on the basis of the tathāgatagarbha that there is a mind that arises and ceases,”ᵀ and so on, down to “this consciousness has two meanings, awakening and nonawakening.”ᵀ What the gateway encompasses extends beyond the arising-and-ceasing mind alone. It takes in both the very reality of that which arises and ceases and its characteristics of arising and ceasing.ᵀ

mind’s arising and ceasing · 心生滅 xīn shēng miè · BDK p. 16 The Mind as phenomena (samsara)

awakening · 覺義 jué yì · BDK p. 16 enlightenment
nonawakening · 不覺 bù jué · BDK p. 16 nonenlightenment
arising and ceasing · 生滅 shēng miè · BDK p. 16 birth and death (samsara) Hakeda adds “(samsara)” when translating this passage.
Why it is called One Mind
BDK 11 ↗The principle of One Mind

Such are the two gateways. What, then, is meant by “One Mind”? Defiled and pure dharmas are nondual in nature. No difference can ultimately be found between the two gateways of the true and the delusive. Hence “one.” This nonduality is what is real in all dharmas. Unlike empty space, its very nature is wondrously aware. Hence “mind.” But if there are no two, how could there be a one? If no one can be found, to what could the word “mind” refer? This truth lies beyond language and conceptual thought. We have no name for it and call it “One Mind” for want of a better term.

How each gateway encompasses all dharmas
BDK 11 ↗Each of these two aspects embraces all states of existence

“Each of these two gateways comprehends all dharmas” explains the earlier statement that this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas. Previously the treatise simply said that mind encompasses all dharmas. Here it shows that each gateway encompasses them all.

Why the two gateways are inseparable
BDK 11 ↗Because these two aspects are mutually inclusive

“Because these two gateways are inseparable” explains how each encompasses everything.ᵀ The gateway of suchness expresses the common characteristic of the defiled and the pure. There are no separate defiled or pure dharmas apart from this common characteristic.ᵀ It can therefore encompass all defiled and pure dharmas. The gateway of arising and ceasing displays the defiled and the pure in their particularity. Nothing falls outside the scope of defiled and pure dharmas. This gateway therefore also encompasses all dharmas.ᵀ The common and the particular differ, yet each gateway excludes nothing. Hence the two are called inseparable. This completes the general explanation.

inseparable · 不相離 bù xiāng lí · BDK p. 11 mutually inclusive
gateway of suchness · 真如門 zhēn rú mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of the absolute
all dharmas · 一切諸法 yī qiè zhū fǎ · BDK p. 12 all things

1. The two gateways together

One Mind and the two gateways

BDK 11 ↗One Mind has two aspects

“On the basis of the dharma of One Mind there are two gateways.”ᵀ As the sūtra underlying this passage says, “Quiescence is called One Mind. One Mind is called the tathāgatagarbha.”

dharma of One Mind · 一心法 yī xīn fǎ · BDK p. 11 principle of One Mind
two gateways · 二種門 èr zhǒng mén · BDK p. 11 two aspects

  1. The expression “the gateway of mind as suchness” explains the sūtra’s “quiescence is called One Mind.”ᵀ

    gateway of mind as suchness · 心真如門 xīn zhēn rú mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of the absolute

  2. “The gateway of mind as arising and ceasing” explains its “One Mind is called the tathāgatagarbha.”ᵀ

    gateway of mind as arising and ceasing · 心生滅門 xīn shēng miè mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of phenomena
1. Quiescence and the gateway of suchness

↥ What does this mean? All dharmas are unborn and unceasing, originally quiescent, solely One Mind.ᵀ One Mind understood in this way is called the gateway of mind as suchness. Hence the words “quiescence is called One Mind.”

All dharmas · 一切諸法 yī qiè zhū fǎ · BDK p. 12 all things
2. Tathāgatagarbha and the gateway of arising and ceasing

↥ The essence of this One Mind is original awakening.ᵀ Yet in dependence on ignorance it moves, taking the form of arising and ceasing.ᵀ Accordingly, in this gateway the nature of a tathāgata lies concealed and does not manifest. Hence the name tathāgatagarbha. As the sūtra says, “The tathāgatagarbha is the cause of the wholesome and the unwholesome. It can bring forth all destinies of rebirth, like an actor who in turn portrays beings of every destiny.” Such meanings belong to the gateway of arising and ceasing. Thus “One Mind is called the tathāgatagarbha” brings out the gateway of the arising and ceasing of One Mind.ᵀ

original awakening · 本覺 běn jué · BDK p. 17 original enlightenment
arising and ceasing · 生滅 shēng miè · BDK p. 16 birth and death (samsara) Hakeda adds “(samsara)” when translating this passage.
gateway of the arising and ceasing of One Mind · 生滅門 shēng miè mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of phenomena

↥ As the text says below, “As for mind as arising and ceasing, it is on the basis of the tathāgatagarbha that there is a mind that arises and ceases,”ᵀ and so on down to “This consciousness has two meanings, original awakening and nonawakening.”ᵀ We can see, then, that the mind that arises and ceases is only part of what this gateway comprises. It takes in both the very substance of arising and ceasing and its characteristics. All count as characteristics of arising and ceasing, all as meanings included within this gateway. The cause, the conditions, and the characteristics of arising and ceasing constitute this gateway. Such, then, is the meaning of the two gateways.

mind as arising and ceasing · 心生滅 xīn shēng miè · BDK p. 16 The Mind as phenomena (samsara)
arises and ceases · 生滅 shēng miè · BDK p. 16 birth and death (samsara) Hakeda adds “(samsara)” when translating this passage.
two meanings · 二種義 èr zhǒng yì · BDK p. 16 two aspects
nonawakening · 不覺 bù jué · BDK p. 16 nonenlightenment

Why the name “One Mind”?

↥ Why “One Mind”? The natures of defiled and pure dharmas are nondual. The gateways of the true and the delusive cannot be different. Hence “one.” This nonduality is what is real in dharmas. Its substance differs from empty space. It is by nature wondrously aware. Hence “mind.” Yet when there is no two, how could there be a one? When no one can be found, what could one call “mind”? This reality is beyond speech and conceptual thought. At a loss how to designate it, one provisionally calls it “One Mind.”

How each gateway encompasses all dharmas

BDK 11 ↗Each of the two aspects embraces all states of existence

“These two gateways each encompass all dharmas” explains the earlier proposition that this mind encompasses mundane and supramundane dharmas.ᵀ “Because the two gateways are inseparable” explains how each can encompass them all.ᵀ How so?

all dharmas · 一切法 yī qiè fǎ · BDK p. 11 all states of existence
inseparable · 不相離 bù xiāng lí · BDK p. 11 mutually inclusive
1. Suchness as the common characteristic

1. Suchness as the common characteristic

The particles and the earthenware

↥ The gateway of suchness is the common characteristic of dharmas.ᵀ No dharmas exist separately outside this common characteristic, and all are encompassed by it. For example, fine particles are the common characteristic of earthenware. There are no pots apart from this common characteristic. All the pots are encompassed by the particles. So too with the gateway of suchness.⁕

gateway of suchness · 真如門 zhēn rú mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of the absolute
2. The particulars that arise and cease

2. The particulars that arise and cease

The earthenware and its particles

↥ What about the gateway of arising and ceasing? This very suchness is the cause of the wholesome and unwholesome. In conjunction with conditions it in turn becomes the various dharmas. Even as it actually takes these forms, its true nature is never impaired. This gateway therefore encompasses suchness too. Fine particles come together to form earthenware, continually retaining their nature and characteristics as particles. Thus the gateway of earthenware itself encompasses the particles. So too with arising and ceasing.

Why the two gateways are inseparable

↥ Suppose that, though the gateways had no separate substance, their characteristics conflicted and they could not interpenetrate. Then the gateway of suchness would encompass reality in principle without encompassing particular phenomena, and the gateway of arising and ceasing would encompass particular phenomena without encompassing their principle.⁕ In fact the gateways interpenetrate, with no boundary dividing them. Hence each encompasses all dharmas, principle and particulars alike. This is why the treatise says the two gateways are inseparable.

What each gateway discloses

↥ Question. If each gateway encompasses both principle and phenomena, why does the gateway of suchness disclose only the essence of the Mahāyāna, whereas the gateway of arising and ceasing discloses essence, attributes, and activity alike?

↥ Answer. To encompass differs from to disclose. How so?

The gateway of suchness

↥ The gateway of suchness effaces the characteristics to disclose reality as such. To efface the characteristics leaves them uneliminated, so the gateway encompasses them. To efface them leaves none standing as characteristics, so the gateway does not disclose them.

The gateway of arising and ceasing

↥ The gateway of arising and ceasing takes up reality as such to constitute particular phenomena. Taking it up leaves it intact, so the gateway encompasses it. Taking it up leaves it uneffaced, so this gateway also discloses the essence.

What each gateway discloses

↥ It is on these grounds that we provisionally distinguish the two. Speaking comprehensively, their two capacities are alike. Thus the gateway of suchness, too, must disclose the characteristics of particular phenomena. The treatise passes this over for brevity.

Principle and particular dharmas in the two gateways
BDK 11 ↗The two aspects are mutually inclusive

Question. We have seen how the two gateways differ. Do the principle and the particulars they encompass also differ according to the gateway?

↥ Answer. When distinguished according to gateway, they too differ. How so?

Particular dharmas
The imagined nature

↥ The particular dharmas encompassed by the gateway of suchness belong to the imagined nature. For dharmas are said to be unborn, unceasing, and originally quiescent.ᵀ Their distinctions depend solely on delusive thought.ᵀ

unborn, unceasing · 不生不滅 bù shēng bù miè · BDK p. 12 unborn and is imperishable
delusive thought · 妄念 wàng niàn · BDK p. 12 illusions
The dependent nature

↥ The particular dharmas discussed in the gateway of the arising and ceasing of mind belong to the dependent nature. For dharmas are said to arise and cease through the conjunction of causes and conditions.

How the two natures are undivided

↥ Although these two natures are not identical, neither are they different. Why? The distinctions among the arising and ceasing dharmas born of causes and conditions cannot be separated from delusive thought. Thus the imagined nature is undivided from the dependent nature and is also present in the gateway of arising and ceasing. Conversely, in conditioned arising, arising from self, from another, or from both is in every case unfindable. Thus the dependent nature is undivided from the imagined and is also present in the gateway of suchness.

How the two natures remain distinct

↥ Although these two natures are undivided, neither are they identical. Why? Dharmas of the imagined nature have never existed, nor can their absence be denied. Dharmas of the dependent nature, though lacking existence of their own, cannot be said to be absent either. The two natures therefore remain distinct.⁕ As the Compendium of the Mahāyāna says, “In their relation to one another, the three natures are undivided and yet not undivided. This is how to speak of them. If one grasps how the three natures are neither identical nor different, there is no dispute among the hundred schools one cannot reconcile.”

Principle

↥ How does the principle encompassed by the two gateways differ?

Suchness and the limit of reality

↥ In the gateway of suchness one calls it “suchness,” although it cannot be apprehended and is not nonexistent either. Whether buddhas appear or do not appear, its nature and characteristic abide, unaltered and indestructible. Within this gateway one provisionally establishes such designations as “suchness” and “the limit of reality,” as in the Larger Sūtra and other Perfection of Wisdom sūtras.

Buddha-nature and original awakening

↥ As for the principle encompassed by the gateway of arising and ceasing, although in its essence it is free of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, it does not hold fast to a nature of permanence. Conditioned by ignorance, it circulates in saṃsāra. Though it actually undergoes defilement, it is intrinsically pure.ᵀ Within this gateway one provisionally establishes such designations as “buddha-nature” and “original awakening,” as in the Nirvāṇa and Flower Garland sūtras.

intrinsically pure · 自性清淨 zì xìng qīng jìng · BDK p. 29 pure in its self-nature
Why the principle is undivided

↥ The Laṅkāvatāra and other sūtras expounded in the present treatise take both gateways together as their central purport.ᵀ These two meanings too are undivided. Although reality is free of arising and ceasing and abides permanently, even that nature cannot be grasped. Though it follows conditions, it is always unmoving, being free of a nature of arising and ceasing. For this reason, within the gateway of suchness one says simply that the true characteristic is taught without destroying provisional names,ᵀ and that the various dharmas are established without disturbing the limit of reality. In the gateway of arising and ceasing, one goes on to say that mind, intrinsically pure,ᵀ is stirred by the wind of ignorance. Undefiled, it undergoes defilement. Defiled, it remains undefiled.

both gateways · 二門 èr mén · BDK p. 11 two aspects
provisional names · 假名 jiǎ míng · Skt. prajñapti · BDK p. 13 provisional
mind, intrinsically pure · 自性清淨心 zì xìng qīng jìng xīn · BDK p. 21 Mind, pure in its own nature
Emptiness and nonemptiness
Can the two be assigned to different gateways?
BDK 11 ↗The two aspects and their respective meanings

Question. In the gateway of suchness, is emptiness alone taught,ᵀ and in the gateway of arising and ceasing, nonemptiness? Is that not how it is?ᵀ

emptiness · 空 kōng · Skt. śūnya (empty), śūnyatā (emptiness) · BDK p. 15 empty Here Wŏnhyo uses the noun “emptiness” for the aspect of suchness that Hakeda calls “empty.”
nonemptiness · 不空 bù kōng · Skt. aśūnya (nonempty) · BDK p. 15 nonempty

↥ Answer. As a first approximation, there is some truth to this pairing. That is why the preceding Outline says solely that suchness can disclose the essence of the Mahāyāna, while the gateway of arising and ceasing also discloses its attributes and activity. Strictly speaking, however, this division does not hold. In the text below nonemptiness is taught in both gateways.⁕

How can emptiness take the form of what exists?
BDK 11 ↗How each gateway encompasses all dharmas

Question. If the gateway of arising and ceasing includes both meanings, I can see how mind, insofar as it is nonempty, can arise and cease in response to conditions. But emptiness means that nothing is there. How, then, can it respond to conditions and take the form of what exists?

↥ Answer. The two meanings are one. We cannot speak of them as different. Even considered in its emptiness, mind can take the form of what exists. Why? If emptiness were fixed as emptiness, it could not take such a form. But this emptiness is itself empty, so it can.⁕

Two meanings of emptiness of emptiness

↥ This “emptiness of emptiness” in turn has two meanings.

1. In the gateway of suchness

↥ Existing things are empty by nature, and this emptiness too is empty. Neither what exists nor its emptiness can be grasped. This is the emptiness of emptiness in the gateway of suchness. As the Larger Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra says, “All dharmas are empty. This emptiness too is empty. This is called the emptiness of emptiness.”

2. In the gateway of arising and ceasing

↥ What exists has no fixed nature that makes it existent, so it can be empty. This is called “emptiness.” In the same way, this emptiness has no fixed nature that makes it empty, so it can take the form of what exists. This is called the “emptiness of emptiness.” This is the emptiness of emptiness in the gateway of arising and ceasing. As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says, “It exists and it does not exist. This is called the emptiness of emptiness. It is so and it is not so. This is called the emptiness of emptiness. Even bodhisattvas at the tenth ground grasp only a hair’s breadth of this emptiness of emptiness. How much less could anyone else grasp?”⁕

1. The two gateways together

↥ This is how to understand the difference between the two gateways. This completes the explanation of the earlier general statement of the dharma.

BDK pp. 12–13

Suchness beyond words

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 12 The Mind in terms of the absolute is the one world of reality (dharma dhātu) and the essence of all phases of existence in their totality.

That which is called “the essential nature of the Mind” is unborn and is imperishable. It is only through illusions that all things come to be differentiated. If one is freed from illusions, then to him there will be no appearances (lakṣana) of objects [regarded as absolutely independent existences]; therefore all things from the beginning transcend all forms of verbalization, description,⁕ p. 13 and conceptualization⁕ and are, in the final analysis, undifferentiated, free from alteration, and indestructible. They are only of the One Mind; hence the name suchness.

All explanations by words are provisional and without validity, for they are merely used in accordance with illusions and are incapable [of denoting suchness]. The term suchness likewise has no attributes [which can be verbally specified]. The term suchness is, so to speak, the limit of verbalization wherein a word is used to put an end to words. But the essence of suchness itself cannot be put an end to, for all things [in their absolute aspect] are real;⁕ nor is there anything which needs to be pointed out as real, for all things are equally in the state of suchness. It should be understood that all things are incapable of being verbally explained or thought of; hence, the name suchness.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. The two gateways explained separately

BDK 12 ↗The Mind in Terms of the Absolute

“Mind as suchness” begins the explanation of the earlier particular statements. There are two sections, one for each gateway.ᵀ

Mind as suchness · 心真如 xīn zhēn rú · BDK p. 12 Mind in terms of the absolute

Digression on whether reality transcends language
Question
BDK 12 ↗Transcends all forms of verbalization

Question. Does reality truly transcend language, or does it not? If it does not transcend language, fundamental wisdom, which is free from language, accords with reality. If reality truly transcends language, subsequently acquired wisdom, which involves language, misrepresents reality. Again, if reality does not transcend language, the treatise’s earlier passage is idle talk. If reality truly transcends language, its later passage is set forth in vain, as though one described empty space as gold or silver.⁕

Reply

↥ Answer. For precisely this reason we should understand that neither “transcends language” nor “does not transcend language” holds of reality. For that very reason both hold of it. In this way each of the foregoing objections has been examined.⁕

1. The gateway of suchness

↥ Let us set aside this digression and return to the base text.

2.1.1. Suchness itself
BDK 12 ↗The one world of reality … and the essence of all phases of existence

  1. A brief statement. ↓

2.1.1.1. Brief statement — the one dharmadhātu

↥ In the brief statement, “it is precisely the one dharmadhātu” identifies the reality on which the gateway of suchness rests,ᵀ for the One Mind is itself the one dharmadhātu. The one dharmadhātu encompasses both gateways.ᵀ Here the gateway of particular characteristics is set aside, and only the Dharma gateway of the common characteristic is taken up.

both gateways · 二門 èr mén · BDK p. 11 two aspects
BDK 12 ↗All phases of existence in their totality

There are four grades of common characteristic. The treatise is speaking of the suchness disclosed by the three kinds of absence of intrinsic nature. Hence “the great common characteristic.”⁕ᵀ It is called a “dharma” because it serves as a norm giving rise to true understanding. It is called a “gateway” because it gives entry into nirvāṇa. Just as the one dharmadhātu in its entirety constitutes the gateway of arising and ceasing, so in its entirety it constitutes the gateway of suchness. The word “essence” brings this out.

↥ In the first statement, “therefore all dharmas” means dharmas of dependent nature, which arise from conditions.

1.3.2. Equal in suchness — birds’ tracks and conditioned appearances
BDK 13 ↗In the final analysis, undifferentiated … hence the name suchness

Consider the different tracks birds make in the sky. The appearance of space varies with the birds’ shapes. What appears really does differ, yet there are no distinct visible features of a track in space itself. Understand dependently arisen dharmas in the same way. They appear differently according to the conditioning of past impressions,ᵀ yet have no distinct natures that words could define. Free of the distinctions that words could express or thought apprehend, they are in this very respect equal in suchness. Hence the words “ultimately equal,” and so on down to “therefore it is called suchness.”ᵀ This is the second statement, which reveals the equality of suchness.

The passage beginning “because all” gives the reason. Suchness is equal and beyond language because verbal expressions are merely provisional designations.ᵀ In the presence of actual nature, words must fall away. Verbal expressions also “merely follow delusive thought.” Direct wisdom must therefore be free of them. This is why the treatise says that suchness is beyond words and thought, continuing down to “because it cannot be apprehended.”

BDK p. 14

According with suchness and entering it

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 14 Question: If such is the meaning [of the principle of the Mahayana], how is it possible for people to conform themselves to and enter into it?

Answer: If they understand that, concerning all things, though they are spoken of, there is neither that which speaks, nor that which can be spoken of, and though they are thought of, there is neither that which thinks, nor that which can be thought of, then they are said to have conformed to it. And when they are freed from their thoughts, they are said to have entered into it.

Next, suchness has two aspects if predicated in words. One is that it is truly empty (śūnya), for [this aspect] can, in the final sense, reveal what is real. The other is that it is truly nonempty (aśūnya), for its essence itself is endowed with undefiled and excellent qualities.

This avoids clinging to the view of existence. To understand in this way is to accord with contemplation of the middle way. Hence “accord with.”

“Distinguished in accordance with verbal expression, it has two meanings,”ᵀ namely, “truly empty” and “truly nonempty.” Yet the latter passage also says, “No conceptual discrimination corresponds to it.” We should understand that no verbal expression corresponds to it either. Distinguished in accordance with verbal expression · 依言說分別 yī yán shuō fēn bié · BDK p. 14 if predicated in words
How the two passages presuppose one another

↥ Again, the first passage must rely on the words “employ words to dispense with words” to bring out how reality transcends language. This in turn shows how reality is inseparable from verbal expression.

Does reality transcend language?
The objection

↥ Question. Does reality truly transcend language? If it does not transcend language, neither does it transcend conceptual thought.

  1. Suppose you say one can state that reality truly transcends language. You incur the fault of contradicting your own thesis, for you exempt the statement about transcending language while maintaining that reality truly transcends language.

  2. Suppose instead that even the statement about transcending language is itself ruled out. You incur the fault of contradicting your own utterance, for you rule out that very statement and then say it can be made.

  3. Furthermore, if reality does not transcend language, fundamental wisdom, being free of language, would go beyond reality. If reality truly transcends language, subsequently acquired wisdom, which involves language, would misconstrue reality.

  4. Again, if reality does not transcend language, the earlier passage of the treatise would be false speech. If reality truly transcends language, the latter passage would be put forward to no purpose, as though one described empty space as blue or yellow.

The reply

↥ Answer. Some give this reply. We should understand, then, that reality neither transcends language nor fails to transcend it. For this very reason it both transcends language and does not transcend it. Such statements apply everywhere and therefore have no single, fixed application. Because they have no fixed application, there is nowhere they do not apply. We have spoken in this way of transcending and not transcending language in the gateway of suchness. The same account holds in the gateway of arising and ceasing.⁕

BDK pp. 14–15

Suchness as empty

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 14 [Suchness is empty] because from the beginning it has never been related to any defiled states of existence, it is free from all marks of individual distinction of things, and it has nothing to do with thoughts conceived by a deluded mind.

It should be understood that the essential nature of suchness is neither with marks nor without marks;⁕ neither not with marks nor not without marks; nor is it both with and without marks simultaneously; it is neither with a single mark nor with different marks; neither not with a single mark nor not with different marks; nor is it both with a single [mark] and with different marks simultaneously.

p. 15 In short, since all unenlightened people discriminate with their deluded minds from moment to moment, they are alienated [from suchness]; hence, the definition “empty”; but once they are free from their deluded minds, they will find that there is nothing to be negated.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2.1.2.3.1.2. Detailed account — the four alternatives
BDK 14 ↗Neither with marks nor without marks

The detailed explanation shows that suchness transcends the four alternatives of predication. There are many sets of four. Two are fundamental, those concerning existence and nonexistence, and those concerning identity and difference. These two sets encompass delusive attachments. Suchness is shown to be truly empty by setting it against them.

The argument of the Expanded Treatise in a Hundred Verses

↥ As the Expanded Treatise in a Hundred Verses says, “Furthermore, this shows that the dharmas grasped by worldly people are all unreal, and shows how the positions held by non-Buddhist schools differ.” The verse accordingly reads,

  • “Existence, nonexistence, both, neither.

  • Identity, nonidentity, both, neither.

  • Match the terms in their respective order.

  • The wise discern that these positions are unreal.”

↥ The explanation follows. Regarding all the categories recognized in the world, such as visible form, which speech designates and the intellect knows, the positions people cling to come under four heads.

  1. Existence. ↓

  2. Nonexistence. ↓

  3. Affirming both. ↓

  4. Denying both. ↓

↥ Match these in order with four mistaken positions, as appropriate.

  1. Identity. ↓

  2. Nonidentity. ↓

  3. Affirming both. ↓

  4. Denying both. ↓

1. Existence and identity

↥ The Sāṃkhyas hold that universals such as existence are identical with the particular dharmas. This corresponds to the alternative of existence. Why is this position untenable?

  • If blue and the other colors were identical with color as such, their natures would all be the same, like color as such.

  • If the sounds of the five kinds of music were identical with sound as such, their natures would all be the same, like sound as such.

  • If the eye and the other faculties were identical with faculty as such, their natures would all be the same, like faculty as such. Any one faculty should apprehend every object, and any one object should be accessible to every faculty.

  • Again, if all dharmas were identical with existence as such, their natures would all be the same, like existence as such.

2. Nonexistence and difference

↥ The Vaiśeṣikas say that universals such as existence are distinct from the particular dharmas. This corresponds to the alternative of nonexistence. Why is this position also untenable? If blue and the other colors were distinct from color as such, they should be beyond the range of the eye, like sounds. The same reasoning applies to sounds and the rest. Again, if all dharmas were distinct from existence as such, they should be intrinsically nonexistent, like a hare’s horns. The text goes on to refute the position at length.

3. Affirming both

↥ The naked ascetics hold that universals such as existence are both identical with the particular dharmas and distinct from them. This corresponds to “both existent and nonexistent.” Why is this position also untenable? If universals such as existence are identical with the particulars, such as form, the Sāṃkhya objection applies. If they are distinct, the Vaiśeṣika objection applies. Identity and difference have contrary characteristics. It is untenable to say that they are one in essence. What is identical would have to be nonidentical, since it is difference itself and so would be like difference. What is different would have to be nondifferent, since it is identity itself and so would be like identity. The refutation continues at length.

4. Denying both

↥ The ascetics described here as practicing “wrong livelihood” hold that universals such as existence are neither identical with the particular dharmas nor distinct from them. This corresponds to “neither existent nor nonexistent.” Why is this position also untenable? When you say “neither identical nor different,” are both expressions merely denials, or does either imply an affirmation? If either implies an affirmation, you cannot deny both. If both are merely denials, you have no position to maintain. If you both deny and affirm, your reasoning contradicts itself. If you neither deny nor affirm, your words are idle conceptual proliferation. The refutation continues at length.

The argument of the Expanded Treatise in a Hundred Verses

↥ Thus four distortions arise in the world. Existence, nonexistence, affirming both, and denying both are, respectively, superimposition, denial, contradiction, and conceptual proliferation. What the world clings to is therefore unreal.

Applying the four denials to suchness

↥ In the present passage, the words are to be understood as follows.

  • “It has no characteristic of existence” disallows the first alternative.ᵀ

    no characteristic of existence · 非有相 fēi yǒu xiàng · BDK p. 14 neither with marks

  • “It has no characteristic of nonexistence” disallows the second.ᵀ

    no characteristic of nonexistence · 非無相 fēi wú xiàng · BDK p. 14 nor without marks

  • “It cannot be characterized either as not existent or as not nonexistent” disallows the fourth alternative, the denial of both.ᵀ

    cannot be characterized either as not existent or as not nonexistent · 非非有相、非非無相 fēi fēi yǒu xiàng, fēi fēi wú xiàng · BDK p. 14 neither not with marks nor not without marks

  • “It has no characteristic of being both existent and nonexistent” disallows the third, the affirmation of both. The order of the last two alternatives depends on the author’s intention. Each ordering has a rationale, and the two are compatible. The four alternatives concerning identity and difference can be understood by the same explanation.

  2. Distinguish its characteristics. ↓

  3. Give it a name. ↓

1.1.1. Its basis — the tathāgatagarbha

↥ In the first clause, “on the basis of the tathāgatagarbha there is a mind that arises and ceases” means that the mind, pure by its very nature, is called tathāgatagarbha.ᵀ Stirred by the wind of ignorance, it moves, arising and ceasing. Hence arising and ceasing are said to depend on the tathāgatagarbha. In the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, “The tathāgatagarbha, perfumed by beginningless unwholesome habits, is called storehouse consciousness.” The same text says, “What is momentary is called storehouse consciousness.”

mind, pure by its very nature · 自性清淨心 zì xìng qīng jìng xīn · BDK p. 21 Mind, pure in its own nature
1.1.2. Its characteristics
BDK 16 ↗What is called “the Storehouse Consciousness

The second clause, beginning “that is to say,” distinguishes the characteristics.

  • BDK 16 ↗Neither birth nor death

    “Neither arising nor ceasing” refers to the tathāgatagarbha just mentioned.ᵀ

    Neither arising nor ceasing · 不生不滅 bù shēng bù miè · BDK p. 16 neither birth nor death (nirvana)
How what neither arises nor ceases is conjoined with arising and ceasing

↥ The mind that neither arises nor ceases moves, taking the form of arising and ceasing. Because the two are inseparable, the text speaks of its being “conjoined with” arising and ceasing.ᵀ As the treatise says below, “The water of the great ocean is stirred into waves by the wind. The characteristics of water and wind are inseparable,” and so on. The water’s movement is the characteristic of wind. The wetness of what moves is the characteristic of water. The water moves in its entirety, so this water is inseparable from the characteristic of wind. Nothing that moves here is without wetness, so the movement is inseparable from the characteristic of water. So it is with mind. The mind that neither arises nor ceases moves in its entirety, and is thereby inseparable from the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Every such characteristic partakes of mind’s wondrous awareness. Arising and ceasing are thereby inseparable from mind’s own characteristic. This inseparability is the sense of “conjoined with.” The text speaks of the mind that neither arises nor ceases as conjoined with arising and ceasing. To reverse the subject and speak of arising and ceasing as conjoined with that mind would miss its point.

conjoined with · 和合 hé hé · BDK p. 16 diffuses harmoniously with
Why the two are neither identical nor different
BDK 16 ↗Neither identical nor different

“Neither identical nor different.” The mind that neither arises nor ceases moves in its entirety, so there is no difference between mind and its arising and ceasing. Yet throughout, the nature of mind remains free of arising and ceasing. In this respect arising and ceasing cannot be identical with mind. Suppose they were identical. When the characteristics of the consciousness that arises and ceases were fully extinguished, mind’s awareness itself would have to perish with them. That is the extreme of annihilation. Suppose they were different. When the wind of ignorance perfumes and stirs the mind, the quiescent mind itself would be unable to respond to conditions. That is the extreme of eternalism. In keeping clear of both extremes, the text says “neither identical nor different.”

↥ As the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “A lump of clay and its minute particles are neither different nor without difference. The same holds of gold and the ornaments made from it. If the lump were different from its particles, it would not be made from them. It is made from them. In this respect they are undivided. If they were in every respect the same, no distinction could be made between a lump and its particles. Likewise, if evolving consciousness and the true characteristic of storehouse consciousness were different, storehouse consciousness could not be its cause.ᵀ If they were in every respect the same, storehouse consciousness would have to cease when evolving consciousness ceased. Yet its own true characteristic does indeed endure. Hence when the karmic characteristic ceases, consciousness in its own true characteristic survives.”ᵀ The author of this treatise is explaining that very passage when he says “neither identical nor different.”

karmic characteristic · 業相 yè xiàng · BDK p. 24 無明業相 activity of ignorance
Activating consciousness, evolving consciousness, and the true characteristic
BDK 16 ↗Storehouse consciousness

“Activating consciousness” takes its name from the words “through the force of ignorance the unawakened mind moves.”ᵀ “Evolving consciousness” takes its name from “on the basis of this movement, mind evolves into a perceiving subject.” Both occur at the level of storehouse consciousness. The ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “The tathāgatagarbha is precisely the ālayavijñāna.ᵀ When it arises together with the seven consciousnesses, this is called the characteristic of evolving and ceasing.” We know from this that the characteristic of evolving is present in the ālayavijñāna.ᵀ

↥ As for “its own true characteristic,” the ten-fascicle text calls the true characteristic its intrinsic characteristic. The mind of original awakening has no need of delusive conditions. Its nature is of itself wondrously aware. This is called “its own true characteristic.” This is said from the standpoint of nonidentity. Again, when the mind follows the wind of ignorance and takes the form of arising and ceasing, its aware nature is the same as it was originally. So here too we can speak of “its own true characteristic.” This is said from the standpoint of nondifference. The matter is treated more fully in the Separate Notes.

1.1.3. Its name — ālayavijñāna

↥ The third clause gives the name ālayavijñāna. What neither arises nor ceases is conjoined with arising and ceasing. Being neither identical nor different, the two are collectively called ālayavijñāna. The translation of the name and its meaning are explained in my Doctrinal Essentials of the Laṅkāvatāra.

1. General account of the underlying reality

↥ This completes the general account of the underlying reality.

1.2. Distinguishing the meanings
BDK 16 ↗This consciousness has two aspects

The second division, which distinguishes the meanings, has three parts.

  1. Introduce the meanings together and briefly state what this consciousness can do. ↓

  2. Explain each meaning and set forth the underlying reality and its characteristics in detail. ↓

  3. Explain sameness and difference. ↓

1.2.1. General statement of what this consciousness can do
BDK 16 ↗It embraces all states of existence and creates all states of existence

The first part says that “this consciousness has two meanings, through which it encompasses all dharmas and brings forth all dharmas.” Its capacity to encompass has been explained above. The earlier passage said that each of the two gateways encompasses everything. Here one consciousness contains two meanings, and it is this one consciousness that encompasses everything. There is no claim that each meaning encompasses everything. These meanings are distinguished only within the gateway of arising and ceasing, so that neither alone can encompass all dharmas. Again, of the two gateways the earlier text spoke only of encompassing. There is no question of bringing forth dharmas from the standpoint of the gateway of suchness. Of this consciousness the text also speaks of bringing forth dharmas, since that function belongs to the gateway of arising and ceasing. How so?

  • Nonawakening perfumes original awakening, giving rise to defiled dharmas.ᵀ

    defiled dharmas · 染法 rǎn fǎ · BDK p. 14 defiled states of existence

  • Original awakening perfumes nonawakening, giving rise to pure dharmas. Together, on the basis of these two meanings, all dharmas can arise. Hence the statement that consciousness “has two meanings” and “brings forth all dharmas.” This passage introduces the later discussion beginning “there are four kinds of perfuming.” Notice the wider scope of One Mind. It comprehends both gateways. The scope of this consciousness is narrower. It falls within the gateway of arising and ceasing. Both its meanings fall within this one gateway, so the gateway is broader than either meaning. For the explanation with scriptural citations, see the Separate Notes.

BDK 16 ↗They are the aspect of enlightenment and the aspect of nonenlightenment

2. The gateway of arising and ceasing

2.1. The detailed exposition

↥ The first part has three subdivisions.

  1. The exposition of the Outline’s “the arising and ceasing of this mind.”ᵀ ↓

    arising and ceasing of this mind · 心生滅 xīn shēng miè · BDK p. 16 The Mind as phenomena (samsara)

  2. From “Furthermore, the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing,” the exposition of those causes and conditions.ᵀ ↓

    causes and conditions of arising and ceasing · 生滅因緣 shēng miè yīn yuán · BDK p. 26 That a person is in samsara results from the fact that Hakeda recasts the Chinese topic as the opening of a sentence. 生滅 means ‘arising and ceasing’, and 因緣 supplies ‘causes and conditions’.

2.1. The arising and ceasing of mind

↥ The first of these in turn has two parts.

  1. A general explanation in terms of essence. ↓

  2. A separate explanation in terms of the meanings distinguished. We begin with the first. ↓

2.1.1. Mind in its essence
On the basis of the tathāgatagarbha

↥ “On the basis of the tathāgatagarbha there is a mind that arises and ceases.” This means that the mind free of arising and ceasing is stirred by the wind of ignorance and takes the form of arising and ceasing. Hence one says that the mind that arises and ceases depends on the mind free of arising and ceasing. Yet the mind that neither arises nor ceases and the mind that arises and ceases are nondual in essence. We distinguish them conceptually by these two meanings so that we can speak of one as depending on the other.

The example of still and moving water

↥ Take still water. When the wind blows on it, it becomes moving water. Movement and stillness differ, but the water itself is one. Nonetheless we can say, “It is on the basis of still water that there is moving water.” The same reasoning applies here. As the treatise says below, “Mind, intrinsically pure, is stirred by the wind of ignorance.” The four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “The tathāgatagarbha, perfumed by beginningless unwholesome habits, is called storehouse consciousness.” It also says, “What is momentary is called storehouse consciousness.” Thus “there is a mind that arises and ceases” refers precisely to storehouse consciousness.

What belongs to this gateway

↥ Here both the tathāgatagarbha as the basis and the mind that arises and ceases in dependence on it are taken together as the gateway of the arising and ceasing of mind. Thus under this gateway the treatise says, “On the basis of the tathāgatagarbha there is a mind that arises and ceases.” It does not mention the tathāgatagarbha only to make the arising and ceasing mind alone the gateway. The later statement “this consciousness has two meanings” shows that both meanings belong to this gateway.

What “conjoined” means
BDK 16 ↗The two are neither identical nor different

“What neither arises nor ceases is conjoined with arising and ceasing. Neither identical nor different, it is called ālayavijñāna.”ᵀ “What neither arises nor ceases” is the tathāgatagarbha just mentioned. “Arising and ceasing” is the arising and ceasing of that very mind that neither arises nor ceases.

What neither arises nor ceases · 不生不滅 bù shēng bù miè · BDK p. 16 neither birth nor death (nirvana)
conjoined with · 和合 hé hé · BDK p. 16 diffuses harmoniously with
ālayavijñāna · 阿梨耶識 ā lí yé shí · Skt. ālayavijñāna · BDK p. 16 storehouse consciousness

  1. In “conjoined with,” the word “with” expresses the mind free of arising and ceasing moving and taking the form of arising and ceasing.

  2. The mind that arises and ceases and the arising and ceasing of mind are inseparable. Hence “conjoined.”

The wind and the water

↥ As the treatise says below, “The waters of the great ocean are set in motion by the wind. The characteristics of the water and of the wind are inseparable.” The movement of the water is the wind’s characteristic. The wetness of what moves is the water’s. These two characteristics have no two separate substances and are therefore inseparable. So too with mind. The arising and ceasing of mind takes shape in dependence on ignorance. The mind that arises and ceases takes shape from original awakening. Having no two separate substances, the two are inseparable. Hence “conjoined.” Precisely speaking, what neither arises nor ceases is conjoined with arising and ceasing. The statement cannot simply be reversed.

Neither identical nor different

↥ What is meant by “neither identical nor different”?

  1. Because mind and the process of arising and ceasing are not identical, mind never loses its nature free of arising and ceasing.

  2. Because mind and the process of arising and ceasing are not different, mind in its entirety takes the form of arising and ceasing. If they were identical, mind would lose its freedom from arising and ceasing when it takes the form of arising and ceasing. If they were different, what neither arises nor ceases would never take the form of arising and ceasing. Hence “neither identical nor different.”

One mind with two meanings

↥ Although there are two meanings, mind in essence is nondual. The nondual mind that unites these two meanings is called ālayavijñāna.

Clay and its particles

↥ As the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “A lump of clay and its particles are neither different nor undifferentiated. The same holds for gold and ornaments. If the lump were different from the particles, it could not be made of them. It is in fact made of them, so they are not different. If they were undifferentiated, there should be no distinction between lump and particles. Likewise, were the functioning consciousness different from the true characteristic of storehouse consciousness, storehouse consciousness would be undifferentiated.ᵀ Were they undifferentiated, storehouse consciousness too would cease when the functioning consciousness ceases. Yet its own true characteristic never ceases. Thus true consciousness does not cease. Only the characteristic of karmic activity ceases.”⁕ᵀ The author of this treatise is explaining precisely this scripture when he says “neither identical nor different.”

functioning consciousness · 轉識 zhuǎn shí · Skt. pravṛttivijñāna · BDK p. 27 evolving mind Here the stirred mind takes on the role of perceiver. Wŏnhyo also discusses broader uses of 轉識.
characteristic of karmic activity · 業相 yè xiàng · BDK p. 24 無明業相 activity of ignorance
Functioning consciousness and its own true characteristic

↥ Here “functioning consciousness” designates the perceiving characteristic that arises and ceases within ālayavijñāna. Within it, the underlying substance is called storehouse consciousness. As the ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “The tathāgatagarbha, ālayavijñāna, arises together with the seven consciousnesses. This is called the characteristic of functioning.”ᵀ We know from this that the characteristic of functioning is also present within ālayavijñāna.

characteristic of functioning · 轉相 zhuǎn xiàng · BDK p. 24 能見相 perceiving subject

↥ As for “its own true characteristic,” the ten-fascicle text calls the true its “own characteristic.” The mind of original awakening needs no delusive condition. It is by nature wondrously aware. Hence the name “its own true characteristic.” This speaks from the standpoint of nonidentity. Yet when it follows the wind of ignorance and takes the form of arising and ceasing, the nature of its wondrous awareness remains as it was. For this reason too one can call it “its own true characteristic.” This speaks from the standpoint of nondifference. Thus the designation “its own true [characteristic]” applies beyond what is free of arising and ceasing.

The two scriptural accounts of consciousness
BDK 16 ↗The storehouse consciousness has two aspects

Question. The Yogācārabhūmi and other works say that ālayavijñāna is resultant consciousness, wholly subject to arising and ceasing. Why, then, does this treatise say that it includes both meanings?

↥ Answer. Each is expounding something different. The accounts are compatible. How so? Broadly, this subtle mind has two meanings.

  1. Insofar as it ripens from karma and afflictions, something previously absent comes into being. In this respect it is wholly subject to arising and ceasing.ᵀ

    afflictions · 煩惱 fán nǎo · Skt. kleśa · BDK p. 29 defilement

  2. Insofar as it is stirred by root ignorance, perfuming sets what is still in motion. Movement and stillness have a single substance.

Resultant consciousness in the Yogācārabhūmi

↥ The treatises just mentioned follow the Sūtra Unraveling the Intent. To dispel the view that consciousness is a unity and is permanent, they consider it as the fruit of karma and the afflictions. They therefore say that this consciousness is wholly subject to arising and ceasing, with mind and its mental factors operating distinctly.

Mind stirred by ignorance in the Laṅkāvatāra

↥ The present treatise follows the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra. To counter the grasping of ultimate and conventional reality as separate substances, it considers mind insofar as ignorance sets it in motion. Thus it says that what neither arises nor ceases is conjoined with and undivided from arising and ceasing. The very form that consciousness takes when stirred by ignorance also ripens from the karma and afflictions mentioned above. The intentions of the two accounts differ, but the substance of consciousness is nondual.

Can the essence of mind itself arise and cease?
BDK 16 ↗The two are neither identical nor different

Question. Is the essence of mind permanent while its characteristics arise and cease, the two being inseparable and together constituting a single consciousness? Or is it the essence of mind itself that both abides permanently and arises and ceases?

↥ Answer. Once their purport is understood, both readings are admissible. How so? We call it “essence” with reference to its abiding permanently, without depending on anything else for what it is. We call it “characteristic” with reference to its impermanence, its arising and ceasing in dependence on something else. In this sense we can say that essence is permanent and characteristics impermanent. Yet we do not use “arising and ceasing” to mean the arising of arising or the ceasing of ceasing. What we call “arising and ceasing” is mind’s arising and mind’s ceasing. In that sense we can say that the essence of mind arises and ceases. We call the movement of water a wave. One could never say that such movement is anything other than the water’s movement. The same reasoning applies here. Suppose mind in its essence were motionless and only the characteristic of ignorance moved. There would be no way for an ordinary being to become a noble one, for the characteristic of ignorance is simply extinguished and the essence of mind would never have constituted an ordinary being in the first place.

Three objections

↥ Objection.

  1. If mind in its essence arises and ceases, true mind perishes, since permanence would be absent during arising and ceasing.

  2. If mind in its essence was originally still and then moved in dependence on conditions, saṃsāra must have a beginning. This is a grave fault, since during that original stillness there would have been no saṃsāra.

  3. If mind changes with conditions and takes the form of arising and ceasing, One Mind could similarly change with conditions and become many minds. These three objections are inescapable. Hence the position is untenable.

Replies in reverse order

↥ Reply. The position entails no such difficulty. I shall answer in reverse order.

To the third objection — One Mind and many minds

↥ We say that the permanent mind, taking ignorance as its condition, in turn becomes an impermanent mind, while its permanent nature never changes. Likewise One Mind, taking ignorance as its condition, in turn becomes the minds of many sentient beings, while this One Mind itself remains nondual.ᵀ As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says, “A medicine of a single flavor takes on various flavors according to where it flows, while its true flavor remains on the mountain.” This is precisely what the sūtra means.

sentient beings · 眾生 zhòng shēng · Skt. sattva · BDK p. 14 people Hakeda also uses “ordinary people” on p. 20 and “sentient beings” on p. 25.
To the second objection — beginningless saṃsāra

↥ “Though one speaks of original stillness followed by movement in dependence on conditions, the fault that saṃsāra has a beginning does not follow. For in such a succession, movement and stillness alike are beginningless. We say, for example, that something is a karmic result first and then in turn becomes a cause. The succession continues indefinitely, for cause and result are both beginningless.” The same reasoning applies here.

To the first objection — permanence and arising

↥ Although mind in its essence arises and ceases, in its essence it always abides, because these two are neither identical nor different. The essence of mind is nondual, yet it has no fixed nature of oneness. Movement and stillness are not identical, yet have no fixed nature of difference. Consider water. Viewed in its continuity it flows. Viewed in terms of momentary arising and ceasing it never moves. It is free of both permanence and annihilation. It neither passes across from one moment to the next nor is it cut off. The same reasoning applies here.

1. Mind in its essence

↥ Thus all three objections are resolved. This completes the general exposition of the essence.

2.1.2. The meanings of this consciousness
BDK 16 ↗The storehouse consciousness has two aspects

From “this consciousness has two meanings” the second part gives the particular explanation in terms of meanings. It has three divisions.

  1. The meanings are announced together and their efficacy briefly stated. ↓

  2. From “what are the two?” each meaning is expounded separately, bringing out its essence and characteristics in detail. ↓

  3. From “furthermore, awakening and nonawakening,” the two are considered together to explain the characteristics of sameness and difference. ↓

↥ In the first division: ↓

1. Their power to encompass and produce
Encompassing every dharma
BDK 16 ↗This consciousness embraces and produces all states of existence

“This consciousness has two meanings and can encompass all dharmas and give rise to all.” We have already explained the capacity to encompass. There, each of the two gateways was said to encompass everything. Here, a single consciousness contains two meanings, and hence the one consciousness encompasses everything. The text does not say that each of the two meanings encompasses everything, because both meanings fall within the single gateway of arising and ceasing, and because neither can separately encompass all dharmas.

Giving rise to every dharma

↥ Again, the earlier account of the two gateways spoke only of encompassing, for the gateway of suchness involves no production. Here the account of consciousness also speaks of production, since it is precisely within the gateway of arising and ceasing that production has a place. What does this mean?

  1. Because nonawakening perfumes original awakening, defiled dharmas arise.ᵀ

    defiled dharmas · 染法 rǎn fǎ · BDK p. 14 defiled states of existence

  2. Because original awakening perfumes nonawakening, pure dharmas arise. Only through the conjunction of these two can all dharmas arise without exception.

↥ Thus the statement that consciousness, having two meanings, gives rise to all dharmas anticipates the later passage beginning “there are four kinds of perfuming.”

The two gateways of mind and the two meanings of consciousness
BDK 16 ↗The storehouse consciousness has two aspects

Question. Above, One Mind was said to have two gateways. Here this consciousness is said to have two meanings. How do “mind” there and “consciousness” here differ?

↥ Reply. The earlier passage spoke of reality in its essence, calling it “One Mind.” Its essence admits of two approaches, transcendence of characteristics and responsiveness to conditions. Thus the text says that One Mind has two gateways. As the source sūtra says, “Quiescence is called One Mind. One Mind is called the tathāgatagarbha.” Its meaning was explained above.

↥ Consciousness here is considered only within the gateway in which One Mind follows conditions. Reality as such and particular phenomena are nondual. There is a single wondrous awareness, called “one consciousness.” Since its essence includes both awakening and nonawakening, the text says that this consciousness has two meanings.

  1. Mind is accordingly broader and consciousness narrower in scope, for mind includes the consciousness discussed in its two gateways.⁕

  2. Again, gateway is broader and meaning narrower, for the gateway of arising and ceasing includes both meanings.

The four- and ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra

↥ As the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “Inseparable and unchanging, it is called tathāgatagarbha-consciousness. The seven consciousnesses keep turning without cessation. Why? Because from that cause and its conditions the consciousnesses arise. This lies outside the sphere of the practice of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.” The ten-fascicle version says, “The tathāgatagarbha is not contained within ālayavijñāna. Thus the seven consciousnesses arise and cease, while the tathāgatagarbha neither arises nor ceases.ᵀ Why? The seven consciousnesses arise in dependence on attending to their several objects. The domain of these seven consciousnesses cannot be realized by any śrāvaka or non-Buddhist practitioner.” Both passages explain how this consciousness neither arises nor ceases. How so?

neither arises nor ceases · 不生不滅 bù shēng bù miè · BDK p. 12 unborn and is imperishable
The ocean and its seven waves
The four-fascicle reading

↥ The point is that, as the wind of objects stirs the ocean of storehouse consciousness, the waves of the seven consciousnesses roll on. Thus the seven consciousnesses arise and cease. The tathāgatagarbha is storehouse consciousness itself. Although inseparable from this functioning, it does not itself change. Since the tathāgatagarbha neither arises nor ceases, the sūtra says “inseparable and unchanging, it is called tathāgatagarbha-consciousness,” and so on.

The ten-fascicle reading

↥ The ten-fascicle version treats the seven consciousnesses as the waves, distinct from the ocean as a whole. Their characteristics are found within the ocean of ālayavijñāna, so they arise and cease.⁕ The tathāgatagarbha is the ocean itself, as distinct from its waves. It cannot reside inside the ocean of ālayavijñāna, and so is free of arising and ceasing. Hence “the tathāgatagarbha is not contained within ālayavijñāna, and thus the seven consciousnesses arise and cease,” and so on. Precisely because the tathāgatagarbha is ālayavijñāna itself, it is said not to be “within” it. If the passage meant that the tathāgatagarbha was absent from a wholly arising-and-ceasing ālayavijñāna, it ought to continue, “thus the eight consciousnesses arise and cease.” Why would it say only that the seven consciousnesses arise and cease? We should understand that the original behind the two scriptural passages is one. The translators differ, and hence their expressions differ.

Scriptural testimony to original awakening and nonawakening

↥ Again, the four-fascicle version says, “Ālayavijñāna is called the tathāgatagarbha. It coexists with ignorance and the seven consciousnesses, is free of the fault of impermanence, and is intrinsically pure. The other seven consciousnesses do not abide from one moment to the next. They are dharmas that arise and cease.” All such passages speak of the original awakening of ālayavijñāna as free of arising and ceasing. Again, the four-fascicle version says, “What is momentary is called storehouse consciousness.” The ten-fascicle version says, “The tathāgatagarbha, ālayavijñāna, arises together with the seven consciousnesses. This is called the characteristic of functioning and ceasing.” Such passages disclose the sense in which ālayavijñāna arises and ceases and is characterized by nonawakening. The present author draws together the purport of that sūtra from beginning to end when he says that this consciousness has two meanings.

2. Particular explanation of each meaning
BDK 16 ↗What are the two?

From “what are the two?” begins the second division, the particular explanation according to meaning.

Awakening and nonawakening distinguished
Root and branch nonawakening
BDK 16 ↗The aspects of enlightenment and nonenlightenment

“The meaning of nonawakening” is likewise twofold.

  1. Root nonawakening. ↓

  2. Derivative or “branch” nonawakening. ↓

1. Root nonawakening

↥ As for [root] nonawakening, the fundamental ignorance within ālayavijñāna is called nonawakening. As the treatise says below, “On the basis of ālayavijñāna one speaks of nonawakening arising.”⁕

2. Branch nonawakening

↥ As for branch nonawakening, every defiled dharma produced by ignorance is called nonawakening. For the treatise says below, “All defiled dharmas are characteristics of nonawakening.”ᵀ

characteristics of nonawakening · 不覺相 bù jué xiàng · BDK p. 25 aspects of nonenlightenment
Which meanings belong to ālayavijñāna?

↥ If we distinguish the characteristics of the consciousnesses and separate the root from its branches, only original awakening and root nonawakening are in ālayavijñāna. If we consider the nondual essence of consciousness and gather the branches back into the root, then inceptive awakening and branch nonawakening too belong to ālayavijñāna.ᵀ Thus the earlier statement that this consciousness has two meanings embraces both approaches. Accordingly the explanation below includes original and inceptive awakening as well as both kinds of nonawakening.

inceptive awakening · 始覺 shǐ jué · BDK p. 18 the process of actualization of enlightenment
BDK p. 17

Original awakening

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 17 The essence of Mind is free from thoughts. The characteristic of that which is free from thoughts is analogous to that of the sphere of empty space that pervades everywhere. The one [without any second, i.e., the absolute] aspect of the world of reality (dharmadhātu) is none other than the undifferentiated dharmakāya, the “essence body” of the Tathāgata. [Since the essence of Mind is] grounded on the dharmakāya, it is to be called the original enlightenment. Why? Because “original enlightenment” indicates [the essence of Mind (a priori)] in contradistinction to [the essence of Mind in) the process of actualization of enlightenment; the process of actualization of enlightenment is none other than [the process of integrating] the identity with the original enlightenment.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

Original awakening
BDK 17 ↗Original enlightenment

“Original awakening” means that the nature of this mind is free of the characteristic of nonawakening.ᵀ Its nature is illuminating awareness. This is called original awakening. As the treatise says below, “Its very essence has the meaning of the light of great wisdom.”

nature of this mind · 心性 xīn xìng · Skt. citta-prakṛti · BDK p. 12 essential nature of the Mind
Does original awakening cut off delusion?
BDK 17 ↗The essence of Mind is free from thoughts

Question. Is the essence of mind called “original awakening” simply because nonawakening is absent, or because mind itself has the illuminating activity of awakened awareness? If mere absence of nonawakening is enough to call it original awakening, one might equally call it nonawakening for its lack of illuminating awareness. If it is called original awakening because it has illuminating awareness, does that awakening cut off delusion? If it does not cut off delusion, it has no illuminating activity. If it cuts off delusion, there are no ordinary beings.ᵀ

ordinary beings · 凡夫 fán fū · Skt. pṛthagjana · BDK p. 29 ordinary people

↥ Answer. There is both freedom from darkness and the presence of illumination. Where there is illumination there is also the cutting off of delusion. What does this mean?

Two senses of being awake

↥ If “awake” means having been asleep before and waking afterward, inceptive awakening involves such an awakening and original awakening does not.

  1. If “awake” means never having slept in the first place, original awakening is awake in this sense and inceptive awakening is not.

Two senses of cutting off delusion

↥ The same holds for “cutting off.”

  1. If it means that what existed earlier is subsequently absent, inceptive awakening involves cutting off and original awakening does not.

  2. If it means being free from delusion from the first, original awakening is cutting off in this sense and inceptive awakening is not. In this latter sense, delusion has been cut off from the first and from the first there are no ordinary beings. As the treatise says below, “From the very beginning all sentient beings have entered the dharma of nirvāṇa and awakening.”

Original and inceptive awakening depend on one another

↥ Although it is said that, given original awakening, there have never been ordinary beings, in the absence of inceptive awakening there have always been ordinary beings. Thus there is no fault. You may object, “If, given original awakening, there have never been ordinary beings, there can never be any inceptive awakening. Relative to what, then, would there be ordinary beings?” The other side may equally reply, “If there can never be inceptive awakening, there is no original awakening. On what original awakening would you base the claim that there are no ordinary beings?”

↥ Understand the successive implications. Given original awakening, there is originally no nonawakening. Without nonawakening there can ultimately be no inceptive awakening. Without inceptive awakening there can originally be no original awakening. We arrive at the absence of original awakening precisely by starting from its presence. Original awakening is spoken of because there is inceptive awakening. Inceptive awakening is spoken of because there is nonawakening. Nonawakening exists in dependence on original awakening. As the treatise says below, “The meaning of original awakening is expressed relative to inceptive awakening, since inceptive awakening is identical with original awakening. As for inceptive awakening, nonawakening exists in dependence on original awakening, and inceptive awakening is spoken of in dependence on nonawakening.” This successive mutual dependence itself discloses that dharmas are neither nonexistent nor existent, neither existent nor nonexistent.

Is original awakening the cause of both defilement and purity?
BDK 17 ↗Original enlightenment as an intrinsic aspect of mind

Question. Does the nature of original awakening serve as the causal nature of both the defiled and the pure, or is it solely the nature of pure dharmas? If it is the cause solely of pure dharmas, why does the sūtra say, “The tathāgatagarbha is the cause of the wholesome and unwholesome,” and so on at length? If it gives rise both to defiled and to pure dharmas, why is it said to possess the full complement of intrinsic virtues,ᵀ and never said to possess the full complement of intrinsically defiling faults?

intrinsic virtues · 性功德 xìng gōng dé · Skt. guṇa (功德) · BDK p. 14 excellent qualities Wŏnhyo’s wording makes 性, ‘intrinsic’, explicit. Hakeda translates the phrase together with 無漏.

↥ Answer. This reality serves as the nature of both the defiled and the pure, and precisely for this reason it is said to possess only intrinsic virtues. What does this mean?

  1. Because reality is free from a fixed nature of purity, in response to conditions it can take the form of defiled dharmas.

  2. Because it is also free from a fixed nature of defilement, in response to conditions it can take the form of pure dharmas. Because it can take both forms, it serves as the nature of defilement and purity alike. Because it is free from fixed natures of defilement and purity, it is wholly intrinsic virtue.

↥ How does being free from the natures of defilement and purity constitute the virtues?ᵀ Because grasping and clinging to such natures is in either case delusive imagining.

virtues · 功德 gōng dé · Skt. guṇa · BDK p. 21 excellent qualities

1. Awakening

1.1. Brief explanation

1.1.2. Inceptive awakening
BDK 18 ↗The process of actualization of enlightenment

Having explained original awakening, the text turns to inceptive awakening. The account has two parts.

  1. It shows how nonawakening, too, arises in dependence on original awakening.

  2. It explains inceptive awakening in relation to nonawakening.

The mutual dependence of the three terms

↥ The point is that inceptive awakening depends on nonawakening, and nonawakening depends on original awakening. Original awakening depends on inceptive awakening. Since each depends on another, none has an intrinsic nature. Where there is no intrinsic nature, no independently existent awakening can be found. That absence of independent awakening follows from mutual dependence. What is established through mutual dependence cannot be dismissed as nonexistent. In this sense one may speak of awakening. It is given the name “awakening” without positing an intrinsic nature.

1. Brief explanation

↥ This concludes the brief explanation of the two kinds of awakening.

Inceptive awakening
BDK 18 ↗The process of actualization of enlightenment

“Inceptive awakening” concerns the essence of this same mind. Conditioned by ignorance, it moves and takes the form of delusive thoughts. Through the perfuming power of original awakening, the activity of awakening gradually emerges, until finally it comes back into accord with original awakening. This is called inceptive awakening.

BDK pp. 18–19

Four degrees of awakening

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 18 What is the meaning of this? An ordinary person becomes aware that his former thoughts were wrong; then he is able to stop (nirodha) such thoughts from arising again. Although this sometimes may also be called enlightenment, [properly it is not enlightenment at all] because it is not enlightenment [that reaches the fountainhead of Mind].

The followers of the Hinayana, who have some insight, and those bodhisattvas who have just been initiated become aware of the changing state (anyathātva) of thoughts and are free from thoughts which are subject to change [such as the existence of a permanent self (atman), etc.]. Since they have forsaken the rudimentary attachments derived from unwarranted speculation (vikalpa), [their experience] is called enlightenment in appearance.

Bodhisattvas [who have come to the realization] of the dharmakāya become aware of the [temporarily] abiding state (sthiti) of thoughts and are not arrested by them. Since they are free from their rudimentary [false] thoughts derived from the speculation [that the components of the world are real, their experience] p. 18–19 is called approximate enlightenment.

Those bodhisattvas who have completed the stages of a bodhisattva and who have fulfilled the expedient means [needed to bring forth the original enlightenment to the fullest extent] will experience the oneness [with suchness] in an instant; they will become aware of how the inceptions of [the deluded thoughts of the mind arise (jāti), and will be free from the rise of any [deluded] thought. Since they are far away even from subtle [deluded] thoughts, they are able to have an insight into the original nature of Mind. [The realization] that Mind is eternal is called the final enlightenment.

It is, therefore, said in a sutra that if there is a man who is able to perceive that which is beyond thoughts, he is advancing toward the Buddha wisdom.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗
