1.2. Degrees of inceptive awakening
BDK 18 ↗Ordinary person … followers of the Hīnayāna … bodhisattvas … final enlightenment

The degrees of awakening are distinguished by way of four characteristics.ᵀ I will explain those characteristics first and then interpret the passage.

four characteristics · 四相 sì xiàng · BDK p. 20 four states
1.2.1. The four characteristics explained
Are the four simultaneous or successive?

↥ Question. Are the four characteristics simultaneous or successive? Why does a doubt arise here?

  • If they are simultaneous, why does the treatise distinguish the times at which one awakens to them?

  • If they are successive, why does it say below that “the four characteristics exist simultaneously”?

Three readings

↥ Several explanations have been proposed.

The Sarvāstivāda account

↥ Some understand the four characteristics according to the Sarvāstivādins. The four exist simultaneously, but their functions are successive. Since their functions are successive, one awakens to them at different times. Since they exist simultaneously, they are said to be present together.

The account of the Chengshi lun

↥ Some understand them as the four successive characteristics taught in the Treatise on Establishing Reality (Chengshi lun). When the treatise says that all four exist simultaneously, it considers them from the standpoint of original awakening. From that standpoint there is no distinction of before and after among them. Hence “they exist simultaneously” and “none stands on its own.”ᵀ

none stands on its own · 無自立 wú zì lì · BDK p. 20 not self-existent
The Mahāyāna’s hidden teaching

↥ Some say these are the four characteristics of the Mahāyāna’s hidden teaching. Awakening to them admits of earlier and later, shallower and deeper stages. The four characteristics to which one awakens exist together.

The Mahāyāna’s hidden teaching — how the four characterize mind

↥ What does the third reading mean? Mind’s nature is originally free of the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Yet ignorance blinds the mind to its own nature. Going against that nature, ignorance departs from quiescence and can give rise to the four characteristics of thought in motion. Through the combined force of ignorance and the four characteristics, mind itself comes to arise, persist, change, and cease.ᵀ An analogy can be found in the discussions of the Lesser Vehicle. While mind is still future, it has yet to undergo arising and ceasing. The force of karma draws forth the four characteristics, which cause this mental dharma to arise, persist, change, and cease. Understand the four characteristics taught in the Mahāyāna in the same way. As a sūtra says, “This very dharmakāya, driven and tossed by afflictions, comes and goes in saṃsāra and is called a sentient being.”ᵀ The treatise means precisely this when it says below, “The mind, pure by nature, is stirred by the wind of ignorance.”ᵀ

arise, persist, change, and cease · 生住異滅 shēng zhù yì miè · BDK p. 20 arise, abide, change, and cease to be
afflictions · 煩惱 fán nǎo · Skt. kleśa · BDK p. 29 defilement
sentient being · 眾生 zhòng shēng · Skt. sattva · BDK p. 14 people Hakeda also uses “ordinary people” on p. 20 and “sentient beings” on p. 25.
mind, pure by nature · 自性清淨心 zì xìng qīng jìng xīn · BDK p. 21 Mind, pure in its own nature
The subdivisions of the four characteristics

↥ Such is the general account. On closer examination each of the four characteristics admits further distinctions. Arising has three, persistence four, change six, and cessation seven.

1. Arising — three characteristics

↥ Arising has three characteristics.

1.1. Activation

↥ The karmic characteristic. Through ignorance and nonawakening, thought stirs. Although it arises and ceases, perceiver and percept have yet to be differentiated. In the analogy, the still-future characteristic of arising is on the point of exercising its function.

1.2. Evolving into a perceiver

↥ The characteristic of evolving. On the basis of the stirring of thought, the mind evolves into a perceiver. In the analogy, arising, still future, has reached the point of exercising its function.

1.3. Manifestation of an object

↥ The characteristic of manifestation. On the basis of a perceiver, the appearance of an object manifests.ᵀ In the analogy, future arising has now reached the present.

characteristic of manifestation · 現相 xiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 境界相 world of objects
1. Arising — three characteristics

↥ Ignorance combines with these three characteristicsᵀ and stirs the One Mind itself, which evolves through to manifestation. In the Lesser Vehicle analogy, mind latent in the future follows its own characteristic of arising and passes into the present. Likewise in the Mahāyāna, the mind that is tathāgatagarbha follows arising through to manifestation. These three characteristics are distinctions within the ālayavijñāna. Their details will be explained below. They are called the three exceedingly profound characteristics of arising.

three characteristics · 三相 sān xiàng · BDK p. 24 三種相 three aspects
2. Persistence — four afflictions of self

↥ Persistence has four characteristics. Ignorance combines with arising, obscuring the absence, in the mind that has arisen, of any self or anything belonging to a self. It can thus produce four characteristics of persistence.

  • Delusion about self.

    • Self-view.

    • Attachment to self.

    • The conceit of self. These four arise in dependence on arising and characterize the mind itself, bringing it to the stage of persistence, where it dwells on an inward object. Hence “characteristics of persistence.” All four belong to the seventh consciousness.

3. Change — six afflictions

↥ Change has six characteristics. Ignorance combines with the characteristics of persistence, failing to recognize the emptiness of the self and the possessions of self it imputes. This produces six characteristics of change.

  • Greed.

    • Aversion.

    • Delusion.

    • Conceit.

    • Doubt.

    • Views. These are what the New Treatise means by “there are only six kinds of affliction by intrinsic nature.” Ignorance combines with these six. They characterize the persisting mind, bringing it to the stage of change, where it turns outwards to apprehend objects. Hence “characteristics of change.” These six occur at the level of the manifestly arising consciousnesses.

4. Cessation — seven bodily and verbal actions

↥ Cessation has seven characteristics. Ignorance combines with the characteristics of change. It fails to recognize that external sense objects are by nature free of being agreeable or disagreeable. This gives rise to the seven characteristics of cessation, the seven kinds of unwholesome bodily and verbal karma. Such karma puts an end to the mind in its stage of change and causes it to fall into a bad destination. Hence “characteristics of cessation.” In the Lesser Vehicle analogy, the characteristic of cessation extinguishes the present mind, which thereby passes into the past. Understand cessation in the Mahāyāna in the same way.

Ignorance as the source of the four characteristics

↥ Thus the four characteristics arise and the One Mind wanders on in saṃsāra. All of this is rooted in fundamental ignorance. As a sūtra says, “The underlying ground of ignorance has the greatest force.” This treatise says, “Understand that the force of ignorance can bring forth all defiled dharmas.”

Primary mind and the mental factors that characterize it

↥ The mind that is characterized comes from One Mind. The characteristics that characterize it arise from ignorance. The function of each characteristic varies with the stage it reaches. These characteristics apprehend the particular features of objects and are called mental factors. Their root, ignorance, goes against the nature of equality. The mind they characterize plays the leading role at every stage. It knows an object under its general aspect and is called the “mind-king,” or primary mind. This is because it is originally One Mind, the common source of all dharmas. As the Treatise on the Middle and the Extremes says, “Cognition of the mere object is called mind. Its distinctions are called mental factors.” The prose explanation says, “Cognizing the general characteristic of an object is called mind. Apprehending its particular characteristics is called a mental factor.” The Yogācārabhūmi gives the same account. This is why followers of other teachings and the like often imagine the primary mind to be a ruler, an agent, or an experiencer. They do not understand that it has no intrinsic nature and moves on in dependence on conditions.

The four characteristics of one thought and the four degrees of awakening

↥ The four characteristics taken together are called a single thought. The four grades of awakening are explained in terms of the four characteristics of this single thought. The point is that the force of ignorance and nonawakening first gives rise to all the dreamlike thoughts that have arising and the other characteristics. They stir the source of mind and evolve as far as the characteristic of cessation. In a long sleep one wanders through the three realms and the six destinations.ᵀ Now, through the inconceivable perfuming of original awakening, disenchantment with saṃsāra and the aspiration for release arise. One gradually turns back toward the source. Cessation is the first characteristic to be stilled, and arising the last. In the clarity of great awakening, one sees that one’s own mind was originally unmoved and that there is now nothing in it to still. Equal from the beginning, it rests upon the bed of a single suchness. The sūtra illustrates this with the analogy of crossing a river in a dream. Although the analogy calls for a fuller explanation here, such is its broad meaning.

three realms · 三界 sān jiè · Skt. traidhātuka · BDK p. 28 triple world

1. Inceptive awakening in detail

1. Inceptive awakening in detail

1.2. Four degrees of inceptive awakening

BDK 18 ↗Four degrees of awakening

We can now explain the wording. The four characteristics distinguish four stages. At each stage the text treats four points.

  1. Who awakens. ↓

  2. The characteristic to which the person awakens. ↓

  3. The benefit of awakening. ↓

  4. How far that awakening extends. ↓

1.2.1. Ordinary person at the ten faiths
1.2.1.1. Who awakens
BDK 18 ↗An ordinary person becomes aware

At the first stage, “an ordinary person” identifies who awakens. The person is at the stage of the ten faiths.

1.2.1.2. Characteristic discerned

↥ “Becomes aware that a previous thought gave rise to evil” identifies the characteristic discerned. Before entering the ten faiths one committed all seven kinds of bodily and verbal misconduct. On entering the stage of faith one recognizes that all seven are unwholesome. Hence “becomes aware that a previous thought gave rise to evil.” This is what it means to awaken to the characteristic of cessation.

1.2.1.3. Benefit
BDK 18 ↗Able to stop such thoughts from arising again

“Can stop a subsequent thought and keep it from arising” is the benefit. Through nonawakening one formerly entertained thoughts of the seven kinds of misconduct. Now that one has awakened, one can put a stop to the characteristic of cessation.

1.2.1.4. Extent of awakening
BDK 18 ↗Although this sometimes may also be called enlightenment

“Although this is called awakening, it is itself nonawakening” indicates its extent. One knows that the characteristic of cessation is unwholesome, yet has still to awaken to the fact that this characteristic is a dream.

1.2.2. Practitioners of the two vehicles and newly resolved bodhisattvas
1.2.2.1. Who awakens
BDK 18 ↗The followers of the Hinayana and newly initiated bodhisattvas

At the second stage the text speaks of “the contemplative insight of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas who have first aroused the resolve, and so forth.”ᵀ The bodhisattvas are those at the three stages of worthiness, beginning with the ten understandings. The first moment of the ten understandings is called the abode of arousing the resolve. Naming the beginner includes those at the subsequent stages. Hence “bodhisattvas who have first aroused the resolve, and so forth.” This identifies who awakens.

contemplative insight · 觀智 guān zhì · BDK p. 18 some insight
two vehicles · 二乘 èr shèng · BDK p. 18 followers of the Hinayana
bodhisattvas who have first aroused the resolve · 初發意菩薩 chū fā yì pú sà · BDK p. 18 bodhisattvas who have just been initiated
1.2.2.2. Characteristic discerned
BDK 18 ↗Become aware of the changing state of thoughts

“Awaken to change in thought” identifies the characteristic discerned.ᵀ The six characteristics of change discussed above discriminate inner from outer and impute a self and what belongs to it. Practitioners of these three vehicles understand selflessness. Hence “awaken to change in thought.” Ignorance has put the mind itself, the bearer of these characteristics, to sleep. It dreams the characteristics of change and gives rise to afflictions. Now, through association with wisdom, it begins to awaken from the dream of change.

change in thought · 念異 niàn yì · Skt. anyathātva (change) · BDK p. 18 changing state (anyathātva) of thoughts
1.2.2.3. Benefit
BDK 18 ↗Free from thoughts which are subject to change

“Thought has no characteristic of change” is the benefit. Once one awakens to the dream of change, those six characteristics of change cease for good. Hence “thought has no characteristic of change.”

1.2.2.4. Extent of awakening
BDK 18 ↗Enlightenment in appearance

“Since they have relinquished the characteristics of coarse discrimination and grasping, this is called semblance awakening” indicates its extent.ᵀ To discriminate the agreeable from the disagreeable and thereby give rise to greed, aversion, and the like is what coarse discrimination and grasping means. One has relinquished these coarse, grasping perceptions but has yet to attain nondiscriminating awakening. Hence “semblance awakening.”

characteristics of coarse discrimination and grasping · 麁分別執著相 cū fēn bié zhí zhuó xiàng · BDK p. 18 rudimentary attachments derived from unwarranted speculation
semblance awakening · 相似覺 xiāng sì jué · BDK p. 18 enlightenment in appearance
1.2.3. Dharmakāya bodhisattvas
1.2.3.1. Who awakens
BDK 18 ↗Bodhisattvas who have realized the dharmakāya

At the third stage “dharmakāya bodhisattvas and the like” identifies who awakens. They are the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds, from the first ground onward.ᵀ

dharmakāya bodhisattvas · 法身菩薩 fǎ shēn pú sà · BDK p. 18 Bodhisattvas [who have come to the realization] of the dharmakāya
1.2.3.2. Characteristic discerned
BDK 18 ↗Become aware of the abiding state of thoughts

“Awaken to the abiding of thought.” In the characteristic of abiding the mind has yet to posit sense objects outside itself. It grasps persons and dharmas, dwelling on them inwardly.ᵀ Dharmakāya bodhisattvas penetrate both kinds of emptiness. The mind itself, which bears the characteristics, had previously awakened to change, yet still slept the dream of abiding. Now, associated with nondiscriminating wisdom, it awakens from that dream. Hence “awaken to the abiding of thought.” This identifies the characteristic discerned.

abiding of thought · 念住 niàn zhù · Skt. sthiti (abiding) · BDK p. 18 [temporarily] abiding state (sthiti) of thoughts
1.2.3.3. Benefit
BDK 18 ↗Are not arrested by them

“Thought has no characteristic of abiding.” The four characteristics of abiding cease and do not arise again. This is the benefit.

1.2.3.4. Extent of awakening
BDK 18 ↗Since they are free from their rudimentary thoughts

“Having left behind discrimination and the characteristics of coarse thought.” Grasping at a self in persons is called “discrimination.”ᵀ To distinguish it from the coarse discrimination of the preceding characteristic of change, the text omits “coarse” here. Grasping at a self in dharmas, however, is called “coarse thought,” to distinguish it from the subtle thought in the characteristic of arising discussed next.

discrimination and the characteristics of coarse thought · 分別麁念相 fēn bié cū niàn xiàng · BDK p. 18 rudimentary [false] thoughts derived from the speculation
BDK 18–19 ↗Approximate enlightenment

One has attained nondiscriminating awakening, yet still sleeps the dream of arising. Hence “awakening according to one's measure.” This indicates its extent.ᵀ

awakening according to one's measure · 隨分覺 suí fèn jué · BDK p. 18–19 approximate enlightenment
1.2.4. Bodhisattva at the culmination of the grounds
1.2.4.1. Who awakens
BDK 19 ↗Bodhisattvas who have completed the stages

At the fourth stage “a bodhisattva at the culmination of the grounds” refers to the Stainless Ground. This names the stage as a whole.⁕ The two phrases that follow distinguish two paths.

1.2.4.1.1. Preparatory path
BDK 19 ↗Fulfilled the expedient means

“Completes the skillful means” refers to the preparatory path.

1.2.4.1.2. Uninterrupted path
BDK 19 ↗Oneness in an instant

“Comes into accord in a single thought-moment” refers to the uninterrupted path.ᵀ

into accord in a single thought-moment · 一念相應 yī niàn xiāng yìng · BDK p. 19 the oneness [with suchness] in an instant
The two paths in vajra-like concentration

↥ As the Abhidharma Treatise says, “The path of culmination is the vajra-like concentration. It is of two kinds, one comprised in the preparatory path and one in the uninterrupted path.” This identifies who awakens.

1.2.4.2. Characteristic discerned
BDK 19 ↗Become aware of how the inceptions arise

“Awakens to the mind’s first arising” identifies the characteristic discerned.ᵀ The mind’s first arising means that, dependent on ignorance, the characteristic of arising comes about. It characterizes the mind itself, setting thought in motion. Only now does one directly realize that apart from original awakening there is no nonawakening. The very thought in motion is the quiescent mind. Hence “awakens to the mind’s first arising.” When disoriented, one calls east “west.” On finding one’s bearings, one sees that what one took for west is east. Such is awakening here.

mind’s first arising · 心初起 xīn chū qǐ · Skt. jāti (arising, in Hakeda’s gloss) · BDK p. 19 the inceptions
1.2.4.3. Benefit
BDK 19 ↗Free from the rise of any deluded thought

“Mind has no initial characteristic” describes the benefit.ᵀ It was through nonawakening that there was a first arising of mind. Now that one has awakened, nothing arises in mind. Hence “mind has no initial characteristic.” At the three preceding stages something had already been relinquished, yet thought in motion still arose and had not come to an end. Hence such expressions as “thought has no characteristic of abiding.” At this final stage thought in motion has ended altogether. Only the One Mind remains. Hence “mind has no initial characteristic.”

initial characteristic · 初相 chū xiàng · BDK p. 20 inception
1.2.4.4. Extent of awakening
BDK 19 ↗Far away even from subtle thoughts

The passage from “far removed” indicates the extent of awakening. It has two statements.

  1. The first states directly how far awakening extends. ↓

    1. BDK 19 ↗It is therefore said in a sutra

      From “therefore,” the text cites a sūtra in confirmation. ↓

1.2.4.4.1. Direct explanation
BDK 19 ↗Far away even from subtle thoughts

The movement of thought at the characteristic of activity is the subtlest of thoughts. Hence “subtle thought.”ᵀ This characteristic comes wholly to an end, leaving nothing whatever. Hence “far removed.” At the very moment of being far removed from it, one stands on the buddha-ground.

characteristic of activity · 業相 yè xiàng · BDK p. 24 無明業相 activity of ignorance
BDK 19 ↗Insight into the original nature of Mind

At the three preceding stages one had yet to reach the source of mind. The characteristic of arising persisted and mind was still impermanent. On reaching this stage ignorance comes forever to an end. One returns to the source, the One Mind, and there is no further stirring. Hence “one comes to see the nature of mind, and mind abides forever.”ᵀ

abides forever · 常住 cháng zhù · BDK p. 19 eternal
BDK 19 ↗The final enlightenment

There is nowhere further to advance. This “is called ultimate awakening.”

↥ Again, until one reaches the source of mind, the thoughts of the dream persist. One wishes to still their movement, hoping to reach the other shore. Now, on seeing the nature of mind, all dream imaginings have ended. One awakens to the fact that one’s own mind originally never wandered in saṃsāra. There is now no movement to bring to rest. Of itself it has always been One Mind, resting on the bed of the one suchness. Hence “one comes to see the nature of mind, and mind abides forever.” Thus inceptive awakening does not differ from original awakening. For that reason it is called ultimate awakening. This completes the direct statement of its extent.

1.2.4.4.2. Scriptural confirmation
BDK 19 ↗Advancing toward the Buddha wisdom

The scriptural proof says, “One who can contemplate freedom from thought is advancing toward a buddha’s wisdom.”ᵀ At the causal stage, although one has yet to be free of thought, one can contemplate what freedom from thought means.ᵀ The sūtra calls such contemplation an advance toward the buddha-ground. This demonstrates that the buddha-ground is free of thought.ᵀ Here the cause is adduced to establish the result.

freedom from thought · 無念 wú niàn · BDK p. 19 that which is beyond thoughts
free of thought · 離念 lí niàn · BDK p. 17 free from thoughts
free of thought · 無念 wú niàn · BDK p. 19 that which is beyond thoughts
The three paths in the Golden Drum Sūtra

↥ For scriptural evidence that covers both cause and result, the Golden Drum Sūtra says the following.⁕

  1. “Through the paths of subduing, the mind that initiates activity ceases. ↓

  2. Through the path of cutting off dharmas, the mind dependent on the fundamental mind ceases. ↓

  3. Through the path of final uprooting, the fundamental mind itself is exhausted.” ↓

  4. The “paths of subduing” refer to the thirty minds [the three sets of ten preliminary stages]. “The mind that initiates activity ceases” corresponds to this treatise’s “relinquishing coarse discriminative and grasping perceptions.” It is the cessation of the characteristic of change.

  5. The “path of cutting off dharmas” is at the stage of the dharmakāya. “The mind dependent on the fundamental mind ceases” corresponds to this treatise’s “relinquishing discrimination and the characteristics of coarse thought.” It is the cessation of the characteristic of abiding.

  6. The “path of final uprooting” is the vajra-like concentration. “The fundamental mind is exhausted” corresponds to this treatise’s “leaving subtle thought far behind.” It is the exhaustion of the characteristic of arising.

1.2.1.2. The four degrees of awakening
BDK 18 ↗The stages of the actualization of enlightenment

With “what does this mean?” begins the second part, the particular exposition. This explains completeness and incompleteness of awakening in relation to the four characteristics.ᵀ

four characteristics · 四相 sì xiàng · BDK p. 20 four states
1.2.1.2.1. Clarification of the four characteristics

↥ I shall first briefly clarify what the four characteristics mean and then explain the words of the treatise. ↓

Are they simultaneous or successive?

↥ Question. Are these four characteristics simultaneous or successive? Where does the difficulty lie? If they are simultaneous, the treatise nevertheless distinguishes four stages at which one awakens to them. If you answer that they are successive, the text says below, “the four characteristics are present simultaneously.”

1. Sarvāstivāda account

↥ Some say that the treatise relies on the Sarvāstivādins’ account of the four characteristics. In substance the four are simultaneous, but their functions are successive. Because their functions are successive, one awakens to them at different times. Because in substance they are simultaneous, they are said to exist together.

2. Account based on the Treatise on Establishing the Truth

↥ Others say it relies on the successive characteristics of the Treatise on Establishing the Truth. It calls them simultaneous because, from the standpoint of original awakening, there is no distinction of earlier and later among them. Hence the four are said to exist simultaneously, with none established in its own right.ᵀ

none established in its own right · 無自立 wú zì lì · BDK p. 20 not self-existent
3. The hidden Mahāyāna account

↥ Others say these are the four characteristics in their hidden Mahāyāna sense. Awakening to the four proceeds successively and by degrees of depth. The four characteristics to which one awakens are present simultaneously.

↥ What does this mean? Mind by nature is originally free from the characteristics of arising and ceasing, yet ignorance fails to recognize the nature of one’s own mind. Because ignorance runs counter to the quiescence of mind’s nature, free of characteristics, it can bring forth the four characteristics of thought in motion.ᵀ Through the power of ignorance in association with the four characteristics, mind itself is made to arise, abide, alter, and cease.ᵀ Compare the account in the treatises of the Lesser Vehicle. Mind in the future passes through arising and ceasing, and karmic force draws it forth so that mind itself arises, abides, alters, and ceases.⁕ The meaning of the four characteristics in the Mahāyāna is similar. As the sūtra says, “This very dharmadhātu, tossed about by the afflictions, circulates through the five destinies and is called ‘sentient beings.’” The present treatise says, “Mind, intrinsically pure, is stirred by the wind of ignorance.” Surely this is just what it means.

mind’s nature · 心性 xīn xìng · Skt. citta-prakṛti · BDK p. 12 essential nature of the Mind
arise, abide, alter, and cease · 生住異滅 shēng zhù yì miè · BDK p. 20 arise, abide, change, and cease to be
The divisions of each characteristic

↥ Such is the general account. Considered individually, each of the four characteristics has further divisions. Arising has three, abiding four, alteration six, and cessation seven.

1. Arising — three characteristics

↥ The three characteristics of arising.

1.1. Karmic activity

↥ Karmic activity. Owing to ignorance, thought stirs unawares.ᵀ Although there is arising and ceasing, the perceiver and what appears have not yet become distinct. It is as though the characteristic of arising in the future were about to exercise its immediate function.

Karmic activity · 業相 yè xiàng · BDK p. 24 無明業相 activity of ignorance
1.2. Turning

↥ Turning. In dependence on thought in motion, there develops a capacity to perceive,ᵀ as when the characteristic of arising reaches the point of exercising its immediate function.

Turning · 轉相 zhuǎn xiàng · BDK p. 24 能見相 perceiving subject
1.3. Manifestation

↥ Manifestation. On the basis of the capacity to perceive, the characteristics of an object have already appeared,ᵀ as when what arises in the future reaches the present.

Manifestation · 現相 xiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 境界相 world of objects
1. Arising — three characteristics

↥ Ignorance associates with these three characteristics, perfuming and stirring mind itself until it is conjoined with them. Following the movement, mind turns, reaching the point of manifestation. It is like mind latent in the future in the Lesser Vehicle account, which, following its characteristic of arising, gradually reaches the present. The same reasoning applies to tathāgatagarbha-mind in the Mahāyāna. All three are distinctions at the level of ālayavijñāna. The details will be given below. These are called the three profound characteristics of arising.

2. Abiding — four characteristics

↥ The four characteristics of abiding. Ignorance conjoins with arising and fails to recognize that the mind that has arisen is free of self and of what belongs to self. It thereby brings forth four characteristics of abiding:

  • delusion about self,

    • the view of self,

    • attachment to self,

    • and conceit of self. These four arise in dependence on the characteristic of arising. They act on mind and bring it to the stage of abiding, where it abides with its object taken inwardly. Hence “abiding.”⁕ All four belong to the level of the seventh consciousness.

3. Alteration — six characteristics

↥ The six characteristics of alteration. Ignorance conjoins with the characteristic of abiding and fails to recognize that the self imagined and what belongs to it are empty. It thereby brings forth six characteristics of alteration:

  • greed,

    • aversion,

    • delusion,

    • conceit,

    • doubt,

    • and views. The newer treatise states that “the afflictions are of precisely six kinds by nature.” This is what it means. Ignorance conjoins with these six and characterizes the abiding mind, bringing it to the stage of alteration, where it reaches outward for objects. Hence “alteration.” These six belong to the level of the actively arising consciousnesses.⁕

4. Cessation — seven characteristics

↥ The seven characteristics of cessation. Ignorance conjoins with the characteristic of alteration and fails to recognize that outer sense objects are in themselves free of opposition or agreement [with one’s wishes]. It thereby gives rise to seven characteristics of cessation, the seven courses of unwholesome bodily and verbal action. These seven bring the mind at the stage of alteration to cessation and propel it into an unfortunate rebirth. Hence “cessation.” Compare the characteristic of cessation in the Lesser Vehicle system. It extinguishes the present mind and consigns it to the past. The Mahāyāna characteristic of cessation has a similar meaning.

The four characteristics and root ignorance

↥ Thus we should understand that both the arising of the four characteristics and the wandering on of One Mind derive entirely from root ignorance. As the sūtra says, “The underlying basis of ignorance has the greatest power.” The treatise says, “Understand that ignorance can give rise to all defiled dharmas.”

The characterized mind and its characterizing mental factors

↥ Furthermore, the mind so characterized traces back to One Mind. The characteristics that characterize it are produced by ignorance. Because they are so produced, their functions differ according to where they arise. In apprehending the particular characteristics of sense objects, they are called mental factors. This is because root ignorance runs counter to the nature of equality. What derives from One Mind, on the other hand, wherever it reaches, acts as the general governor. It cognizes the common characteristics of sense objects and is called the ruling mind, because the original One Mind is the common source of all dharmas.⁕ Consequently, many non-Buddhist thinkers take this ruling mind to be a sovereign, an agent, and an experiencer, because they fail to understand that, lacking an intrinsic nature of its own, it wanders on in dependence on conditions. As the Treatise Distinguishing the Middle and the Extremes says, “Cognition of the object alone is called mind. [Cognition of] its distinctions is called mental factors.” The prose commentary explains, “Cognizing the object’s common characteristic is called mind. Apprehending its particular characteristics is called mental factors.” The Yogācārabhūmi gives the same account. Such in brief is the Mahāyāna account of the four characteristics as they characterize mind and manifest its course.⁕

1.2.1.2.2. Explanation of the treatise’s wording
The four characteristics of a single thought-moment

↥ We now turn to the wording itself. The four characteristics, taken together, are called a single thought-moment. Distinguishing the four characteristics of this one thought-moment reveals the gradual progression through four stages. Originally, through the power of ignorance and nonawakening, all sorts of dream-thoughts arise, beginning with the characteristic of arising. They stir the very source of mind and proceed as far as the characteristic of cessation. Beings sleep a long sleep in the three realms,ᵀ wandering on from time without beginning. Now, through the inconceivable activity of original awakening,ᵀ there arises a mind disenchanted with saṃsāra and intent on nirvāṇa. Little by little one advances, first bringing the characteristic of cessation to rest and finally returning to the source of mind.ᵀ In the full light of great awakening one realizes that one’s own mind originally had no movement and now has nothing to bring to rest. From the beginning all is equal in one and the same awakening. It is like the sūtra’s simile of crossing a river in a dream. The simile deserves fuller treatment here. Such is its general import.

three realms · 三界 sān jiè · Skt. traidhātuka · BDK p. 28 triple world
inconceivable activity · 不思議業 bù sī yì yè · BDK p. 20 suprarational functions
source of mind · 心源 xīn yuán · BDK p. 18 fountainhead of Mind
Outline of the exposition

↥ The passage has two parts.

  1. It distinguishes the four characteristics to explain what “ultimate” means. ↓

  2. From “Again, as for the arising of mind,” it explains in what sense ultimate awakening is the same awakening.ᵀ ↓

    ultimate awakening · 究竟覺 jiū jìng jué · BDK p. 18 final enlightenment
1.2.1.2.2.1. Gradual awakening to the four characteristics

↥ Each of the four stages is considered under four headings.

  1. Who awakens. ↓

  2. The characteristic to which one awakens. ↓

  3. The benefit of that awakening. ↓

  4. The extent of that awakening. ↓

1. Ordinary people at the ten faiths

↥ In the first stage: ↓

1.1. Who awakens
BDK 18 ↗An ordinary person

“An ordinary person” identifies who awakens. The stage is that of the ten faiths.

1.2. The characteristic recognized

↥ “Recognizes that the preceding thought gave rise to evil” identifies the characteristic to which one awakens. Before entering this stage, one committed all seven kinds of unskillful bodily and verbal action. On entering the ten faiths, one recognizes that those earlier misdeeds were indeed unskillful. Hence “recognizes that the preceding thought gave rise to evil.” This is what it means to awaken to the characteristic of cessation.

1.3. The benefit of awakening
BDK 18 ↗Able to stop such thoughts from arising again

“Can stop the subsequent thought from arising” states the benefit of awakening. Earlier, nonawakening gave rise to unskillful thoughts. Now, having awakened, one can bring the characteristic of cessation to a stop.

1.4. The extent of awakening
BDK 18 ↗Although this sometimes may also be called enlightenment

“Although it is called awakening, it is precisely nonawakening” shows how far this awakening goes. One knows that the characteristic of cessation is unskillful but has yet to awaken to the fact that this characteristic is itself a dream.

2. Practitioners of the three vehicles

↥ In the second stage: ↓

2.1. Who awakens
BDK 18 ↗Those bodhisattvas who have just been initiated

“Bodhisattvas who first arouse the resolve, and so forth” means the bodhisattvas at the three stages of the worthy, beginning with the ten understandings.ᵀ The first of the ten understandings is called the abode of arousing the resolve for awakening. Hence the phrase “first arouse the resolve.”

Bodhisattvas who first arouse the resolve · 初發意菩薩 chū fā yì pú sà · BDK p. 18 bodhisattvas who have just been initiated
2.2. The characteristic recognized
BDK 18 ↗Aware of the changing state of thoughts

“Awaken to the changing of thought.”ᵀ In the characteristic of change one discriminates between inner and outer and imputes an “I” and a “mine.” Practitioners of all three vehicles can recognize that inwardly there is no abiding self and outwardly nothing belonging to such a self. The point concerns mind itself, which undergoes these characteristics. Put to sleep by ignorance, it dreams the characteristic of change. As it gradually comes into accord with wisdom, it begins to awaken from this dream. Hence “awaken to the changing of thought.”

changing of thought · 念異 niàn yì · Skt. anyathātva (change) · BDK p. 18 changing state (anyathātva) of thoughts
2.3. The benefit of awakening

↥ Through this awakening, the six modes of change cease, never to arise again. Hence “thought has no characteristic of change.” This is the benefit of awakening.

2.4. The extent of awakening
BDK 18 ↗Enlightenment in appearance

“Because they relinquish coarse attachment, this is called a semblance of awakening.”ᵀ Discriminating inner from outer and imputing “I” and “mine” is called coarse attachment. Although they relinquish these coarse discriminative perceptions, they have yet to realize directly the true nature of consciousness-only. Hence “a semblance of awakening.” This is the extent of their awakening.

semblance of awakening · 相似覺 xiāng sì jué · BDK p. 18 enlightenment in appearance
3. Bodhisattvas of the dharmakāya

↥ In the third stage: ↓

3.1. Who awakens
BDK 18 ↗Bodhisattvas … of the dharmakāya

“Dharmakāya bodhisattvas and so forth” means bodhisattvas on the ten grounds, beginning with the first.ᵀ

Dharmakāya bodhisattvas · 法身菩薩 fǎ shēn pú sà · BDK p. 18 Bodhisattvas [who have come to the realization] of the dharmakāya
3.2. The characteristic recognized
BDK 18 ↗Aware of the … abiding state of thoughts

“Awaken to the abiding of thought.” In the characteristic of abiding, one no longer imputes sense objects exterior to mind,ᵀ yet still clings to persons and dharmas as abiding through causes and conditions. Dharmakāya bodhisattvas awaken to the fact that the characteristics of persons and dharmas are consciousness alone. Mind itself, which undergoes these characteristics, had previously awakened to change but still slept in the dream of abiding. Now, in accord with true knowledge of consciousness-only, it awakens from the dream of abiding. Hence “awaken to the abiding of thought.”

abiding of thought · 念住 niàn zhù · Skt. sthiti (abiding) · BDK p. 18 [temporarily] abiding state (sthiti) of thoughts
3.3. The benefit of awakening

↥ Through this awakening the four modes of abiding cease and do not arise again. Hence “thought has no characteristic of abiding.”

3.4. The extent of awakening
BDK 18 ↗Free from their rudimentary … thoughts

“Because they have left behind discrimination and the characteristic of coarse thought.”ᵀ The view of a personal self is called “discrimination.” To distinguish this from the coarse discrimination proper to change, the text leaves “discrimination” unqualified by “coarse.” Clinging to a self is called “coarse thought.” It is called “coarse” to distinguish it from the “subtle thought” proper to arising.⁕ Although one has realized the true nature of consciousness-only, one still sleeps in the dream of arising. Hence “awakening in part.”ᵀ

↥ In the fourth stage: ↓

4.1. Who awakens
BDK 19 ↗Completed the stages of a bodhisattva

“The bodhisattva at the end of the grounds” means the stainless ground.⁕ This names the stage as a whole. As the Sūtra of Fundamental Deeds says, “A bodhisattva on the stainless ground abides there for a hundred thousand eons.” The next two phrases distinguish two paths. ↓

BDK 19 ↗Fulfilled the expedient means

“Completes the skillful means” refers to the preparatory path.ᵀ

skillful means · 方便 fāng biàn · Skt. upāya · BDK p. 19 expedient means
BDK 19 ↗Experience the oneness … in an instant

“In accord in a single thought-moment” refers to the uninterrupted path.ᵀ As the Abhidharma treatise says, “The path of consummation is the vajra-like concentration. It has two forms, the one included in the preparatory path and the other in the uninterrupted path.” Together these three phrases identify the one who awakens.

In accord in a single thought-moment · 一念相應 yī niàn xiāng yìng · BDK p. 19 the oneness [with suchness] in an instant
4.2. The characteristic recognized

↥ “Awakens to mind as it first arises” identifies that to which one awakens.ᵀ ↓

mind as it first arises · 心初起 xīn chū qǐ · Skt. jāti (arising, in Hakeda’s gloss) · BDK p. 19 the inceptions
BDK 19 ↗Aware of how the inceptions … arise

“Awakens to mind as it first arises.” Through ignorance there is the characteristic of arising. It deludes mind itself and sets thought in motion. Only now does one directly realize that, apart from original awakening, there is no nonawakening. The thought in motion is itself the quiescent mind. Hence “awakens to mind as it first arises.” When disoriented, one takes east for west. On regaining one’s bearings, one recognizes that what one wrongly called west is precisely due east. The meaning of awakening to mind’s first arising is just the same.ᵀ

mind’s first arising · 心初起 xīn chū qǐ · Skt. jāti (arising, in Hakeda’s gloss) · BDK p. 19 the inceptions
4.3. The benefit of awakening

↥ Originally, owing to nonawakening, mind moved without [truly] arising.⁕ Now that one has awakened, there is nothing that arises in mind. Hence “mind has no initial characteristic.”ᵀ At the preceding three stages a characteristic is eliminated at each stage, but thoughts in motion have not yet been exhausted. Hence such expressions as “thought has no characteristic of abiding.” At the ultimate stage, all motion of thought ends at once and only One Mind remains. Hence “mind has no initial characteristic.” This is the benefit of awakening.

initial characteristic · 初相 chū xiàng · BDK p. 20 inception
4.4. The extent of awakening
BDK 19 ↗Far away even from subtle … thoughts

From “far removed” the text describes how far this awakening goes. The stirring of thought in the characteristic of activity is the subtlest of thoughts. Hence “subtle thought.” This characteristic ends completely, never leaving any remainder. Hence “far removed.” When this separation is accomplished, one is at precisely the ground of Buddhahood. At the earlier stages one had yet to awaken to the source of mind. The characteristic of arising had yet to end, and mind was still impermanent. Now, at this stage, ignorance ceases forever. One returns to the source of mind, with no further stirring. Hence “comes to see the nature of mind.” Mind abides constantly, with no further advance possible.ᵀ This is called ultimate awakening.

abides constantly · 常住 cháng zhù · BDK p. 19 eternal

↥ To put it another way, before one has returned to the source of mind, dream-thoughts have yet to end. One wishes to stop this motion and hopes to reach that stillness. Now that one has seen the nature of mind, dream-perceptions end altogether. One awakens to the fact that one’s own mind never wandered in saṃsāra and that now there is nothing to bring to cessation. It was always One Mind, as when one has been lying on the same bed throughout. Hence “comes to see the nature of mind, and mind abides constantly.” Inceptive awakening is thus altogether identical with original awakening. This is called “ultimate awakening.” This shows the extent of that awakening.

Permanence and the fruition of practice
BDK 19 ↗Mind is eternal … the final enlightenment

Question. If inceptive awakening is identical with original awakening and free of arising and ceasing, how can this be reconciled with the following statement? The Compendium of the Great Vehicle says, “The root is already permanent. What issues from it depends on the root and persists as a continuum,” and so on at length.⁕

↥ Answer. The two authors have different points in view, so their reasoning is consistent. How so?

  1. The author of the present treatise means that nonawakening originally set the quiescent mind in motion. Now nonawakening comes to rest and mind returns to its original quiescence. In this sense it comes to abide permanently.

  2. The Compendium means that the dharmakāya has always been abiding and unmoving. On its basis one undertakes the two practices of merit and wisdom, which bring to fruition the innumerable excellent qualities. Since this fruit arises through causes and conditions, it is subject to arising and ceasing. Hence the Compendium speaks of a continuum.

↥ To give a full account of newly attaining the innumerable excellent qualities requires both senses.⁕ In the first sense there is permanence. In the second there is arising and ceasing. Arising and ceasing and permanent abiding do not obstruct each other. Each single thought-moment pervades the three times without exceeding one moment.⁕ It is as if each pore pervaded the ten directions. Even in pervading the ten directions, the pore does not grow any larger. So it is with every Buddha, freely and without obstruction. How could one cling exclusively to one approach?

↥ As a Flower Garland Sūtra verse says, “The Sage transcends the three times, fully endowed with the major and minor bodily characteristics. He abides where there is no abiding. The whole dharma-realm is pure. Through causes and conditions dharmas arise. Through causes and conditions dharmas cease. To contemplate the Tathāgata in this way is to put delusion behind one for good.” Each author expounds one of these meanings. How do they conflict?

Scriptural confirmation through the three paths
BDK 19 ↗He is advancing toward the Buddha wisdom

Again, as a sūtra puts it:

  1. “Through the paths of subduing, the mind that initiates activity ceases.

  2. Through the path of cutting off dharmas, the mind that depends on the fundamental mind ceases.

  3. Through the path of decisive uprooting, the fundamental mind is exhausted.”

↥ The terms correspond as follows.

  1. The “paths of subduing” are the thirty stages of mind. “The mind that initiates activity ceases” corresponds to the relinquishing of coarse discriminative attachment in this treatise.ᵀ This concerns the characteristic of change.

    coarse discriminative attachment · 麁分別執著相 cū fēn bié zhí zhuó xiàng · BDK p. 18 rudimentary attachments derived from unwarranted speculation

  2. The path of cutting off dharmas occurs at the dharmakāya stage. “The mind that depends on the fundamental mind ceases” corresponds to relinquishing discrimination and the characteristic of coarse thought. This concerns the characteristic of abiding.

  3. The path of decisive uprooting is the unobstructed vajra-like path. “The fundamental mind is exhausted” corresponds to becoming free of subtle thought here. This concerns the characteristic of arising.

↥ From “Therefore,” the treatise cites a sūtra in support.

BDK p. 20

The four characteristics of a thought

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 20 Though it is said that there is [an inception of] the rising of [deluded) thoughts in the mind, there is no inception as such that can be known [as being independent of the essence of Mind]. And yet to say that the inception [of the rising of deluded thoughts] is known means that it is known as [existing on the ground of] that which is beyond thoughts [i.e., the essence of Mind]. Accordingly, all ordinary people are said not to be enlightened because they have had a continuous stream of [deluded] thoughts and have never been freed from their thoughts; therefore, they are said to be in a beginningless ignorance.

If a person gains [insight into] that which is free from thoughts, then he knows how those [thoughts] that characterize the mind [i.e., deluded thoughts] arise, abide, change, and cease to be, for he is identical with that which is free from thoughts. But, in reality, no difference exists in the process of the actualization of enlightenment, because the four states [of rising, abiding, etc.] exist simultaneously and each of them is not self-existent; they are originally of one and the same enlightenment [in that they are taking place on the ground of original enlightenment, as its phenomenal aspects].

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

1. Inceptive awakening in detail

1. Inceptive awakening in detail

1.3. Acquired and original awakening are undivided

BDK 20 ↗There is no inception as such that can be known

The passage beginning “Again, as for the arising of mind” is the third part. It explains in general why inceptive awakening does not differ from original awakening. It has two divisions.

  1. A further account of the characteristic of ultimate awakening. ↓

  2. A direct explanation of its lack of difference from original awakening. ↓

1.3.1. Ultimate awakening

↥ The first division has three steps.

  1. It describes ultimate awakening directly. ↓

  2. It brings out what awakening is by pointing to what falls short of it. ↓

  3. It shows the fullness of wisdom by considering what wisdom knows. ↓

1.3.1.1. Its characteristic

↥ In the first step, “Again, as for the arising of mind” takes up the earlier words “awakens to the mind’s first arising.” Awakening does not mean discerning an initial characteristic as something that exists. Hence “there is no initial characteristic to be known.” Nevertheless the text speaks of awakening to the mind’s first arising. It is like finding one’s bearings and recognizing that what one took for west is east. In just this way, when a tathāgata awakens to mind, he knows that the very first stirring has been quiescent all along. Hence “this is what is meant by freedom from thought.”

1.3.1.2. What falls short of awakening
BDK 20 ↗Accordingly, all ordinary people are said not to be enlightened

The passage from “therefore” brings out the point by showing its converse. As explained above, freedom from thought is awakening. Thus where there is thought one cannot speak of awakening. Among all beings up to and including the vajra mind, none has yet left behind the thought of beginningless ignorance. In this respect they cannot be called awakened. The earlier passage distinguished the dreams of the four characteristics, and so spoke of gradual awakening. The present passage considers the sleep of ignorance that is the same in them all. Hence “nonawakening.” As the Sūtra for Humane Kings says, “From the acceptance attained through subduing up to the summit samādhi, one illuminates ultimate truth. This is not called seeing. What is called seeing is omniscience.”

1.3.1.3. What fully awakened wisdom knows
BDK 20 ↗Then he knows how those thoughts arise, abide, change, and cease

From “if one attains,” the objects known reveal the range of wisdom. When one reaches the source of mind and attains freedom from thought, one knows comprehensively the four distinct characteristics through which the One Mind of every being moves. Hence “one knows mind’s characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.”ᵀ

arising, abiding, change, and cessation · 生住異滅 shēng zhù yì miè · BDK p. 20 arise, abide, change, and cease to be
BDK 20 ↗For he is identical with that which is free from thoughts

“Because [all] are equal in freedom from thought” gives the reason for this statement. A difficulty may arise here. A buddha has attained freedom from thought, whereas sentient beings have thoughts. Given this divide between absence and presence, how can one who is free of thought know those who have thoughts? The text dispels the doubt as follows. Sentient beings have thoughts, yet are originally free of thought. One who attains freedom from thought is in this respect their equal. Hence “because [all] are equal in freedom from thought.” Having realized this common freedom from thought, one can fully know the four characteristics of their thoughts.

1.3.2. Why inceptive awakening is undivided from original awakening
BDK 20 ↗No difference exists in the process of the actualization of enlightenment

The second division now directly explains the absence of any difference. One speaks of first attaining awakening free of thought, yet what one awakens to is that the four characteristics have never arisen. In relation to what nonawakening, then, could there be an inceptive awakening? Hence “in truth, there is no distinct inceptive awakening.”

BDK 20 ↗The four states exist simultaneously

The following words explain why. All four characteristics exist together, constituted by mind. Apart from the One Mind, none has a separate being of its own. Hence “they exist simultaneously and none stands on its own.” Since none stands on its own, they are “originally equal,” one and the same original awakening.

1. Awakening

1.2. Detailed explanation of the two awakenings

1.2.1. Inceptive awakening
1.2.1.2. The four degrees of awakening

1. Awakening › 2. Detailed explanation of the two awakenings › 1. Inceptive awakening › 2. The four degrees of awakening › 2. Explanation of the treatise’s wording

1.2.1.2.2.2. Why inceptive and original awakening do not differ
BDK 20 ↗Though it is said that there is … the rising … in the mind

From “Again, as for the arising of mind,” the second part explains how inceptive awakening is no different from original awakening. This too has two parts. First, the preceding expression occasions a closer examination of the extent of inceptive awakening. ↓

BDK 20 ↗In reality, no difference exists

From “But in reality there is no …,” the treatise directly explains the absence of any difference. ↓

1.2.1.2.2.2.1. The extent of inceptive awakening
BDK 20 ↗All ordinary people are said not to be enlightened

“No sentient beings are called awakened.” All beings up to and including the vajra-like stage have long slept in ignorance, never once parted from it. In this sense they cannot be called awake. Only permanent freedom from sleep merits the name. Considered in relation to the distinctions among the four characteristics, there is a gradual awakening, as explained above. Here, considered in relation to the undifferentiated sleep of ignorance, all are unawakened.⁕ As the Sūtra for Humane Kings says, “From acceptance through subduing up to the stage of equal awakening, one illuminates ultimate truth, yet this is not called seeing. What is called seeing belongs only to the Buddha Tathāgata.”

BDK 20 ↗How those … thoughts … arise, abide, change, and cease

“If one attains freedom from thought, one knows the characteristics of mind—arising, abiding, change, and cessation.”ᵀ Before attaining freedom from thought, one cannot know comprehensively that all characteristics of mind are dreams. Hence one cannot be called awake. A Buddha has attained freedom from thought and can therefore know fully how all sentient beings sleep in ignorance and dream the four characteristics. Only then can one be called awake.

freedom from thought · 無念 wú niàn · BDK p. 19 that which is beyond thoughts
arising, abiding, change, and cessation · 生住異滅 shēng zhù yì miè · BDK p. 20 arise, abide, change, and cease to be
BDK 20 ↗For he is identical with that which is free from thoughts

“Because of equality in freedom from thought” establishes the foregoing point. There is a tacit objection: “A Buddha has attained freedom from thought, while sentient beings have thoughts. Given this separation, how can one’s own freedom from thought yield knowledge of the thoughts of others?” It is because the nature of every one of their thoughts has been free of thought from the beginning.ᵀ The freedom from thought that a Buddha attains is equal to theirs, without duality. Hence “because of equality in freedom from thought.” Having attained this equality in freedom from thought, a Buddha can know thoughts comprehensively.

free of thought · 無念 wú niàn · BDK p. 19 that which is beyond thoughts
1.2.1.2.2.2.2. The absence of any difference
BDK 20 ↗No difference exists in the process of the actualization of enlightenment

The text now directly establishes that there is no difference. We speak of inceptive awakening only when freedom from thought is first attained. Yet one awakens to the fact that the four characteristics never arose in the first place. What nonawakening could one find in relation to which there would be an inceptive awakening? Hence “in reality, inceptive awakening has no distinction [of its own].”

BDK 20 ↗The four states … exist simultaneously

How is there no distinction? In the order of their arising, the four characteristics have a before and after, yet from the beginning they have depended on each other simultaneously. Moreover, mind constitutes all four. Apart from mind they have no distinct substance of their own. Hence “the four characteristics exist simultaneously, and none stands on its own.”ᵀ When seawater moves, we speak of waves. A wave has no substance of its own, so there is no movement belonging to the wave itself. Water has substance, so there is a movement of the water. Mind stands in the same relation to the four characteristics.

none stands on its own · 無自立 wú zì lì · BDK p. 20 not self-existent

↥ To make this point, the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says, “Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not wander through saṃsāra, do not experience pleasure and pain, and are not the cause of nirvāṇa. It is the tathāgatagarbha that experiences pleasure and pain and, together with its causes, arises or ceases.”

↥ The Śrīmālādevī Sūtra likewise says, “Take the six consciousnesses and the cognitive mental factor. Momentary as they are, these seven dharmas do not sow the various sufferings.ᵀ They cannot become disenchanted with suffering or desire to seek nirvāṇa. Blessed One, the tathāgatagarbha has no discernible beginning and is a dharma that neither arises nor ceases. It sows the various sufferings and can become disenchanted with suffering and desire to seek nirvāṇa.” Again, “Birth and death are two dharmas. It is by worldly convention that birth and death are predicated of the tathāgatagarbha. Birth and death are not dharmas inherent in the tathāgatagarbha.”

sufferings · 苦 kǔ · Skt. duḥkha · BDK p. 24 anxiety (duḥkha)

↥ Both sūtras make the same point. It is the very tathāgatagarbha that wanders in birth and death. Birth and death are fundamentally without substance of their own. Lacking any substance of their own, they have no separate movement through saṃsāra. If the characteristics themselves undergo no such movement, how could the underlying reality be moved? Hence the statement that birth and death do not belong to the tathāgatagarbha. For this reason the four characteristics are One Mind alone. Nonawakening is itself identical with original awakening. Hence “from the beginning they are equal, one and the same awakening.”

BDK pp. 20–21

Purified wisdom and inconceivable activity

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 20 And, again, original enlightenment, when analyzed in relation to the defiled state [in the phenomenal order], presents itself as having two attributes.⁕ One is the “purity of wisdom” and the other is the “suprarational functions.”

p. 20–21 By virtue of the permeation (vāsanā, perfuming) of the influence of Dharma [i.e., the essence of Mind or original enlightenment], a person comes to truly discipline himself and fulfills all expedient means [of unfolding enlightenment]; as a result, he breaks through the compound consciousness (i.e., the storehouse consciousness that contains both enlightenment and nonenlightenment), puts an end to the manifestation of the stream of [deluded] mind, and manifests the dharmakāya (i.e., the essence of Mind), for his wisdom (prajñā) becomes genuine and pure.

What is the meaning of this? All modes (lakṣana) of mind and consciousness [under the state of nonenlightenment] are [the products of] ignorance. Ignorance does not exist apart from enlightenment; therefore, it cannot be destroyed [because one cannot destroy something that does not really exist], and yet it cannot not be destroyed [insofar as it remains].

This is like the relationship that exists between the water of the ocean (i.e., enlightenment) and its waves (i.e., modes of mind) stirred by the wind (i.e., ignorance). Water and wind are inseparable; but water is not mobile by nature, and if the wind stops the movement ceases. But the wet nature remains undestroyed. Likewise, a person’s Mind, pure in its own nature, is stirred by the wind of ignorance. Both Mind and ignorance have no particular forms of their own and they are inseparable. Yet Mind is not mobile by nature, and if ignorance ceases, then the continuity [of deluded activities] ceases. But the essential nature of wisdom (i.e., the essence of Mind, like the wet nature of the water) remains undestroyed.

[He who has fully uncovered the original enlightenment] is capable of creating all manner of excellent conditions because his wisdom is pure. The manifestation of his numberless excellent qualities is incessant; accommodating himself to the capacity of other people he responds spontaneously, reveals himself in manifold ways, and benefits them.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. Original awakening in detail

BDK 20 ↗Original enlightenment analyzed in relation to the defiled state

The passage from “furthermore” treats original awakening in detail. It has two divisions.

  1. Original awakening as it follows defilement. ↓

  2. Original awakening as pure by nature. ↓

2.1. As it follows defilement

↥ The first division has three steps.

  1. A general statement. ↓

  2. The names. ↓

  3. An explanation of the characteristics. ↓

2.1.1. General statement

↥ In the general statement, “[it] gives rise to two characteristics.” The two belong to the aspect in which awakening follows the movement of mind. Hence “gives rise.” Neither is separable from original awakening in its intrinsic purity. Hence “they never part from it.”

2.1.2. Names of the two characteristics
BDK 20 ↗Purity of wisdom and suprarational functions

In the second step, naming the two, “the characteristic of purified wisdom” describes original awakening as it follows defilement.ᵀ ↓ “The characteristic of inconceivable activity” describes the activity of this original awakening when it returns to purity.ᵀ ↓

2.1.3. The characteristics explained
1. Purified wisdom

↥ In the third step the text explains purified wisdom first. Its explanation has three parts.ᵀ

purified wisdom · 智淨相 zhì jìng xiàng · BDK p. 20 purity of wisdom

  1. The teaching itself. ↓

1.1. The teaching

↥ The teaching itself has two parts.

  1. A direct statement. ↓

  2. A further explanation. ↓

1.1.1. Direct statement
BDK 20–21 ↗By virtue of the permeation of the influence of Dharma

In the direct statement, “perfuming by the power of Dharma” is the power with which suchness conditions the mind from within. By virtue of this perfuming one cultivates the requisites for awakening and can undertake “practice in accordance with reality” on the bodhisattva grounds.ᵀ

practice in accordance with reality · 如實修行 rú shí xiū xíng · BDK p. 21 truly discipline himself
BDK 21 ↗Fulfills all expedient means

At the Stainless Ground one “completes the skillful means.”

BDK 21 ↗Breaks through the compound consciousness

One can thereby “break through” the characteristic of arising and cessation within “the compound consciousness” and reveal its nature, which neither arises nor ceases.ᵀ Hence “breaking through the characteristic of compound consciousness, one manifests the dharmakāya.”

arising and cessation · 生滅 shēng miè · BDK p. 16 birth and death (samsara) Hakeda adds “(samsara)” when translating this passage.
BDK 21 ↗Puts an end to the manifestation of the stream of mind

At this point one can “extinguish” the characteristics of activity and turning within “the continuing mind.”ᵀ The mind of original awakening as it follows defilement can then return to its source and become utterly pure wisdom. Hence “extinguishing the characteristic of the continuing mind” and “wisdom is utterly pure.”ᵀ

continuing mind · 相續心 xiāng xù xīn · BDK p. 21 stream of [deluded] mind
wisdom is utterly pure · 智淳淨 zhì chún jìng · BDK p. 21 his wisdom (prajñā) becomes genuine and pure

↥ Here “continuing consciousness” is the very mind that arises and ceases within compound consciousness.ᵀ The text speaks of breaking through compound consciousness with a view to revealing the Dharma [body]. It speaks of extinguishing the characteristic of continuing consciousness with a view to perfecting the pure wisdom of the response body. What ceases is the characteristic of the continuing mind. The continuing mind itself does not cease. As the sūtra says, “Therefore, Mahāmati, the individual characteristic of the consciousnesses ceases. By the cessation of their individual characteristic is meant the cessation of the characteristic of activity. If the individual characteristic itself ceased, this would amount to the speculative annihilationism of the non-Buddhist schools. Those schools say, ‘Once objects are left behind, continuing consciousness ceases. Once it ceases, all the consciousnesses cease.’ Mahāmati, if continuing consciousness ceased, the consciousnesses should already have ceased in the beginningless past.” The sūtra continues at length.

continuing consciousness · 相續識 xiāng xù shí · BDK p. 28 continuing mind On p. 27 this is the fifth mode of mind. In discussing purity of wisdom, Wŏnhyo uses the same Chinese name more broadly for the stream of mind that arises and ceases.
1.1.2. What ceases and what remains
BDK 21 ↗What is the meaning of this?

The passage from “What does this mean?” further explains what was said above to cease and what does not cease.

BDK 21 ↗All modes of mind and consciousness are products of ignorance

“All the characteristics of mind and consciousness are ignorance” refers to the characteristics of the activating consciousness, the evolving consciousness, and the rest.ᵀ Ignorance gives rise to them, and they are all nonawakening. Hence the text calls them all ignorance. These characteristics of nonawakening in the consciousnesses are inseparable from the nature of original awakening as it follows defilement. Hence “inseparable from the nature of awakening.”ᵀ

characteristics of mind and consciousness · 心識之相 xīn shí zhī xiàng · BDK p. 21 modes (lakṣana) of mind and consciousness
nature of awakening · 覺性 jué xìng · BDK p. 21 enlightenment
BDK 21 ↗It cannot be destroyed, and yet it cannot not be destroyed

This characteristic of ignorance and the nature of original awakening are neither one nor different. Insofar as they are not different, ignorance cannot be destroyed. Insofar as they are not one, it is not indestructible. From the standpoint of non-difference and indestructibility, one says that when ignorance turns about, it becomes illumination. From the standpoint of non-identity and destructibility, one says that ignorance ceases while the nature of awakening remains intact. The present passage adopts the standpoint of non-identity. Thus it speaks of extinguishing the characteristic of the continuing mind.

1.2. Simile of water and wind
BDK 21 ↗Water is not mobile by nature

In the simile, “water does not move by nature” means that its present movement is not intrinsic. It moves under another’s influence. If it moved by its own nature, then, when the characteristic of movement ceased, its wetness too would cease.ᵀ Because something else makes it move, its characteristic of movement can cease and its wetness remain intact.

characteristic of movement · 動相 dòng xiàng · BDK p. 21 movement
1.3. Application of the simile
BDK 21 ↗If ignorance ceases, then the continuity ceases

In the application, “ignorance ceases” means that fundamental ignorance ceases. It corresponds to the wind dropping. “Continuity then ceases” means that the activating consciousness and the rest cease. It corresponds to the movement subsiding.

BDK 21 ↗The essential nature of wisdom remains undestroyed

“The nature of wisdom remains intact.” The inherently illuminating discernment of original awakening as it follows defilement is called the nature of wisdom.ᵀ It corresponds to wetness remaining intact.

nature of wisdom · 智性 zhì xìng · BDK p. 21 essential nature of wisdom
2. Inconceivable activity
BDK 21 ↗Suprarational functions

In the explanation of inconceivable activity that follows, “by virtue of purified wisdom” refers to the mind of original awakening as it follows defilement, discussed above.ᵀ When it first becomes utterly pure, this is the wisdom of inceptive awakening. Through the power of that wisdom the bodies of response and transformation appear. Hence “manifestations of immeasurable virtues.”ᵀ

inconceivable activity · 不思議業相 bù sī yì yè xiàng · BDK p. 20 suprarational functions
virtues · 功德 gōng dé · Skt. guṇa · BDK p. 21 excellent qualities
BDK 21 ↗The manifestation of his numberless excellent qualities is incessant

What thus appears has neither beginning nor end and continues without interruption. Hence “incessant.” As the Golden Drum Sūtra says, “The response body continues unbroken from beginningless saṃsāra. The qualities unique to all buddhas sustain it. Sentient beings are inexhaustible and its activity is likewise inexhaustible. Hence it is called ever-abiding.”

↥ The Treatise on the Jewel Lineage says, “What is the accomplishment of benefit for oneself? What is the accomplishment of benefit for others? Having accomplished one’s own benefit, one spontaneously relies on those two buddha bodies, from the beginningless past, to display sovereign activity in the world. This is called accomplishing benefit for others.”

How can benefit for others be beginningless?

↥ Question. Only after first accomplishing benefit for oneself does one begin to act for others. How, then, can one speak of activity for others as beginningless?

↥ Answer. In a single thought-moment a tathāgata responds throughout past, present, and future. Since those to whom he responds are beginningless, his response is beginningless. Likewise, perfect wisdom in a single thought-moment comprehends the boundless objects of all three times. Because its objects are boundless, wisdom too is boundless. The manifestations of boundless wisdom can therefore be both beginningless and endless. No calculation by discriminating consciousness can fathom this. Hence “inconceivable activity.”ᵀ

1.2.2.1.1. Purified wisdom
Purification of conjoined consciousness
BDK 21 ↗Fulfills all expedient means

“Completing the skillful means” occurs at the stainless ground.

BDK 21 ↗Breaks through the compound consciousness

“Breaks through the characteristics of the conjoined consciousness.”ᵀ When what neither arises nor ceases is joined to what arises and ceases, this is called the conjoined consciousness. Now one breaks through the characteristic of arising and ceasing with which it was joined. Freed from that characteristic, the essence that neither arises nor ceases becomes manifest. Hence the ensuing words about “making the dharmakāya manifest.” This is original awakening.⁕

conjoined consciousness · 和合識 hé hé shí · BDK p. 21 compound consciousness
BDK 21 ↗Puts an end to the manifestation of the stream of … mind

“The characteristic of the continuing mind.”ᵀ This mind is still the ālayavijñāna. When it includes both arising-and-ceasing and what neither arises nor ceases, it is called the conjoined consciousness, bringing out the original awakening of the dharmakāya. When one singles out its own characteristic within the aspect of arising and ceasing, it is called the continuing mind, bringing out the inceptive awakening of the response body. Its characteristic [here to be ended] is the characteristic of activity. What ceases is only the characteristic of the continuing mind. The continuing mind itself does not cease. When that characteristic ceases, the continuing mind is forever free of the characteristics of consciousness. It is transformed into consummate wisdom. Hence “because wisdom is pure.” This is the sense of inceptive awakening as it pertains to the response body. Yet this inceptive awakening has no separate inception. It is the very essence of original awakening that conforms to defilement and takes on defilement. Now, out of those conditions of defilement, it regains its purity. This alone is called inceptive awakening. Thus “inceptive awakening” means original awakening insofar as it accords with conditions.

continuing mind · 相續心 xiāng xù xīn · BDK p. 21 stream of [deluded] mind

The water and wind simile
BDK 21 ↗The water-and-wind simile

In the simile: ↓

BDK 21 ↗Water is not mobile by nature

“Water is not by nature in motion.” Although it is not still at present, its motion does not come from its own nature. It moves only in response to something else. Mind is likewise moved by conditions. Its own nature does not account for its movement. Hence “not by nature in motion.”

Applying the simile to mind
BDK 21 ↗If ignorance ceases, then the continuity … ceases

“When ignorance ceases, the continuity ceases.” It is the characteristic of continuity that ceases.

BDK 21 ↗The essential nature of wisdom … remains undestroyed

“The nature of wisdom is undestroyed.”ᵀ The essence of the continuing mind continues without ceasing. This is its own characteristic. Its innate capacity for knowing is called the nature of wisdom.

nature of wisdom · 智性 zhì xìng · BDK p. 21 essential nature of wisdom
BDK pp. 21–22

The four mirrors

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 21 The characteristics of the essence of enlightenment have four great significances that are identical with those of empty space p. 21–22 or that are analogous to those of a bright mirror.

First, [the essence of enlightenment is like] a mirror that is really empty [of images]. It is free from all marks of objects of the mind and it has nothing to reveal in itself, for it does not reflect any images.

Second, [it is, as it were] a mirror, influencing (vāsanā) [all human beings to advance toward enlightenment], serving as the primary cause [of their attaining enlightenment]. That is to say, it is truly nonempty; appearing in it are all the objects of the world which neither go out nor come in; which are neither lost nor destroyed. It is eternally abiding One Mind. [All things appear in it] because all things are real. And none of the defiled things are able to defile it, for the essence of wisdom (i.e., original enlightenment) is unaffected [by defilements], being furnished with an unsoiled quality and influencing all human beings [to advance toward enlightenment].

Third, [it is like] a mirror that is free from [defiled] objects [reflected in it]. This can be said because the nonempty state [of original enlightenment] is genuine, pure, and bright, being free from hindrances both affectional and intellectual, and transcending characteristics of that which is compounded (i.e., the storehouse consciousness).

Fourth, [it is like] a mirror influencing [a person to cultivate his capacity for goodness], serving as a coordinating cause [to encourage him in his endeavors]. Because [the essence of enlightenment] is free from [defiled] objects, it universally illumines the mind of a human being and induces him to cultivate his capacity for goodness, presenting itself in accordance with his desires [as a mirror presents his appearance].

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. Original awakening in detail

2. Original awakening in detail

2.2. As intrinsically pure

BDK 21 ↗The characteristics of the essence of enlightenment

From “furthermore,” the text next explains the characteristics of original awakening in its intrinsic purity. It has two divisions.

  1. A general statement. ↓

  2. A separate explanation of each characteristic. ↓

2.2.1. General comparison with space and a mirror
BDK 21 ↗Identical with empty space or analogous to a bright mirror

In the general statement, “equal to space” means that it pervades everywhere. “Like a clean mirror” means that it is free of stains and shows reflections.ᵀ Of the four meanings, the first and third use freedom from stains to draw the comparison with a clean mirror. The second and fourth draw on its capacity to show images, which also implies purity.

clean mirror · 淨鏡 jìng jìng · BDK p. 21–22 bright mirror
2.2.2. The four mirrors explained

↥ The detailed explanation sets out the four separately. The first two concern the nature present as cause, the last two the stage of fruition.

BDK 22 ↗The first and second mirrors

The first two explain emptiness and wisdom. As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says, “Buddha-nature is emptiness in the ultimate sense. Emptiness in the ultimate sense is called wisdom. The wise see both emptiness and nonemptiness. Fools see neither emptiness nor nonemptiness.” The sūtra continues at length.ᵀ

nonemptiness · 不空 bù kōng · Skt. aśūnya (nonempty) · BDK p. 15 nonempty
1. Mirror of true emptiness

↥ In the first mirror, “free of all the characteristics of objects of mind” brings out the sūtra’s emptiness in the ultimate sense.ᵀ “There is no dharma to be reflected. Here awakening does not mean illumination” explains “do not see emptiness and nonemptiness.”

characteristics of objects of mind · 心境界相 xīn jìng jiè xiàng · BDK p. 22 marks of objects of the mind
2. Mirror of perfuming as cause
BDK 22 ↗Appearing in it are all the objects of the world

In the second, “all the objects in the world appear in it” explains the sūtra’s statement that the wise see both emptiness and nonemptiness. For that sūtra says, “What is empty is the whole of saṃsāra. What is nonempty is great nirvāṇa.” Here only the objects of saṃsāra are shown. Since they appear in the mirror, “they do not go out.” Since they do not stain the mirror, “they do not enter.”

BDK 22 ↗Neither lost nor destroyed

Whatever images appear have the same extent as original awakening. They equal the whole of space and extend throughout the three times. Thus they do not slip away from moment to moment or perish through extinction. Hence “neither lost nor destroyed, ever abiding in the One Mind,” and so forth.

BDK 22 ↗Influencing as the primary cause

The preceding lines explain the clean mirror. The passage from “furthermore, all” explains “perfuming as cause.”ᵀ

perfuming as cause · 因熏習 yīn xūn xí · BDK p. 22 serving as the primary cause Hakeda also renders 熏習 as “influencing” in this mirror simile.
3. Mirror of the Dharma freed from obstructions
BDK 22 ↗Free from hindrances both affectional and intellectual

In the third mirror, “emerges from both obstructions, wholly pure and clear” concerns the mirror of perfuming as cause just discussed. When it emerges from the bonds of affliction, it is the dharmakāya.

4. Mirror of perfuming as condition
BDK 22 ↗Universally illumines the mind of a human being

In the fourth mirror, “because the Dharma has emerged free, it illuminates the minds of beings everywhere.”ᵀ When original awakening becomes manifest, it illuminates the capacities of beings equally and displays myriad transformations. Hence “[it] manifests in accord with their thoughts.”ᵀ

the Dharma has emerged free · 法出離 fǎ chū lí · BDK p. 22 [the essence of enlightenment] is free from [defiled] objects
manifests in accord with their thoughts · 隨念示現 suí niàn shì xiàn · BDK p. 22 presenting itself in accordance with his desires
Comparison with inconceivable activity
BDK 22 ↗Presenting itself in accordance with his desires

How does this differ from the inconceivable activity explained earlier? That passage explains the activity of inceptive awakening in the response body. This one explains the functioning of original awakening as the dharmakāya. Every single transformation has both meanings. Within this general account a further distinction can be made.

  1. Considered as brought forth by inceptive awakening, the benefit a being receives follows conditions and particular connections. Its root is original awakening as it follows defilement, and the connections it has had all along vary in intimacy.

  2. Considered as manifested by original awakening, it benefits all whose capacities have matured, regardless of any particular connection. Original awakening has always been pure by nature and extends equally to all, without dividing them into near and distant.
