1.2.2. Original awakening
BDK 21 ↗The characteristics of the essence of enlightenment

The second division, from “Again, the essence and characteristics of awakening,” explains the essence and characteristics of original awakening.ᵀ ↓ Its characteristics are of four kinds.

essence and characteristics of awakening · 覺體相 jué tǐ xiàng · BDK p. 21 characteristics of the essence of enlightenment
1.2.2.2. Its essence and characteristics — the four mirrors

↥ From “Again” the second division explains the essence and characteristics of original awakening. Of the four mirrors, take the second. ↓

1.2.2.2.2. The mirror that perfumes as cause
BDK 22 ↗A mirror … serving as the primary cause

“Perfuming as cause.”ᵀ The qualities inherent in this nature act as the direct cause, perfuming sentient beings’ minds. They can give rise to disenchantment with saṃsāra, aspiration for nirvāṇa, and the various preparatory practices, all the way to the fruit of Buddhahood. Hence “perfuming as cause.” All dharmas without exception appear in it. Hence it is called a mirror. As the Flower Garland Sūtra says, “The deep, vast ocean holds a wealth of jewels that can never be exhausted. There the images of the forms of every kind of being appear. Deep is the ocean of causes and conditions. Inexhaustible are its jewels of excellent qualities. In the pure dharmakāya there is no image that fails to appear.” This is precisely the point here.

Perfuming as cause · 因熏習 yīn xūn xí · BDK p. 22 serving as the primary cause Hakeda also renders 熏習 as “influencing” in this mirror simile.
1.2.2.2.4. The mirror that perfumes as condition
BDK 22 ↗A mirror … serving as a coordinating cause

In the fourth, “perfuming as condition,” consummate wisdom newly arises and acts as a dominant condition.ᵀ It perfumes the minds of sentient beings, causing disenchantment, aspiration, and the preparatory practices to arise, all the way to the fruit of Buddhahood. Hence “perfuming as condition.” The qualities of all these practices are inseparable from consummate wisdom. They are reflections of that wisdom, hence the designation “mirror.”⁕ As the Buddha Ground Sūtra says, “The wisdom of the great perfect mirror can give rise to the reflections of all the skillful dharmas of sentient beings.” That is what is meant.

perfuming as condition · 緣熏習 yuán xūn xí · BDK p. 22 serving as a coordinating cause Hakeda also renders 熏習 as “influencing” in this mirror simile.

BDK p. 23

Nonawakening

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 23 Because of not truly realizing oneness with suchness, there emerges an unenlightened mind and, consequently, its thoughts. These thoughts do not have any validity to be substantiated; therefore, they are not independent of the original enlightenment.

It is like the case of a man who has lost his way: he is confused because of [his wrong sense of] direction. If he is freed from [the notion of] direction altogether, then there will be no such thing as going astray. It is the same with human beings: because of [the notion of] enlightenment, they are confused. But if they are freed from [the fixed notion of] enlightenment, then there will be no such thing as nonenlightenment. Because [there are people] of unenlightened, deluded mind, for them we speak of true enlightenment, knowing well what this [relative] term stands for. Independent of the unenlightened mind, there are no independent marks of true enlightenment itself that can be discussed.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

Nonawakening

BDK 23 ↗The aspect of nonenlightenment

The explanation of nonawakening has three parts.

  1. Fundamental nonawakening. ↓

  2. Derivative nonawakening. ↓

  3. A conclusion bringing together fundamental and derivative nonawakening. ↓

1. Fundamental nonawakening

↥ The first part itself has two divisions.

  1. Nonawakening is established in dependence on original awakening. ↓

  2. Original awakening in turn depends on nonawakening. ↓

1.1. Nonawakening depends on original awakening

↥ The first division has three steps.

  1. The teaching itself. ↓

  2. The simile. ↓

  3. Its application. ↓

1.1.1. Teaching

↥ In the teaching, “because one does not know in accordance with reality that the dharma of suchness is one” is fundamental ignorance. It is like losing one’s bearings.ᵀ

the dharma of suchness is one · 真如法一 zhēn rú fǎ yī · BDK p. 23 oneness with suchness
BDK 23 ↗There emerges an unenlightened mind and, consequently, its thoughts

“Through nonawakening the mind arises and thoughts occur” is the stirring of thought that characterizes activity. It is like taking a direction wrongly. The west one mistakenly supposes to be there has no existence apart from the east that is actually there. Hence “thought has no characteristic of its own and is inseparable from original awakening.”ᵀ

1.2. Original awakening depends on nonawakening
BDK 23 ↗For them we speak of true enlightenment

The next division explains how original awakening in turn depends on nonawakening. There are two points.

1.2.1. The name “true awakening”

↥ “Because there is the deluded thinking mind of nonawakening” refers to the imaginative discrimination that ignorance gives rise to.ᵀ Through this imagining one “can understand names and meanings.” Speech is therefore possible and one can speak of true awakening.ᵀ In this sense the name “true awakening” depends on deluded imagining.

names and meanings · 名義 míng yì · BDK p. 23 what this [relative] term stands for

1.2.2. The awakening spoken of
BDK 23 ↗No independent marks of true enlightenment itself that can be discussed

“Apart from nonawakening, true awakening has no characteristic of its own that can be spoken of.” The true awakening spoken of necessarily depends on nonawakening. Without such a relation it has no characteristic of its own. What exists in dependence on another likewise has no characteristic of its own. In the absence of an own-characteristic, how could there be a characteristic belonging to another? This shows that no dharma can be apprehended.ᵀ As a later passage says, “Know that defiled and pure dharmas alike depend upon one another. None has a characteristic of its own of which one could speak.” The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says, “Were there even a hairbreadth of substantial reality in conventional truth, there would have to be substantial reality in ultimate truth as well.” This is the point.

BDK 23 ↗The aspect of nonenlightenment

The ensuing account of nonawakening has two parts.

  1. Fundamental nonawakening. ↓

  2. Derivative nonawakening, beginning with “Again.” ↓

2.1. Fundamental nonawakening

↥ The first part in turn establishes two points.

  1. Nonawakening is established in dependence on original awakening. ↓

  2. Original awakening exists in relation to nonawakening. ↓

2.1.1. Nonawakening depends on original awakening

↥ “Because one does not know in accordance with reality that the dharma of suchness is one, mind stirs in nonawakening.”ᵀ This is fundamental ignorance. It is like losing one’s bearings.

the dharma of suchness is one · 真如法一 zhēn rú fǎ yī · BDK p. 23 oneness with suchness
BDK 23 ↗Consequently, its thoughts

“And there is thought” means the stirring of thought in the characteristic of activity and the characteristics that follow. This is like a mistaken direction. Apart from the actual direction there is no separate mistaken one. The direction one misidentifies is the actual one. Hence “thought has no characteristic of its own and is inseparable from original awakening.”ᵀ

characteristic of its own · 自相 zì xiàng · Skt. svalakṣaṇa · BDK p. 23 independent marks
2.1.2. Original awakening is spoken of in relation to nonawakening

↥ The next passage explains in what sense original awakening depends on nonawakening. ↓

BDK 23 ↗Because [there are people] of unenlightened, deluded mind

“Nonawakening” again means ignorance.

↥ “Mind of delusive imaginings” means all the states of mind that arise from nonawakening and grasp at characteristics. The text names the root to bring in its offshoots.ᵀ

Mind of delusive imaginings · 妄想心 wàng xiǎng xīn · BDK p. 23 deluded mind
BDK 23 ↗True enlightenment, knowing well what this … term stands for

“Can know names and meanings, and so one speaks to them of true awakening.”ᵀ Only because the mind of delusive imaginings knows names and their meanings can there be speech that speaks of true awakening.ᵀ That is to say, the words by which one speaks of true awakening necessarily depend on the delusive imaginings that arise from nonawakening.

names and meanings · 名義 míng yì · BDK p. 23 what this [relative] term stands for
true awakening · 真覺 zhēn jué · BDK p. 23 true enlightenment
names and their meanings · 名義 míng yì · BDK p. 23 what this [relative] term stands for
BDK 23 ↗No independent marks of true enlightenment itself

“Apart from nonawakening there is no characteristic of true awakening itself of which one can speak.” This shows that true awakening, insofar as one speaks of it, necessarily presupposes nonawakening. Apart from this relation it has no characteristic of its own. What exists only in relation to another likewise lacks a characteristic of its own. If a characteristic of one’s own is absent, how could there be a characteristic belonging to another? This shows that no dharma can be apprehended. As the text says below, “Know that all defiled dharmas and all pure dharmas are mutually dependent. There is no characteristic of their own of which one can speak.” The Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise says, “If conventional truth had even a hair’s breadth of substantial reality, ultimate truth too would have to be substantially real.” This is what is meant.

BDK p. 24

Three subtle characteristics

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 24 Because of its nonenlightened state, [the deluded mind] produces three aspects which are bound to nonenlightenment and are inseparable from it.

First is the activity of ignorance. The agitation of mind because of its nonenlightened state is called activity. When enlightened, it is unagitated. When it is agitated, anxiety (duḥkha) follows, for the result (i.e., anxiety) is not independent of the cause (i.e., the agitation contingent upon ignorance).

Second is the perceiving subject. Because of the agitation [that breaks the original unity with suchness], there appears the perceiving subject. When unagitated, [the mind] is free from perceiving.

Third is the world of objects. Because of the perceiving subject, the world of objects erroneously appears. Apart from the perceiving, there will be no world of objects.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. Derivative nonawakening

BDK 24 ↗Three aspects inseparable from nonenlightenment

The detailed account of derivative nonawakening has two divisions.

  1. The subtle characteristics. ↓

  2. The coarse characteristics. ↓

2.1. The three subtle characteristics

↥ The first division in turn has two steps.

  1. A general statement. ↓

  2. A separate explanation of each characteristic. ↓

1. General statement
BDK 24 ↗Bound to nonenlightenment and inseparable from it

In the general statement, the three “are associated with that nonawakening and inseparable from it.” Root and branches depend on one another. Hence “associated.”ᵀ “Associated” here has a different sense from the association of mind and mental factors. This is precisely the defiled mind termed “unassociated.”ᵀ

defiled mind · 染心 rǎn xīn · BDK p. 29 defiled [state of] mind
2. Individual characteristics
2.1. Activity due to ignorance
BDK 24 ↗The activity of ignorance

In the separate explanations, the first is “the characteristic of activity due to ignorance.” The mind moves in dependence on ignorance. Hence “characteristic of activity.”ᵀ To stir into motion is what “activity” means. Thus the text calls the stirring of mind activity.ᵀ

characteristic of activity due to ignorance · 無明業相 wú míng yè xiàng · BDK p. 24 activity of ignorance
stirring of mind · 心動 xīn dòng · BDK p. 24 agitation of mind
BDK 24 ↗When enlightened, it is unagitated

“When awakened, it does not move” illustrates the point by considering the converse. On attaining inceptive awakening there is no stirring of thought. Thus we know that the present movement comes solely from nonawakening.

BDK 24 ↗When it is agitated, anxiety follows

“Where there is movement, there is suffering.” Just as attaining quiescence is supreme happiness, here movement itself is suffering.ᵀ

suffering · 苦 kǔ · Skt. duḥkha · BDK p. 24 anxiety (duḥkha)
BDK 24 ↗The result is not independent of the cause

The characteristic of activity is “no suffering,” ignorance “no origination.”⁕ Cause and result are present together. Hence “the result is inseparable from the cause.” Although thought moves at the characteristic of activity, it is so subtle that subject and object have yet to differentiate. The fundamental ignorance underlying it is the same in this respect.

↥ The Treatise on Nonperception asks, “What is the characteristic of this consciousness, and what is its object?⁕ Answer. Its characteristic and its object cannot be distinguished. They are one in substance, without differentiation. Question. In that case, how do we know it exists? Answer. We know this consciousness exists through what it does. It can give rise to all the workings of affliction, karma, and karmic result. Take ignorance, which is constantly arising. Can one distinguish that ignorance as one wishes? If one could distinguish it, it would not be called ignorance. If it cannot be distinguished, it would seem not to exist. Yet it does exist. One knows ignorance exists from such things as desire and aversion. Fundamental consciousness is like this also.” Passages like this reveal fundamental consciousness specifically in terms of its characteristic of activity.

2.2. The perceiver
BDK 24 ↗The perceiving subject

The second, “the characteristic of the perceiver,” is the characteristic of turning.ᵀ On the basis of the preceding characteristic of activity, consciousness turns and becomes that which apprehends. Hence “through movement it can see.” From the standpoint of its quiescent nature, there is no perceiver. Hence “without movement there is no seeing.”ᵀ The converse thus shows that the perceiver necessarily depends on movement. At this turning there is already that which apprehends, yet it cannot display the characteristic of an apprehended object. There is simply an orientation outward, without resting on any object. As the Compendium of the Great Vehicle says, “Mental consciousness apprehends the three times and objects outside the three times.”ᵀ One can thus understand why the object of this [fundamental] consciousness is called unknowable. It is called unknowable because no object is there to be known, just as the beginning of the twelve links of dependent arising is said to be unknowable. So it is here. This reveals fundamental consciousness in terms of its characteristic of turning.

characteristic of the perceiver · 能見相 néng jiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject
characteristic of turning · 轉相 zhuǎn xiàng · BDK p. 24 能見相 perceiving subject
perceiver · 能見 néng jiàn · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject
Mental consciousness · 意識 yì shí · Skt. manovijñāna · BDK p. 29 consciousness (vijñāna) The full Chinese compound specifies mental consciousness. Hakeda’s parenthesis gives the broader vijñāna.
2.3. The world of objects
BDK 24 ↗The world of objects

The third, “the characteristic of objects,” is the characteristic of manifestation.ᵀ The preceding turning makes the manifestation of objects possible. Hence “because there is a perceiver, objects appear delusively.” As the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says, “Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness. Stated fully, there are eight characteristics. What are the three? True consciousness, manifesting consciousness, and consciousness that discriminates objects.ᵀ Just as a clear mirror bears visible images, so it is with manifesting consciousness.” The same sūtra says further, “Take storehouse consciousness. All at once it discerns the body, the place in which the body dwells, and the objects it uses, all manifestations of one’s own mind.” Later this treatise says of manifesting consciousness, “It can make all objects appear. Just as a clear mirror shows visible images, so does manifesting consciousness. For at all times it arises spontaneously and is constantly present.” These passages reveal fundamental consciousness in terms of its characteristic of manifestation. Since even manifestation belongs to fundamental consciousness, how could turning and activity, from which it derives, be placed instead in the sixth and seventh consciousnesses?

characteristic of objects · 境界相 jìng jiè xiàng · BDK p. 24 world of objects
manifesting consciousness · 現識 xiàn shí · Skt. khyātivijñāna (in the Laṅkāvatāra parallel) · BDK p. 27 reproducing mind The third mode manifests the field of objects, as a mirror displays images.

2. Nonawakening

2.2. Derivative nonawakening

BDK 24 ↗[The deluded mind] produces three aspects

From “Again” the second part explains derivative nonawakening. The first three characteristics are subtle and still fall within the domain of ālayavijñāna. ↓ The six coarse characteristics that follow belong to the other seven consciousnesses.ᵀ ↓ In relation to fundamental ignorance, however, all are offshoots that it gives rise to. Hence their common designation “derivative nonawakening.”⁕

six coarse characteristics · 六麁相 liù cū xiàng · BDK p. 24 六種相 six aspects
2.2.1. The three subtle characteristics
1. The activity of ignorance
BDK 24 ↗The activity of ignorance

“The characteristic of the activity of ignorance” is the characteristic of activity to which ignorance gives rise.ᵀ To stir into motion is the meaning of “activity” here. Hence the “stirring of mind” is called the characteristic of activity.ᵀ

characteristic of the activity of ignorance · 無明業相 wú míng yè xiàng · BDK p. 24 activity of ignorance
stirring of mind · 心動 xīn dòng · BDK p. 24 agitation of mind
BDK 24 ↗When enlightened, it is unagitated

“In awakening there is no motion” explains the point from the opposite side. When one attains inceptive awakening, movement is gone forever. One can thus see that the present motion is due solely to nonawakening.

BDK 24 ↗When it is agitated, anxiety … follows

“With movement there is suffering.” Consider the attainment of quiescence. Quiescence is bliss, and so the text here calls movement itself suffering.

BDK 24 ↗The result … is not independent of the cause

“The result is inseparable from the cause.” Ignorance is “no origination.” The characteristic of activity is “no suffering.” “No suffering” and “no origination” are present at the same time and are inseparable.⁕ Although the characteristic of activity arises and ceases, it is exceedingly subtle. Subject and object have yet to differentiate. The same holds for ignorance.

↥ As the Treatise on the Absence of Perception puts it, “Question. What is the characteristic of this consciousness and what is its object?⁕ Answer. Its characteristic and its object cannot be distinguished. They are a single undifferentiated reality. Question. If so, how do we know this consciousness exists? Answer. We know it exists from its effects. This consciousness can give rise to all the afflictions, karma, and the events in which karmic results ripen. Consider ignorance, which continually arises. Can you distinguish this ignorance? If it could be distinguished, it would not be what we call ignorance. If it cannot be distinguished, one would expect it not to exist. And yet it does exist.⁕ It is from such effects as desire and anger that we know ignorance exists. The same applies to the fundamental consciousness.” The Abhidharma Treasury Sūtra says the same. Passages of this kind specifically concern the characteristic of activity.

2. The perceiver
BDK 24 ↗Second is the perceiving subject”; “Third is the world of objects

The second characteristic, that of the perceiver, is the seeing aspect of ālayavijñāna.ᵀ

that of the perceiver · 能見相 néng jiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject
3. The object

↥ The third, that of the object, is its appearance aspect.

Textual evidence for perceiver and object

↥ As the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “Take the storehouse consciousness: in one act it distinguishes the body manifest in its own mind, its dwelling, its means of support, and so on.” “Distinguishes in one act” is the characteristic of the perceiver.ᵀ “Its own mind manifests,” and what follows, is the characteristic of the object.ᵀ The Yogācārabhūmi says the same. Passages like these concern the latter two characteristics. Although these two comprise two aspects, they are inseparable from the characteristic of activity. This is the approach of “cognition alone.” Although the characteristic of activity has no [differentiated] subject and object, it comprises the two aspects. This is “the two alone.”⁕

characteristic of the perceiver · 能見相 néng jiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject
characteristic of the object · 境界相 jìng jiè xiàng · BDK p. 24 world of objects
All three belong to maturation consciousness

↥ All three belong to maturation consciousness. Considered simply as deluded by karma and affliction, no distinction is drawn between activity, the differences in its motion, and the characteristic of transformation and the rest.⁕ For this reason they are spoken of collectively as maturation consciousness. Considered as moved by the wind of ignorance, they differ in the way they move, from subtle to coarse. Hence the finer distinction into three characteristics.ᵀ Furthermore, these three are moved by ignorance alone, and so belong to the eighth consciousness. The subsequent six are stirred by objects, and so belong to the [other] seven consciousnesses. For just this reason, the seven consciousnesses are spoken of solely in terms of arising and ceasing. The ālayavijñāna, by contrast, comprises both aspects [arising-and-ceasing and what neither arises nor ceases].

three characteristics · 三種相 sān zhǒng xiàng · BDK p. 24 three aspects
BDK pp. 24–25

Six coarse characteristics

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 24 Conditioned by the [incorrectly conceived] world of objects, [the deluded mind] produces six aspects.

First is the aspect of the [discriminating] intellect. Depending on the [erroneously conceived] world of objects, the mind develops the discrimination between liking and disliking.

Second is the aspect of continuity. By virtue of [the discriminating function of] the intellect, the mind produces an awareness of pleasure and pain [with regard to things] in the world of objects. The mind, developing [deluded] thoughts and being bound to them, will continue uninterrupted.

Third is the aspect of attachment. Because of the continuity [of deluded thoughts], the mind, superimposing its deluded thoughts on the world of objects and holding fast to [the discriminations of liking and disliking] develops attachments [to what it likes].

p. 25 Fourth is the aspect of the speculation (vikalpa) on names and letters (i.e., concepts). On the basis of erroneous attachments, [the deluded mind) analyzes words which are provisional [and therefore devoid of validity].

Fifth is the aspect of giving rise to [evil] karma. Relying on names and letters (i.e., concepts that have no validity), [the deluded mind] investigates names and words and becomes attached to them, and creates manifold types of evil karma.

Sixth is the aspect of anxiety attached to the [effects of evil] karma. Because of the [law of] karma, the deluded mind suffers the effects and will not be free.

It should be understood that ignorance is able to produce all types of defiled states; all defiled states are aspects of nonenlightenment.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

Nonawakening

2. Derivative nonawakening

2. Derivative nonawakening

2.2. The six coarse characteristics
BDK 24 ↗Conditioned by the world of objects, the mind produces six aspects

From “because there is,” the text takes up the coarse characteristics. Here again there are two steps.

  1. A general statement. ↓

  2. A separate explanation of each characteristic. ↓

1. General statement

↥ The opening words, “because objects are present as conditions,” refer to the objects displayed by the manifesting consciousness described above. On the basis of these objects the six coarse characteristics arise within the seven consciousnesses. This explains the sūtra’s words, “Stirred by the wind of objects, the waves of the seven consciousnesses roll.”

2. Individual characteristics

↥ In the explanation that follows, the six are distributed as follows.

  • The first characteristic is the seventh consciousness. ↓

  • The next four belong to the actively arising consciousnesses. ↓

  • The last is the result they produce. ↓

2.1. Discriminating cognition
BDK 24 ↗The aspect of the discriminating intellect

First, “the characteristic of discrimination” is the seventh consciousness, the starting point of the coarse characteristics. Here for the first time the mental factor of discernment distinguishes self and sense object. Hence its name.ᵀ As the Śrīmālā Sūtra says, “As for these six consciousnesses and the mental factor of discernment, these seven dharmas do not abide for a moment.” Here “mental discernment” means discernment as a mental factor.

characteristic of discrimination · 智相 zhì xiàng · BDK p. 24 aspect of the [discriminating] intellect
BDK 24 ↗The discrimination between liking and disliking

In a fortunate destination of rebirth, it discriminates agreeable objects and imputes “I” and “mine.” In a bad destination it discriminates disagreeable objects and imputes “I” and “mine.” Hence “depending on objects, the mind arises and distinguishes what it likes from what it dislikes.” More precisely, it takes fundamental consciousness as its object and imputes “I.” It takes the objects manifested there and imputes “mine.” Here the text singles out what is coarser and more apparent. Hence “the mind arises dependent on objects.” Moreover, these objects are inseparable from manifesting consciousness, just as reflections are inseparable from a mirror’s surface. The seventh consciousness simply turns inward and imputes “I” and “mine.” It does not separately posit sense objects outside the mind. Thus other texts say that it takes that very consciousness as its object.

What objects does manas apprehend?
BDK 24 ↗Depending on the world of objects

Question. How do we know that seventh consciousness, manas, takes both consciousness and the six kinds of sense objects as its objects?ᵀ

six kinds of sense objects · 六塵 liù chén · BDK p. 29 objects of the five senses and of the mind

↥ Answer. There are two proofs.

  1. Inference. ↓

  2. Authoritative testimony. ↓

2.1.1. Proof by inference

↥ The inference runs as follows.

  • The thesis. The mind faculty necessarily has the same object as mental consciousness.

  • The reason. It is the support peculiar to that consciousness.

  • The statement of agreement. Whatever serves as a support peculiar to a consciousness necessarily shares the object of the consciousness it supports. The eye faculty and the other sense faculties are examples.

  • The statement of exclusion. If something can have a different object, it cannot be the peculiar support. An example is the mind faculty understood as the immediately preceding, just-ceased moment of cognition. Since this thesis, reason, and example are free of fault, we know that the mind faculty also takes the six kinds of sense objects as its objects.

↥ On this account, when the dependent mental consciousness takes the mind faculty as its object, that supporting faculty in turn faces itself. There is no fault in this, for cognition has a reflexive aspect. It also apprehends the mental factors associated with it, since nothing bars their apprehension. Mind and mental factors each cognize themselves directly. This does not preclude their having one and the same object. This reasoning cannot be extended to the five sensory consciousnesses. They arise dependent on material faculties and have a restricted range. Each encounters only its own kind of object, such as visible form.

2.1.2. Proof by authoritative testimony

↥ For authoritative testimony there is scriptural evidence.⁕ The Golden Drum Sūtra says, “The eye faculty receives visible form, the ear faculty distinguishes sound,” and so on, through “the mind faculty distinguishes all dharmas.” In the Mahāyāna the mind faculty is manas. Hence we know that it takes all dharmas as objects.

↥ Again, among its ten kinds of discrimination the Abhidharma Treatise says, “The first, discrimination of appearances, comprises the body, its dwelling place, and what it uses. These respectively take as their appearances the material faculties, the receptacle world, and objects such as visible forms. The second, discrimination in which appearances manifest, comprises the six groups of consciousness and manas. They apprehend appearances and make them manifest in the manner just stated.ᵀ Of these, the five sensory consciousnesses manifest only the five kinds of sensible object, beginning with form.ᵀ Mental consciousness and manas manifest the entire range, including the material faculties, the receptacle world, and objects such as visible forms.” If manas did not apprehend the material faculties, the receptacle world, and the rest, the discrimination that manifests them ought to comprise only the six consciousnesses. But the passage adds “and manas.” Hence we know that manas also apprehends them.

manas · 意 yì · Skt. manas · BDK p. 26 mind (manas) Wŏnhyo also discusses the Yogācāra usage in which manas designates the seventh consciousness.
five kinds of sensible object · 五塵 wǔ chén · BDK p. 27 objects of the five senses
1. Discriminating cognition

↥ Let us leave the digression there and return to the treatise.

2.2. Continuity
BDK 24 ↗The aspect of continuity

The second, “the characteristic of continuity,” is actively arising consciousness. The consciousness aggregate is coarse discrimination.ᵀ It constructs all dharmas conceptually, and thus continues at length. It also gives rise to craving and clinging, drawing forward and sustaining past karmic fabrications without interruption. It also nourishes rebirth and thereby enables future karmic results to continue. For these reasons it is called the characteristic of continuity. Its sense differs from that of the “continuing mind” discussed earlier.

characteristic of continuity · 相續相 xiāng xù xiàng · BDK p. 24 aspect of continuity
BDK 24 ↗By virtue of the discriminating function of the intellect

“Depending on discrimination” means that it arises with the preceding characteristic of discrimination as its faculty. The supporting faculty is subtle and has only neutral feeling. The consciousness that depends on it is coarse and can give rise to both pain and pleasure. Hence “gives rise to pain and pleasure.” Again, the discriminating faculty on which it depends abides apprehending inwardly and does not posit external sense objects. It resembles sleep. Continuing consciousness, by contrast, imputes both inner and outer. It discriminates through directed thought and evaluation, as though one had woken up.

BDK 24 ↗The mind, developing thoughts, will continue uninterrupted

Hence “the waking mind gives rise to thoughts.” The thoughts that arise are discriminations that grasp dharmas as real. The consciousness aggregate, associated with this coarse grasping, runs after objects everywhere. Hence “because it continues in association without interruption.”

2.3. Grasping
BDK 24 ↗The aspect of attachment

The third, “the characteristic of grasping,” is the feeling aggregate.ᵀ On the basis of the consciousness aggregate, it discriminates the disagreeable from the agreeable and experiences pain and pleasure. Hence the passage from “dependent upon continuity” through “dwelling on pain and pleasure.”

characteristic of grasping · 執取相 zhí qǔ xiàng · BDK p. 24 aspect of attachment
2.4. Imputing names
BDK 25 ↗Speculation on names and letters

The fourth, “the characteristic of imputing names,” is the perception aggregate.ᵀ On the basis of the preceding feeling aggregate it distinguishes verbal designations such as “disagreeable” and “agreeable.” Hence the passage from “on the basis of deluded grasping” through “the characteristics of verbal designations.”

characteristic of imputing names · 計名字相 jì míng zì xiàng · BDK p. 25 aspect of the speculation (vikalpa) on names and letters (i.e., concepts)
2.5. Initiating karma
BDK 25 ↗Giving rise to karma

The fifth, “the characteristic of initiating karma,” is the aggregate of fabrications.ᵀ Depending on the names and characteristics apprehended by the perception aggregate, the mental factor of intention arises and performs wholesome and unwholesome actions. Hence the passage from “dependent on names” through “creates various kinds of karma.”ᵀ

characteristic of initiating karma · 起業相 qǐ yè xiàng · BDK p. 25 aspect of giving rise to [evil] karma
dependent on names · 依於名字 yī yú míng zì · BDK p. 25 Relying on names and letters 名字 in this clause refers to linguistic designations.
2.6. Suffering under the bondage of karma
BDK 25 ↗Anxiety attached to the effects of karma

The sixth is “the characteristic of suffering under the bondage of karma.”ᵀ As a consequence of the karma produced by the preceding aggregate of fabrications, one experiences painful results in the three realms of becoming and six destinations of rebirth. Hence “one receives the results of karma and has no freedom.”

characteristic of suffering under the bondage of karma · 業繫苦相 yè xì kǔ xiàng · BDK p. 25 aspect of anxiety attached to the [effects of evil] karma

3. Fundamental and derivative nonawakening taken together

BDK 25 ↗Ignorance is able to produce all types of defiled states

“One should understand” begins the third part, the conclusion. As explained above, the six coarse characteristics arise in dependence on the objects displayed in manifestation. The three subtle characteristics depend directly on ignorance. These six and three together comprise all defilement. Thus one should know that the underlying ground of ignorance is the root that gives rise to every defiled dharma.

BDK 25 ↗All defiled states are aspects of nonenlightenment

Defiled characteristics may be coarse or subtle, but all fail to awaken to the true characteristic of dharmas. The characteristic of nonawakening is the influence of ignorance. Hence “all defiled dharmas exhibit the characteristic of nonawakening.”

Wŏnhyo · Separate NotesT1845 ↗

2. The six coarse characteristics of derivative nonawakening

BDK 24 ↗Conditioned by the world of objects, the mind produces six aspects

“With an objective field as condition, six characteristics arise.”ᵀ Among the preceding subtle characteristics, the field of objects manifests in dependence on the power of seeing.ᵀ There the field does not stir the power of seeing. These subsequent six characteristics are stirred by the field manifested there. These six do not themselves manifest that field. Such is the distinction when each is considered separately. Speaking generally, the former, too, depend in turn on the field they themselves manifest, and the latter can in turn produce the field on which they depend. Here the treatise appropriately takes each separately. Hence it says that the presence of the field gives rise to six characteristics.ᵀ The scripture itself says, “Stirred by the wind of objects, the waves of the seven consciousnesses roll.” This is precisely what it means.

objective field · 境界 jìng jiè · Skt. viṣaya · BDK p. 24 world of objects
field of objects · 境界 jìng jiè · Skt. viṣaya · BDK p. 24 world of objects
six characteristics · 六種相 liù zhǒng xiàng · BDK p. 24 six aspects

The six in relation to consciousness and the aggregates

BDK 24 ↗The six aspects and their relation to the aggregates

Of the six characteristics,

  • the first is the seventh consciousness, ↓

  • the next four are the four aggregates of the consciousnesses that arise in activity,

  • and the last is the karmic result produced with the aggregate of fabrications as its cause.⁕

2.1. Discernment

BDK 24 ↗The aspect of the discriminating intellect

As for “the characteristic of discernment,” the seventh consciousness is the first of the coarse characteristics.ᵀ Here for the first time it associates with the mental factor of discernment and distinguishes self and what belongs to self. Hence “characteristic of discernment.”ᵀ As Queen Śrīmālā’s Sūtra says, “In these six consciousnesses, the mental factor of discernment does not abide for a moment.”⁕ “Discernment as a mental factor” means the factor of discernment (prajñā). Thus we know that the characteristic of discernment here belongs precisely to the seventh consciousness.

characteristic of discernment · 智相 zhì xiàng · BDK p. 24 aspect of the [discriminating] intellect
self and what belongs to self · 我我所 wǒ wǒ suǒ · Skt. ātman and ātmīya · BDK p. 29 “I” and “mine”
BDK 24 ↗Depending on the world of objects, the mind discriminates liking and disliking

“Depending on the field of objects, the mind arises” means that the seventh consciousness arises in dependence on the preceding characteristic of an objective field.ᵀ In a favorable destiny it distinguishes desirable dharmas as self and mine.ᵀ In an unfavorable destiny it distinguishes undesirable dharmas as self and mine. Hence “distinguishes the desirable and the undesirable.”

characteristic of an objective field · 境界相 jìng jiè xiàng · BDK p. 24 world of objects
self and mine · 我我所 wǒ wǒ suǒ · Skt. ātman and ātmīya · BDK p. 29 “I” and “mine”

↥ To state the matter fully, it conceives the seeing aspect as selfᵀ and the manifested field as mine. Here the treatise speaks only of the more evident feature. Hence it says simply “depending on the field of objects.”

seeing aspect · 能見相 néng jiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject

↥ Again, the seventh consciousness takes as objects both the seeing aspect of the ālayavijñāna and its aspect as an objective field.ᵀ Yet that field is inseparable from the seeing, as a reflection is inseparable from the surface of its mirror. The seventh consciousness simply turns inward and itself conceives self and mine. Since it does not conceive them as external, other passages say it takes the ālayavijñāna as its object and omit any mention of an objective field. Moreover, in speaking briefly they consider only the object of grasping at self and thus say that its object is consciousness. They leave aside the object grasped as mine and thus omit its also taking the objective field as object.

aspect as an objective field · 境界相 jìng jiè xiàng · BDK p. 24 world of objects
What does the seventh consciousness apprehend?

↥ Question. How do we know that the seventh consciousness takes both mind and an objective field as its objects?

↥ Answer. We have two means of establishing this.

  1. Inferential reasoning. ↓

  2. Authoritative scriptural testimony. ↓

2.1.1. Proof by inference

↥ The inference runs as follows.

  1. The mental faculty necessarily shares an object with mental consciousness. This is the thesis.ᵀ

    mental consciousness · 意識 yì shí · Skt. manovijñāna · BDK p. 29 consciousness (vijñāna) The full Chinese compound specifies mental consciousness. Hakeda’s parenthesis gives the broader vijñāna.

  2. It is the support specific to mental consciousness. This is the reason.

  3. Whatever is a specific support necessarily shares an object with what it supports, as the eye faculty does. This gives the concordant example.

  4. Whatever does not share an object cannot be such a specific support. The immediately preceding, now ceased, mind faculty is an example. This gives the exclusion by dissimilarity.

↥ This thesis, reason, and example stand without fault.⁕ Thus we know that the mental faculty also apprehends the six kinds of sense object.ᵀ If you say that manas need not share an object with mental consciousness,⁕ᵀ you could equally say that the eye need not share an object with visual consciousness, since both faculties are specific supports. That cannot hold of the faculties of vision and the other consciousnesses. Without a similar instance your proposition fails. If you say that manas is no specific support, mental consciousness would lack a specific support and should fail to arise, as visual consciousness would [without its faculty]. This incurs the fault of contradicting your own scriptures. For the Buddha’s scriptures say, “Because the eye is unimpaired, visual consciousness can arise,” and so on through “because the mental faculty is unimpaired, mental consciousness can arise,” with further explanation. The treatise, too, calls this “the specific support.” Thus the claim that manas takes consciousness alone as its object and no other field fails.

six kinds of sense object · 六塵 liù chén · BDK p. 29 objects of the five senses and of the mind
manas · 意 yì · Skt. manas · BDK p. 26 mind (manas) Wŏnhyo also discusses the Yogācāra usage in which manas designates the seventh consciousness.
Self-awareness and the mental factors as objects

↥ If mental consciousness, which depends on manas, has all dharmas as its field, its support, the mental faculty, must also confront all dharmas. Consequently manas also takes itself as object, since it possesses the aspect of self-awareness. It also takes its associated mental factors as objects, since nothing prevents it. Those mental factors in turn directly know their own being and have an aspect of self-awareness. This does not invalidate the requirement that they share a single object.⁕ Understand that this applies to all eight consciousnesses. How do we know?⁕ The Ornament [of the Mahāyāna Sūtras] says, “The investigation of defilement and purity has been explained.” Its verse establishing consciousness-only says, “Grasper and grasped are both simply the radiance of mind.⁕ The radiance of greed and the radiance of faith are two radiances without two separate dharmas.”

↥ The explanation says that the first half instructs one who establishes consciousness-only to understand that grasper and grasped are merely the radiance of mind. In the second half, one radiance is that of greed and the other afflictions, the other that of faith and the other wholesome dharmas. These two radiances likewise entail no two distinct dharmas, defilement and purity. For apart from the radiance of mind there are no separately existing dharmas of greed, faith, and the like. This passage establishes the point. The mental factors, too, are illumined by the radiance of mind and so are inseparable from it. Being inseparable from it, they are themselves its radiance. A mirror’s image is illumined by the mirror’s light and therefore inseparable from it. Being inseparable from the light, the image is that very light. The same reasoning applies here. Although they resemble reflected images, there are no separate originals that remain unapprehended. If the mental factors taken as originals differed from the mental factors taken as images, the claim that they share one object would fail.

2.1.2. Proof by scripture

↥ For scriptural testimony, the ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “The seven consciousnesses arise through attention to and examination of their fields.” It also says, “Stirred by the wind of objects, the waves of the seven consciousnesses roll.” This treatise explains the intent of that scripture when it says, “With the field of objects as condition, six further characteristics arise.”ᵀ From passages like these we can know the answer.

six further characteristics · 六種相 liù zhǒng xiàng · BDK p. 24 six aspects
2. The six coarse characteristics of derivative nonawakening

↥ Next comes the following characteristic.

2.2. Continuity

BDK 24 ↗The aspect of continuity

The second characteristic, continuity, is the consciousness aggregate. It is coarse discrimination, ranges over all objects, and can continue for a long time. Hence “characteristic of continuity.”ᵀ This consciousness also gives rise to craving and draws forward and sustains past karma. It also nourishes rebirth, allowing future karmic results to follow in succession. Hence “continuing consciousness.”

characteristic of continuity · 相續相 xiāng xù xiàng · BDK p. 24 aspect of continuity
BDK 24 ↗By virtue of the intellect, the mind produces an awareness of pleasure and pain

“Depending on discernment” means that continuity first arises in dependence on the preceding characteristic of discernment. Its support is subtle and has only neutral feeling. What depends on it is coarse and gives rise to both pain and pleasure. Hence “gives rise to pain and pleasure.” The supporting characteristic of discernment abides with its object inwardly, as if asleep.⁕ Continuing consciousness races out over external objects, as if awake. Hence “the mind becomes aware and gives rise to thought.” This thought is discrimination that grasps at dharmas. The consciousness aggregate associates with this coarse grasping and races over every field. Hence “associated without interruption.”

2.3. Grasping

BDK 24 ↗The aspect of attachment

The next, “the characteristic of grasping,” is the feeling aggregate (vedanā).ᵀ

characteristic of grasping · 執取相 zhí qǔ xiàng · BDK p. 24 aspect of attachment

2.4. Imputing names

BDK 25 ↗Speculation on names and letters

The next, “the characteristic of imputing names,” is the perception aggregate (saṃjñā).ᵀ

characteristic of imputing names · 計名字相 jì míng zì xiàng · BDK p. 25 aspect of the speculation (vikalpa) on names and letters (i.e., concepts)

2.5. Producing karma

BDK 25 ↗Giving rise to karma

The next, “the characteristic of producing karma,” is the fabrications aggregate (saṃskāra).ᵀ The text is clear and requires no elaborate explanation.

characteristic of producing karma · 起業相 qǐ yè xiàng · BDK p. 25 aspect of giving rise to [evil] karma
BDK p. 25

What awakening and nonawakening share

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 25 Two relationships exist between the enlightened and nonenlightened states. They are “identity” and “nonidentity.”

Just as pieces of various kinds of pottery are of the same nature in that they are made of clay, so the various magiclike manifestations (māyā) of both enlightenment (anāsrava: nondefilement) and nonenlightenment (avidyā) are aspects of the same essence, suchness. For this reason, it is said in a sutra that “all sentient beings intrinsically abide in eternity and are entered into nirvana. The state of enlightenment is not something that is to be acquired by practice or to be created. In the end, it is unobtainable. [for it is given from the beginning].” Also it has no corporeal aspect that can be perceived as such. Any corporeal aspects [such as the marks of the Buddha] that are visible are magic-like products [of suchness manifested] in accordance with [the mentality of human beings in] defilement. It is not, however, that these corporeal aspects [which result from the, suprarational functions] of wisdom are of the nature of nonemptiness (i.e., substantial); for wisdom has no aspects that can be perceived.

3.3.2.2. Applying the pottery simile

↥ In the application, “illusory differences that follow defilement” refers to untainted dharmas.ᵀ “Illusory differences whose nature is defiled” refers to the dharmas of ignorance.ᵀ Why? Ignorance, in both root and branches, runs counter to the nature of equality. Differences therefore belong to its very nature. Untainted dharmas accord with the nature of equality. If one considered their nature alone, there would be no difference among them. We speak of differences among them only insofar as they follow the differences among defiled dharmas.

illusory differentiations that accord with defilement · 隨染幻差別 suí rǎn huàn chā bié · BDK p. 26 magic-like manifestations [of suchness manifested] in accordance with [the mentality of human beings in] defilement
illusory differentiations inherently defiled · 性染幻差別 xìng rǎn huàn chā bié · BDK p. 26 those [of people of ignorance] who are defiled (i.e., blinded) as to the essential nature [of suchness]

  1. What is free of effluents has illusory differentiations in accord with defilement.ᵀ

    illusory differentiations in accord with defilement · 隨染幻差別 suí rǎn huàn chā bié · BDK p. 26 magic-like manifestations [of suchness manifested] in accordance with [the mentality of human beings in] defilement

  2. Ignorance has illusory differentiations inherently defiled.

↥ Why? Ignorance is at odds with the nature of equality. Hence all defiled dharmas it produces are differentiated by nature. Dharmas free of effluents accord with the nature of equality. Considered simply in their nature, they should be undifferentiated. Only because they accord with the differences among defiled dharmas do we speak of differences among what is free of effluents.

↥ How so? Corresponding to the illusory differences among defilements such as activating consciousness, there are different inherent, effluent-free qualities of original awakening.ᵀ Again, as antidotes to those different defilements, the myriad distinct qualities of inceptive awakening are perfected. Thus what is free of effluents has differences only in relation to these defilements, with no differences deriving from its intrinsic nature. Defilement and purity depend entirely on one another and have no independent nature. Hence “illusory.”

activating consciousness · 業識 yè shí · Skt. karmavijñāna (proposed) · BDK p. 27 activating mind Mind first stirs under the influence of ignorance. Suzuki marks the Sanskrit identification as tentative.
effluent-free · 無漏 wú lòu · Skt. anāsrava · BDK p. 25 enlightenment (anāsrava: nondefilement)

The causes and conditions of arising and ceasing

1. The mind that arises and ceases

BDK 26 ↗The cause and conditions of being in samsara

The extensive commentary on “this mind's arising and ceasing” in the Outline is complete.

2. Causes and conditions of arising and ceasing

↥ The second division now explains its causes and conditions. It has two parts.

  1. It explains how arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions. ↓

  2. It shows the essence and characteristics of those causes and conditions. ↓

2.1. Dependence on causes and conditions

↥ The first of these in turn has two parts.

  1. A general statement. ↓

  2. A detailed explanation. ↓

2.1.1. General statement

↥ “Causes and conditions” in the general statement can be explained in two ways.

  1. The mind that is ālayavijñāna is itself transformed into the various dharmas. It is the cause of arising and ceasing. Root ignorance perfumes and sets this mind itself in motion. It is the condition of arising and ceasing.

  2. Again, the abiding ground of ignorance is the root of all defilements. It gives rise to all forms of arising and ceasing and is thus called their cause. The objects of the six senses set the waves of the seven consciousnesses in motion, making them arise and cease. These objects are the condition of arising and ceasing.ᵀ

    objects of the six senses · 六塵 liù chén · BDK p. 29 objects of the five senses and of the mind

↥ Cause and condition are explained in these two senses.

BDK 26 ↗Sentient beings depend on mind

The characteristics of arising and ceasing come into being in combination. Hence the expression “sentient being” [literally, “multitude-born”]. They have no separate essence and depend entirely on mind itself. Hence “dependent on mind.” This mind is ālayavijñāna in its own defining character. The sentient being that depends on it consists of mentation and mental consciousness.ᵀ Hence the words “mentation and mental consciousness operate.”

mentation · 意 yì · Skt. manas · BDK p. 26 mind (manas) Here 意 is the collective name of the five modes.
2.1.2. Detailed explanation
BDK 26 ↗What does this mean?” — dependence on the storehouse consciousness

“What does this mean?” begins the detailed explanation. It has three parts.

  1. Dependence on mind. ↓

  2. The operation of mentation. ↓

  3. The operation of mental consciousness. ↓

1. Dependence on mind

↥ In the first, “storehouse consciousness” is the mind mentioned above, the cause of arising and ceasing. “There is ignorance” speaks of the ignorance within storehouse consciousness, the condition of arising and ceasing. The point is that mentation and mental consciousness operate in dependence on this cause and condition. Hence “it is on the basis of ālayavijñāna that we speak of the presence of ignorance.” The earlier general statement briefly identified the cause, speaking only of dependence on mind. The present detailed explanation sets out both cause and condition, so it speaks also of dependence on the ignorance within ālayavijñāna.

Wŏnhyo · Separate NotesT1845 ↗

2. Causes and conditions of arising and ceasing

BDK 26 ↗The causes and conditions of being in samsara

“Further” begins the second section, expanding on the cause of arising and ceasing. It has two divisions.

  1. The treatise explains directly how arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions. ↓

  2. Beginning “consciousness that arises through the perfuming of ignorance,” it returns to the nature and characteristics of those causes and conditions.ᵀ ↓

    perfuming of ignorance · 無明熏習 wú míng xūn xí · Skt. vāsanā (熏習), avidyā (無明) · BDK p. 29 permeation of ignorance

2.1. How arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions

↥ The first division begins with a general statement and then explains its terms separately.

2.1.1. General statement of causes and conditions

↥ “Causes and conditions” admits two readings.

  1. The underlying mind of the ālayavijñāna itself turns into the arising and ceasing of dharmas. This is their cause. The dharmas that arise and cease, subtle and coarse, arise by supporting one another. These are their conditions. As the sūtra says, “The tathāgatagarbha is the cause of the wholesome and the unwholesome.”

  2. Again, the underlying ground of ignorance perfumes the mind itself, which turns into the various consciousnesses. This is called their cause of arising and ceasing. The consciousnesses thus produced in turn support one another as causes and conditions. As the text says below, “The cause of all defilement is called ignorance.”

↥ Both meanings are present here.

BDK 26 ↗Sentient beings depend on mind

“Sentient beings depend on mind.” The dharmas that arise and cease come into being in conjunction, hence “sentient beings.”⁕ They have no independent being and depend wholly on mind itself. Hence “depend on mind.” The sentient beings that thus depend consist simply in manas and mental consciousness (manovijñāna). Hence “manas and mental consciousness operate.” This states the headings of the two sections.

2.1.2. Explanation of the two headings

2. Explanation of the two headings

2.1.2.1. Manas
BDK 26 ↗On the basis of the storehouse consciousness, ignorance arises

“What does this mean?” introduces the explanation of the two headings. The first, manas, is treated in three parts.

  1. A brief account of manas. ↓

  2. A detailed exposition of manas. ↓

  3. Beginning “therefore,” a conclusion establishing mind-only.ᵀ ↓

    mind-only · 唯心 wéi xīn · Skt. cittamātra · BDK p. 28 of mind only
2.1.2.1.1. Manas in brief

↥ In the first part, “depending on the ālayavijñāna” explains the earlier “depending on mind.” The ignorance underlying the characteristics [of consciousness] depends directly on consciousness itself. Hence “in dependence on consciousness we speak of ignorance.” The text above said, “This consciousness has two meanings, first, awakening, and second, nonawakening.” It meant precisely this. The four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “Perfumed since beginningless time by false and unwholesome habits, the tathāgatagarbha is called the storehouse of consciousness. It gives rise to the underlying ground of ignorance and accompanies the seven consciousnesses.” Understand that this underlying ignorance is neither included in the seven consciousnesses nor a seed deposited by their perfuming.

BDK pp. 27–28

The five modes of mind

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 27 [The mentality] that emerges in the state of nonenlightenment, which [incorrectly] perceives and reproduces [the world of objects] and, conceiving that the [reproduced] world of objects is real, continues to develop [deluded] thoughts, is what we define as mind.

This mind has five different names.

The first is called the “activating mind,” for, without being aware of it, it breaks the equilibrium of mind by the force of ignorance.

The second is called the “evolving mind,” for it emerges, contingent upon the agitated mind as [the subject] that perceives [incorrectly].

The third is called the “reproducing mind,” for it reproduces the entire world of objects as a bright mirror reproduces all material images. When confronted with the objects of the five senses, it reproduces them at once. It arises spontaneously at all times and exists forever [reproducing, the world of objects] in front [of the subject].

The fourth is called the “analytical mind,” for it differentiates what is defiled and what is undefiled.

p. 28 The fifth is called the “continuing mind,” for it is united with [deluded] thoughts and continues uninterrupted. It retains the entire karma, good and bad, accumulated in the immeasurable lives of the past, and does not permit any loss. It is also capable of bringing the results of the pain, pleasure, etc., of the present and the future to maturity; in doing so, it makes no mistakes. It can cause one to recollect, suddenly the things of the present and the past and to have sudden and unexpected fantasies of the things to come.

The triple world, therefore, is unreal and is of mind only. Apart from it there are no objects of the five senses and of the mind. What does this mean? Since all things are, without exception, developed from the mind and produced under the condition of deluded thoughts, all differentiations are no other than the differentiations of one’s mind itself. [Yet] the mind cannot perceive the mind itself; the mind has no marks of its own [that can be ascertained as a substantial entity as such].

It should be understood that [the conception of] the entire world of objects can be held only on the basis of a person’s deluded mind of ignorance. All things, therefore, are just like the images in a mirror that are devoid of any objectivity that one can get hold of; they are of the mind only and are unreal. When the [deluded] mind comes into being, then various conceptions (dharmas) come to be; and when the [deluded] mind ceases to be, then these various conceptions cease to be.

2. The operation of mentation
BDK 27 ↗The mentality that emerges in the state of nonenlightenment

From “nonawakening” onward the treatise explains the operation of mentation. There are three parts.

  1. It explains its operation briefly. ↓

  2. It describes that operation in detail. ↓

  3. It concludes by establishing the meaning of dependence on mind. ↓

1. The five functions in brief

↥ The brief explanation already describes the characteristics of five kinds of consciousness.

1.1. Activating consciousness

↥ “Arises in nonawakening.” The mind on which these depend, perfumed by ignorance, stirs in its entirety. This is activating consciousness.

1.2. Evolving consciousness

↥ “Can perceive.” This same mind is transformed into that which perceives. This is evolving consciousness.

1.3. Manifesting consciousness

↥ “Can manifest.” Again, this same mind comes to manifest objects. This is manifesting consciousness.

1.4. Discriminating consciousness

↥ “Can apprehend objects.” It apprehends the objects manifested by manifesting consciousness. This is discriminating consciousness.ᵀ

discriminating consciousness · 智識 zhì shí · BDK p. 27 analytical mind The fourth mode distinguishes defiled and pure dharmas.
1.5. Continuing consciousness

↥ “Gives rise to thoughts in succession.” It gives rise to various coarse thoughts concerning the objects apprehended. This is continuing consciousness.

1. The five functions in brief

↥ Through the successive unfolding of these five functions, mental consciousness arises in the presence of objects. This is why the five are collectively called mentation [manas].

2. The five functions in detail
BDK 27 ↗This mind has five different names

From “this mentation” onward the second part gives a detailed account under two heads.

  1. A general statement.

  2. A detailed explanation. ↓

2.2. Explanation of the five names
2.2.1. Activating consciousness
BDK 27 ↗The activating mind

In the detailed explanation, “the power of ignorance” identifies the condition on which it depends. “The mind stirs in nonawakening” explains activation [業], since to stir and set in motion is the sense of “activity.”ᵀ

mind stirs · 心動 xīn dòng · BDK p. 24 agitation of mind
2.2.2. Evolving consciousness
BDK 27 ↗The evolving mind

“Because a perceiving aspect arises in dependence on the mind in motion” means that on the basis of the movement of activating consciousness, the capacity to perceive develops.ᵀ There are, however, two senses of evolving consciousness.

perceiving aspect · 能見相 néng jiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject
capacity to perceive · 能見 néng jiàn · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject

  1. When ignorance impels the transformation that gives rise to perceiving, this occurs within the root consciousness.

  2. When objects impel the transformation that gives rise to perceiving, this is called the seventh consciousness.

↥ The characteristic of evolving in this passage has the first sense.

2.2.3. Manifesting consciousness
BDK 27 ↗The reproducing mind

“Can manifest all objects” means that the capacity to manifest objects arises in dependence on the perceiving of the foregoing evolving consciousness. As the text said above, “It is through dependence on perceiving that objects appear delusively.” Manifesting consciousness therefore depends on evolving consciousness. The function of perceiving and the function of manifesting are distinct. Hence the earlier expression “can perceive and can manifest.”

The mirror simile
BDK 27 ↗A bright mirror and the objects of the five senses

A simile follows, and then its application.

Application to sense objects

↥ The application singles out “the five sense objects,” the most readily apparent ones, to match the visible images in the simile.ᵀ In fact this consciousness manifests every kind of object.

five sense objects · 五塵 wǔ chén · BDK p. 27 objects of the five senses
3. Manifesting consciousness
BDK 27 ↗It arises spontaneously at all times

“Because at all times it arises spontaneously and is constantly present” distinguishes it from the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which are sometimes interrupted. On this textual evidence we know that the three [activating, evolving, and manifesting] are distinct functions within root consciousness.

2.2.4. Discriminating consciousness
BDK 27 ↗The analytical mind

Fourth is discriminating consciousness, the seventh consciousness and the first of the six characteristics discussed above, the characteristic of discrimination. Its meaning was explained earlier. Desirable and undesirable results are called defiled and pure dharmas.ᵀ It discriminates among them and construes them as “I” and “mine.” Hence “discriminates between defiled and pure dharmas.”

defiled and pure dharmas · 染淨法 rǎn jìng fǎ · BDK p. 27 what is defiled and what is undefiled
2.2.5. Continuing consciousness
BDK 28 ↗The continuing mind

Fifth is continuing consciousness, namely mental consciousness, called the characteristic of continuity among the six previously described.

Continuity in its own operation

↥ “Because it is associated with thoughts and is uninterrupted” means that its association with grasping at dharmas enables it to continue over time. This explains continuity in terms of the uninterrupted character of this consciousness itself.

Continuity through its functions
BDK 28 ↗It retains the entire karma, good and bad

From “maintains and holds” onward the treatise explains continuity in terms of this consciousness's functions.

  1. It can give rise to the afflictions of craving and clinging. It can therefore draw on and sustain fabrications set in motion by past ignorance, enabling them to constitute the becoming capable of bearing future fruit. Hence the passage from “maintains and holds” through “because it allows none to be lost.”

  2. It can also give rise to afflictions that nourish rebirth, allowing karmic results to arise one after another without interruption. Hence “it brings them to fulfillment without discrepancy.”

↥ The unbroken round of causes and effects across the three times is thus the work of mental consciousness. It is called continuing consciousness in this sense.

5. Continuing consciousness
BDK 28 ↗Recollect the things of the past and think of things to come

The next words, “recalling past affairs and considering future affairs,” show that this consciousness makes coarse, readily apparent discriminations. These differ from the subtle discriminations of discriminating consciousness. We know from this that continuing consciousness here belongs solely to mental consciousness. Its reference differs from that of “continuing mind” earlier in the treatise.

3. Dependence on mind
BDK 28 ↗The triple world is of mind only

“Therefore” introduces the third part, which concludes by clarifying dependence on mind. It has two parts.

  1. A brief statement. ↓

  2. An extensive explanation. ↓

3.1. The three realms are mind-only

↥ In the brief statement, “therefore” refers back to the five kinds of consciousness and the rest, which are constituted in dependence on mind. On these grounds, all dharmas in the three realms are made by mind alone.ᵀ This is the meaning of the Sūtra of the Ten Grounds when it says, “Children of the Buddha, the three realms are made by the One Mind alone.”

mind alone · 唯心 wéi xīn · Skt. cittamātra · BDK p. 28 of mind only
3.2. The meaning of mind-only
BDK 28 ↗All differentiations are differentiations of one's own mind

“What does this mean?” begins the extensive explanation. There are two parts.

  1. Dharmas are not altogether absent, yet do not exist [as apprehended]. ↓

  2. Dharmas have no such existence, yet are not altogether absent. ↓

3.2.1. Dharmas appear yet have no apprehensible existence

↥ In the first, “all dharmas arise from mind, born of deluded thought” establishes that dharmas do appear.ᵀ “Every act of discrimination discriminates one's own mind. Mind does not see mind, and no characteristic can be apprehended.”ᵀ This establishes in what sense dharmas have no existence.

deluded thought · 妄念 wàng niàn · BDK p. 28 deluded thoughts
Every act of discrimination · 一切分別 yī qiè fēn bié · BDK p. 28 all differentiations
no characteristic can be apprehended · 無相可得 wú xiàng kě dé · Skt. lakṣaṇa (相) · BDK p. 28 the mind has no marks of its own
BDK 28 ↗Mind cannot perceive mind itself

As the ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says, “If body, means of livelihood, and dwelling arise as in a dream, there would have to be two kinds of mind, yet mind has no such dual character. A knife cannot cut itself, nor can a fingertip point to itself. The same holds for mind's inability to see itself.”

↥ I explain it as follows. If the things seen in a dream really existed just as they were seen, there would be the two aspects of perceiver and perceived. Yet in a dream no two such dharmas actually exist. The minds of the three realms are all like this dream. Outside mind there is nothing for discrimination to discriminate. Hence “every act of discrimination discriminates one's own mind.” As for one's own mind, it cannot see itself, just as in the examples of the knife and the fingertip. Hence “mind does not see mind.” Since there is no other to be seen and mind cannot see itself either, the absence of anything perceived entails the absence of a perceiver. Neither aspect, perceiver or perceived, can be apprehended. Hence “no characteristic can be apprehended.” For a detailed treatment of the difficulty here, reconciling the newer and older accounts, see my Separate Notes.

3.2.2. Dharmas have no such existence yet do appear
BDK 28 ↗Images in a mirror and the arising and ceasing of dharmas

From “one should understand” onward the treatise explains the second point, that things have no such existence yet are not altogether absent.

  1. From “one should understand that the world” through “no essence can be apprehended, for it is only mind's delusion,” it explains their lack of such existence.

  2. Beginning with “when mind arises, dharmas arise,” it shows in what sense they are not absent. Under the influence of ignorance, mind stirs in nonawakening and comes even to manifest all objects. Hence “when mind arises, the manifold dharmas arise.” When the ignorant mind ceases, its objects cease along with it, and the discriminating consciousnesses can cease altogether. Hence “when mind ceases, the manifold dharmas cease.” The arising and ceasing explained here is other than moment-by-moment arising and ceasing.

↥ This concludes the extensive explanation of mentation.
