2. Causes and conditions of arising and ceasing

2.1. How arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions

2.1.2. Explanation of the two headings

2. Causes and conditions of arising and ceasing › 1. How arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions › 2. Explanation of the two headings

2.1.2.1. Manas
2.1.2.1.1. Manas in brief
BDK 27 ↗What emerges in the state of nonenlightenment is called mind

“Arises without awakening”: mind itself is perfumed by this ignorance and stirs into arising and ceasing, hence the word “arises.” This very mind, perfumed by ignorance, turns into that which sees and so on, until it becomes the successive arising of thoughts. Mind itself thus has five functions. In confrontation with an object it can produce mental consciousness, hence its name manas. The fifth function is itself mental consciousness, but insofar as it produces a subsequent moment it too is included under manas.

2.1.2.1.2. The five modes of manas
BDK 27 ↗This mind has five different names

“This manas” begins the second, detailed explanation. It distinguishes the five functions mentioned above and assigns five names to consciousness.

2.1.2.1.2.1. Activating consciousness

↥ The meaning of the first, activating consciousness, has already been explained.

2.1.2.1.2.2. Evolving consciousness
BDK 27 ↗The evolving mind

“Evolving consciousness” is the aspect that sees. It operates with an object, hence “evolving consciousness.”ᵀ The term, however, has two applications.

Evolving consciousness · 轉識 zhuǎn shí · Skt. pravṛttivijñāna · BDK p. 27 evolving mind Here the stirred mind takes on the role of perceiver. Wŏnhyo also discusses broader uses of 轉識.
aspect that sees · 能見相 néng jiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject

  1. When the power of seeing stirred by ignorance is called “evolving consciousness,” it belongs to the ālayavijñāna.ᵀ

    power of seeing · 能見 néng jiàn · BDK p. 24 perceiving subject

  2. When the power of seeing stirred by objects is called “evolving consciousness,” the seven consciousnesses are meant.

↥ These two meanings must be kept distinct. Elsewhere, all that is capable of seeing is called “evolving consciousness.” The term then extends to all eight consciousnesses. The aspect of turning here is understood in the first sense.

2.1.2.1.2.3. Manifesting consciousness
BDK 27 ↗The reproducing mind

The third, the aspect of manifestation, corresponds to the objective field among the three characteristics above.ᵀ Here the author wants to show that apart from evolving consciousness there is no separate objective appearance. He therefore speaks of what manifests in order to explain the field manifested.

aspect of manifestation · 現相 xiàn xiàng · BDK p. 24 境界相 world of objects
BDK 27 ↗As a bright mirror reproduces all material images

“Like a bright mirror displaying visible forms.” The four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “Mahāmati, in an extended account there are three kinds of consciousness, and in an extended account eight characteristics.⁕ What are the three? True consciousness, manifesting consciousness, and consciousness that discriminates objects.ᵀ Just as a bright mirror holds the images of visible forms, so too does manifesting consciousness display them.” The treatise explains “manifestation” here by saying, “It arises spontaneously at all times and is always present.” Manifesting consciousness, then, belongs definitely to the eighth consciousness. Activating consciousness and the others that underlie it are subtler still. How could one possibly insist on placing them among the seven consciousnesses?

manifesting consciousness · 現識 xiàn shí · Skt. khyātivijñāna (in the Laṅkāvatāra parallel) · BDK p. 27 reproducing mind The third mode manifests the field of objects, as a mirror displays images.
consciousness that discriminates objects · 分別事識 fēn bié shì shí · Skt. vastuprativikalpavijñāna (in the Laṅkāvatāra parallel) · BDK p. 29 object-discriminating consciousness
BDK 27 ↗When confronted with the objects of the five senses, it reproduces them at once

“As the five sense objects come before it, they immediately appear.” Whatever appearance arises is inseparable from seeingᵀ and appears only in the mirror of the power of seeing. Hence “as they come before it, they immediately appear.” Strictly speaking, mental objects appear as well. The text briefly names the five more evident types of object.

five sense objects · 五塵 wǔ chén · BDK p. 27 objects of the five senses
The range of its objects
BDK 27 ↗It reproduces the entire world of objects: the scope of manifesting consciousness

Question. How broad is the field of this consciousness? Our treatise names only the five sense objects. The Laṅkāvatāra says, “The ālayavijñāna discerns the manifested field: one’s own body, the means of sustaining life, the world as receptacle, and so forth. It cognizes them all at once, without a before and after.”

↥ The Yogācārabhūmi says, “It operates by discerning two kinds of field.

  1. It discerns what it appropriates internally. It discerns the dispositions of delusive grasping at an imagined intrinsic nature, and the material sense faculties and their bodily bases. This applies where there is material form. In the formless realm only the dispositions of delusive grasping are discerned.

  2. It discerns externally the undifferentiated appearance of the receptacle world. In dependence on the ālayavijñāna that takes what is inwardly appropriated as its object, the appearance of the receptacle world is present continuously at all times. It is like a lamp flame which, when it arises, takes up the oil and wick inwardly and emits light outwardly.⁕ Thus the ālayavijñāna has the appropriated field as its inward object, and the receptacle world as its outward object. Understand that it arises on the same principle.”

↥ The Distinction between the Middle and the Extremes says, “This consciousness apprehends four types of field, comprising sense objects, faculties, self, and consciousness. Since what is apprehended is absent, the root consciousness apprehending it can likewise arise in this way.”⁕

↥ On the account of the Distinction and the Laṅkāvatāra, dispositions and the like would fall outside this consciousness’s field. On the Yogācārabhūmi’s account, sound and the seven consciousnesses, among other things, would fall outside it. On our treatise’s account, the currently manifest sense faculties, the consciousnesses, and the like would also fall outside the field it manifests. How can these contradictions be reconciled?

↥ Answer. They do not contradict one another. Why? None says it takes only the dharmas named as its objects. None says the other dharmas fall outside its field.

Why the scriptural accounts differ

↥ Question. Even if they do not contradict one another, their accounts differ. May we hear what each intends?

↥ Answer. Each difference has its reason.

  1. The Distinction aims to show that all dharmas now manifest in activity are manifested by root consciousness, and that outside consciousness there is no separate dharma. Hence it speaks only of dharmas manifest in activity. Dispositions and seeds have no evident appearance and are indistinguishable from consciousness. Hence it leaves them unmentioned.

  2. The Yogācārabhūmi and related works aim to show that appearances have no independent continuity apart from seeing. They therefore describe all continuously occurring dharmas other than mind and mental factors as discerned by this consciousness. Mental dharmas themselves are not established apart from objects. Their status is clear and so requires no separate mention.

↥ By analogy one can understand what the other treatises bring to the fore or leave implicit. One must not cling to a single corner of the teaching and disparage an account that embraces its full scope.

3. Manifesting consciousness

↥ Enough of this digression. We return to explaining the main text.

2.1.2.1.2.4. Discerning consciousness
BDK 27 ↗The analytical mind discriminates the defiled and the undefiled

The fourth, “discerning consciousness,” is the seventh consciousness, the first, discernment, among the six characteristics discussed above.ᵀ Desirable results [and their opposites] are termed defiled and pure dharmas. It differentiates these dharmas and conceives them as self and mine. Hence “discriminates defiled and pure dharmas.”⁕ᵀ

discerning consciousness · 智識 zhì shí · BDK p. 27 analytical mind The fourth mode distinguishes defiled and pure dharmas.
defiled and pure dharmas · 染淨法 rǎn jìng fǎ · BDK p. 27 what is defiled and what is undefiled
2.1.2.1.2.5. Continuing consciousness
BDK 28 ↗The continuing mind

“Continuing consciousness” is mental consciousness, the characteristic of continuity among the earlier six.

BDK 28 ↗United with thoughts, it continues uninterrupted

“Because it associates with thought without interruption” explains the name “continuing” by the unbroken course of the consciousness itself.

BDK 28 ↗It retains the entire karma accumulated in past lives

Beginning “sustains,” the text explains its name “continuing” in terms of its function. This consciousness can give rise to craving and clinging, and thus draw forward and sustain the fabrications set in motion by past ignorance, enabling them to mature into the becoming (bhava) capable of yielding a future result. Hence “sustains the results of the past, preventing their loss.”⁕ The Yogācārabhūmi explains this fully. Moreover, consciousness can give rise to the afflictions that nourish rebirth, so that karmic results keep arising without interruption. Hence “brings about corresponding results in the present, the future, and so forth, without discrepancy.” That causes and results revolve unceasingly through the three times is the work of mental consciousness. Hence “continuing.”

BDK 28 ↗It recollects past things and entertains thoughts of things to come

“Recollects past events and considers future ones” shows that the function of this consciousness differs from discerning consciousness, which takes only a present field as object. This passage establishes that continuing consciousness here is mental consciousness. It differs from the “continuing mind” discussed earlier.

2.1.2.1.3. Conclusion establishing mind-only
BDK 28 ↗The triple world is unreal and of mind only

“Therefore” introduces the conclusion establishing consciousness-only. The five modes of consciousness explained above have no separate existence of their own. All depend on the One Mind. Hence the three realms are deceptive and fashioned by mind alone.ᵀ

mind alone · 唯心 wéi xīn · Skt. cittamātra · BDK p. 28 of mind only
Mind does not see mind
BDK 28 ↗All differentiations are differentiations of one’s own mind

“Since all dharmas arise from deluded thought, all discrimination discriminates one’s own mind. Mind does not see mind, and no characteristic can be found.”ᵀ A verse in the ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “If the body, its means of subsistence, and its supports were as seen in a dream, there should be two kinds of mind there. Yet there are no two characteristics. A knife cannot cut itself, nor a finger point to itself. As the eye cannot see itself, so it is here.”

deluded thought · 妄念 wàng niàn · BDK p. 28 deluded thoughts
all discrimination · 一切分別 yī qiè fēn bié · BDK p. 28 all differentiations
no characteristic can be found · 無相可得 wú xiàng kě dé · Skt. lakṣaṇa (相) · BDK p. 28 the mind has no marks of its own

↥ What does this mean? If the things seen in a dream really existed just as seen, then there would be two. But in the dream there are in fact no two characteristics of grasper and grasped. All minds throughout the three realms are like this dream. Hence “all discrimination discriminates one’s own mind.” Yet one’s own mind cannot see itself, just as in the examples of the knife and the finger. Hence “mind does not see mind.” When there is no other thing to be seen and mind does not see itself, there is nothing seen. Without anything seen, seeing is not established. Neither seer nor seen can be found. What other characteristic could there be? Hence “no characteristic can be found.” That verse says, “No other, no cause, no discrimination or thing discriminated. Of the five dharmas and the two minds, in quiescence there is nothing of the sort.”

Reconciling mind-only with reflexive awareness
BDK 28 ↗The mind cannot perceive the mind itself

Question. Works such as the Compendium of Valid Cognition (Pramāṇasamuccaya) say, “Mind and mental factors each directly know themselves. This is direct perception. Otherwise recollection should be impossible, just as one does not remember what one has never seen.” Here the sūtra says, “It does not see itself.” How do you reconcile this contradiction?

↥ Answer. The two statements have different intentions, which allow them to stand together. How so?

  1. The sūtra and our treatise aim to show that apart from the seeing aspect there is no distinct object aspect. On the side of the object there is nothing to be seen. Nor can one say that the seeing aspect turns around and sees that very seeing aspect. Its function is single and directed outward. Hence the knife and finger exemplify the point at issue.

  2. The Compendium holds that although the seeing aspect cannot see itself, the faculty of reflexive awareness can directly know the seeing aspect itself. Its function is distinct and directed inward. Hence the lamp flame exemplifies this point.

↥ For this reason the two statements are compatible. Again, the sūtra and our treatise aim to disclose the true characteristic of things. From the standpoint of their nonexistence, they deny that mind sees itself. The author of the Compendium aims to establish a conventional designation. From the standpoint of nonabsence, he affirms reflexive awareness. Conventional designation leaves reality as it is. Reality does not destroy conventional designation. If neither destroys nor disturbs the other, where is the contradiction?⁕

↥ Here it says, “Apart from seeing there is no objective appearance. Therefore seeing does not see an objective appearance.” Elsewhere it says, “The object aspect is distinct from the seeing aspect. Therefore seeing can see the object aspect.” Why should these apparently contradictory claims cause surprise? Understand that, as before, neither invalidates the other. It is also said, “To disclose conventional presence, one speaks of an objective appearance and a seeing. To disclose conventional absence, one speaks of neither appearance nor seeing. Conventional presence does not amount to absolute presence, so it leaves absence undisturbed. Conventional absence does not amount to absolute absence, so it does not destroy presence. With presence undestroyed, things are plainly present. With absence undisturbed, they are plainly absent.” In so profound a principle of dependent arising there is nowhere to take a stand and nothing to obstruct the way. What room is there for conflicting claims?

BDK pp. 29–30

Mental consciousness and ignorance

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 29 What is called “consciousness (vijñāna)” is the “continuing mind.” Because of their deep-rooted attachment, ordinary people imagine that “I” and “mine” are real and cling to them in their illusions. As soon as objects are presented, this consciousness rests on them and discriminates the objects of the five senses and of the mind. This is called “vijñāna” (i.e., the differentiating consciousness) or the “separating consciousness.” Or, again, it is called the “object-discriminating consciousness.” [The propensity for discrimination of] this consciousness will be intensified by both [the intellectual] defilement of holding fast to perverse views and [the affectional] defilement of indulgence in passion.

That the [deluded mind and] consciousness arise from the permeation of ignorance is something that ordinary people cannot understand. The followers of the Hinayana, with their wisdom, likewise fail to realize this. Those bodhisattvas who, having advanced from their first stage of correct faith by setting the mind [upon enlightenment] through practicing contemplation, have come to realize the dharmakāya, can partially comprehend this. Yet even those who have reached the final stage of bodhisattvahood cannot fully comprehend this; only the Enlightened Ones (Buddhas) have thorough comprehension of it. Why? The Mind, though pure in its self-nature from the beginning, is accompanied by ignorance. Being defiled by ignorance, a defiled [state of] mind comes into being. But, though defiled, the Mind itself is eternal and immutable. Only the Enlightened Ones are able to understand what this means.

What is called the essential nature of Mind is always beyond thoughts. It is, therefore, defined as “immutable.” When the one world of reality is yet to be realized, p. 29–30 the Mind [is mutable and] is not in perfect unity [with suchness]. Suddenly, [a deluded] thought arises; [this state] is called ignorance.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

3. The operation of mental consciousness
BDK 29 ↗Consciousness is the continuing mind

Next comes the explanation of mental consciousness. This is the continuing consciousness discussed earlier. Considered in association with the discrimination that grasps at dharmas, insofar as it gives rise to what follows, it is termed “mentation.” Considered in its capacity to give rise to the afflictions of views and craving, insofar as it arises from what precedes it, it is called “mental consciousness.”ᵀ Hence the passage from “mental consciousness is this very continuing [consciousness]” through “it discriminates the six sense objects and is called mental consciousness.”ᵀ The treatise adopts the account in terms of a single mental consciousness. It accordingly does not list eye-consciousness and the other four separately, and speaks of mental consciousness as discriminating the objects of all six senses.ᵀ

afflictions of views and craving · 見愛煩惱 jiàn ài fán nǎo · BDK p. 29 [the intellectual] defilement of holding fast to perverse views and [the affectional] defilement of indulgence in passion
six sense objects · 六塵 liù chén · BDK p. 29 objects of the five senses and of the mind
objects of all six senses · 六塵 liù chén · BDK p. 29 objects of the five senses and of the mind
BDK 29 ↗The separating consciousness

“Also called the differentiating consciousness.” Depending on the six distinct sense faculties, it apprehends their six respective objects.ᵀ Manas, by contrast, operates without dependence on such distinct faculties. Hence “differentiating.”

differentiating consciousness · 分離識 fēn lí shí · BDK p. 29 separating consciousness Hakeda reserves “separating consciousness” here for 分離識. His preceding explanatory gloss “the differentiating consciousness” belongs to 意識.
BDK 29 ↗The object-discriminating consciousness

It can also discriminate the different features of things past and future, internal and external. Hence “it is also called consciousness that discriminates particular things.”ᵀ

consciousness that discriminates particular things · 分別事識 fēn bié shì shí · Skt. vastuprativikalpavijñāna (in the Laṅkāvatāra parallel) · BDK p. 29 object-discriminating consciousness
BDK 29 ↗Intensified by the defilement of holding fast to perverse views and by cravings

“Because it grows through the afflictions of views and craving” explains the name “consciousness that discriminates particular things.” Nourished by the afflictions abandoned through seeing and through cultivation, it can discriminate all sorts of things. Among the six characteristics discussed earlier, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and fabrications are accordingly included under this mental consciousness.

1. Dependence on causes and conditions

↥ This concludes the extensive explanation of how arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions.

2.2. Nature of the causes and conditions

BDK 29 ↗The depth of ignorance and its perfuming influence

The second part now revisits the essence and characteristics of the causes and conditions on which arising and ceasing depend. It has two divisions.

  1. A brief account of the profundity of cause and condition. ↓

  2. A full account of their differences. ↓

2.2.1. Their profundity

↥ The brief account has three steps.

  1. It states that the matter is profound. ↓

  2. It explains why. ↓

  3. It draws the conclusion. ↓

2.2.1.1. Statement of profundity
BDK 29 ↗Only the Buddhas comprehend it thoroughly

In the first step, “the consciousness that arises through the perfuming of ignorance” recapitulates the earlier passage on how, on the basis of ālayavijñāna, we speak of ignorance and of [mentation] arising in nonawakening.ᵀ No other can know it. “Only a buddha understands it exhaustively” states its profundity.

perfuming of ignorance · 無明熏習 wú míng xūn xí · Skt. vāsanā (熏習), avidyā (無明) · BDK p. 29 permeation of ignorance
2.2.1.2. Its explanation
BDK 29 ↗Mind is pure in its essential nature yet is accompanied by ignorance

“Why?” begins the explanation of this profundity. “From the beginning its own nature has been pure, yet ignorance defiles it and a defiled mind exists.” This explains how it is pure and yet continually defiled. “Although a defiled mind exists, it remains forever unchanged.” This explains how it is in motion yet forever still.ᵀ That is what makes this matter profound and difficult to fathom.

remains forever unchanged · 常恒不變 cháng héng bù biàn · BDK p. 29 is eternal and immutable

↥ As the Śrīmālā Sūtra says, “It is difficult to comprehend the mind that is intrinsically pure.ᵀ That this very mind is defiled by afflictions is likewise difficult to comprehend.”

intrinsically pure · 自性清淨 zì xìng qīng jìng · BDK p. 29 pure in its self-nature

↥ The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says, “The tathāgatagarbha has the characteristic of purity, yet adventitious afflictions stain it and render it impure. It was on this account that I taught Queen Śrīmālā and the other bodhisattvas that the tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, arises together with the seven consciousnesses. This is called the characteristic of evolving and ceasing. Mahāmati, concerning the domain of the tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, I, together with you and those bodhisattvas of profound wisdom, can fully distinguish these two dharmas. The other śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and followers of other paths who cling to names cannot understand these two dharmas.”

2.2.1.3. Conclusion

↥ “Therefore only a buddha can know this” is the third step, the concluding statement of profundity.

2.2.2. Their distinctions
BDK 29 ↗The essential nature of mind and the arising of ignorance

Beginning with “that is to say,” the second division sets out the differences among causes and conditions at length. It has six parts.

  1. Mind's nature, the cause, in its essence and characteristics. ↓

  2. Ignorance, the condition, in its essence and characteristics. ↓

  3. The various conditions of the defiled mind. ↓

  4. The stages of counteracting and abandoning ignorance. ↓

  5. The meanings of “associated” and “unassociated.” ↓

  6. The meanings of the obstacle to wisdom and the obstacle of the afflictions.ᵀ ↓

    obstacle to wisdom · 智礙 zhì ài · BDK p. 33 hindrance originating from misconceptions of objects
    obstacle of the afflictions · 煩惱礙 fán nǎo ài · BDK p. 32–33 hindrance originating from defilements
1. Mind's nature as cause

↥ In the first, “the nature of mind is always free of thought and is therefore called unchanging” explains the earlier statement that even in the presence of a defiled mind, it remains unchanged.ᵀ Although the mind stirs in its entirety, it is quiescent from the beginning. Hence “the nature of mind is always free of thought.”

unchanging · 不變 bù biàn · BDK p. 29 immutable
2. Ignorance as condition
BDK 30 ↗Suddenly a deluded thought arises

In the second, the words “unassociated with mind” indicate that this ignorance is exceedingly subtle.ᵀ As yet there is no differentiation of subject and object, or of mind and its mental factors. Hence “unassociated with mind.” This alone is the root. No other defiled dharma is subtler or stands prior to it. In this sense it is said to “arise suddenly.” As the Sūtra of Fundamental Activities says, “Prior to the four abiding grounds no further dharma arises. Hence the name ‘abiding ground of beginningless ignorance.’” That is, there is nothing else prior to it to serve as a beginning. It alone is the root. Hence “beginningless.” This is precisely the sense of “suddenly” in the present treatise. It is with respect to the dependence of the coarse and subtle on one another that we say nothing precedes it, and that it “arises suddenly.” “Suddenly” here carries no implication about a point in time. I distinguish the characteristics of this ignorance at length in my Treatise on the Two Hindrances. This explains the earlier words that the mind is intrinsically pure, yet ignorance defiles it and a defiled mind exists.

unassociated with mind · 心不相應 xīn bù xiāng yìng · BDK p. 29–30 is not in perfect unity [with suchness] Wŏnhyo reads 心不相應 as describing the subtlety of ignorance, before subject and object or mind and mental factors are differentiated.

2. Causes and conditions of arising and ceasing

2.1. How arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions

2.1.2. Explanation of the two headings

1. How arising and ceasing depend on causes and conditions › 2. Explanation of the two headings

2.1.2.2. Mental consciousness
BDK 29 ↗What is called consciousness is the continuing mind

“Further” begins the second division, explaining the heading “mental consciousness.” Mental consciousness is the continuing consciousness mentioned above. Insofar as it associates with coarse thoughts that grasp at dharmas and produces a subsequent moment, it is called continuing consciousness. Insofar as it arises from a preceding thought and can produce afflictions of views and craving, it is called mental consciousness.ᵀ Hence “mental consciousness is this very continuing consciousness.” The aggregates of feeling, perception, and fabrications among the six characteristics above are included here by association with mental consciousness.⁕ Furthermore, the treatise adopts here the approach that speaks of a single mental consciousness, so it does not describe the five sensory consciousnesses separately. The wording is clear.

afflictions of views and craving · 見愛煩惱 jiàn ài fán nǎo · BDK p. 29 [the intellectual] defilement of holding fast to perverse views and [the affectional] defilement of indulgence in passion

2.2. The nature and characteristics of the causes and conditions

BDK 29 ↗Consciousness originates from the influence of ignorance

“Depending on the perfuming of ignorance” begins the second division, returning to the nature and characteristics of causes and conditions. It has two parts.

  1. Considering mind itself, the treatise shows how hard it is to fathom the defilement and purity of the underlying cause. ↓

  2. Beginning “failing to comprehend,” it considers the various defiled and pure dharmas and distinguishes the nature and characteristics of the conditions. ↓

2.2.1. Purity and defilement of mind as cause

↥ In the first part, “consciousness that arises through the perfuming of ignorance” takes up the earlier statement that in dependence on the ālayavijñāna there is ignorance and [mind] stirs without awakening. This passage explains precisely how the intrinsically pure mind is stirred by the wind of ignorance. Hence “consciousness arisen through ignorance.” If mind itself simply arose and ceased and was a defiled mind through and through, it would be easy to understand.ᵀ If it simply endured forever and was a wholly pure mind, that too would be easy to know. Even if it were genuinely pure in itself and merely appeared defiled, that too could readily be understood. Or if consciousness itself moved while its empty nature was still, what difficulty would there be?

defiled mind · 染心 rǎn xīn · BDK p. 29 defiled [state of] mind

↥ Yet here this mind itself is pure and itself defiled. The mind moves and the mind is still.ᵀ Defilement and purity are nondual, motion and stillness indistinguishable. And yet, for all that nonduality and lack of distinction, neither pair is simply one. It is because mind eludes determination in this way that it is so difficult to know.

mind moves · 心動 xīn dòng · BDK p. 24 agitation of mind
BDK 29 ↗Mind, though pure in its self-nature, is accompanied by ignorance

“Mind is intrinsically pure, yet there is a defiled mind” shows how, though pure, it is continually defiled.

BDK 29 ↗Though defiled, the Mind itself is eternal and immutable

“Although there is a defiled mind, it remains constantly unchanged” shows how, though in motion, it is always still. For this reason only a buddha understands it exhaustively. The ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “The tathāgatagarbha has purity as its characteristic, yet the stains of adventitious afflictions soil it. On this basis I taught Queen Śrīmālā and the other bodhisattvas that the tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, arises together with the seven consciousnesses. This is called the characteristic of transformation and cessation. Mahāmati, as for the domain of the tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, I, you, and those bodhisattvas of profound wisdom can discern these two dharmas clearly. Other śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and followers of other paths who cling to names cannot comprehend these two dharmas.” Is this not exactly what is meant?

2.2.2. The conditioning factors and their distinctions
BDK 29 ↗When the one world of reality is yet to be realized

“Failing to comprehend” introduces the nature and characteristics of the conditions and their distinctions. There are three parts.

  1. The treatise distinguishes the characteristics of defilement and briefly indicates the stages at which each is counteracted and abandoned. ↓

  2. Beginning “the meaning of association,” it explains how the several defiled dharmas are associated or unassociated. ↓

  3. Beginning “further, the meaning of defiled mind,” it explains the two hindrances in terms of those defiled dharmas. ↓

1. The defilements and the stages of their abandonment

↥ The first of these is itself threefold.

  1. The characteristic of ignorance.

    1. The different defiled minds and how they are counteracted and abandoned. ↓

    2. Only then, how the ignorance mentioned first is counteracted and abandoned.

Why the abandonment of ignorance is explained last

↥ Why does the explanation proceed out of order? If one looks directly at ignorance, its gradual treatment is difficult to discern. As the defiled minds alone are removed, from the coarse to the subtle, fundamental ignorance itself is correspondingly relinquished and brought to a stop by degrees.⁕ That is why the treatment and abandonment of ignorance are discussed last.

BDK pp. 31–32

The six defiled states of mind

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 31 Six kinds of defiled states of mind [conditioned by ignorance] can be identified.

The first is the defilement united with attachment [to atman], from which those who have attained liberation in the Hinayana and those [bodhisattvas] at the “stage of establishment of faith” are free.

The second is the defilement united with the “continuing mind,” from which those who are at the “stage of establishment of faith” and who are practicing expedient means [to attain enlightenment] can gradually free themselves and free themselves completely at the “stage of pure-heartedness.”

The third is the defilement united with the discriminating “analytical mind,” from which those at the “stage of observing precepts” begin to be liberated and finally are liberated completely when they arrive at the “stage of expedient means without any trace.”

The fourth is the [subtle] defilement disunited from the represented world of objects, from which those at the “stage of freedom from the world of objects” can be freed.

The fifth is the [subtler] defilement disunited from the “[evolving] mind that perceives” (i.e., the defilement existing prior to the act of perceiving), p. 31–32 from which those at the “stage of freedom from the [evolving] mind” are freed.

The sixth (and most subtle] is the defilement disunited from the basic “activating mind,” from which those bodhisattvas who have passed the final stage and have gone into the “stage of Tathāgatahood” are freed.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

3. The six defilements
BDK 31 ↗Six kinds of defiled states of mind

The treatment of the defilements has two parts.

  1. A general statement. ↓

  2. A detailed explanation. ↓ The detailed explanation also indicates how they are counteracted and abandoned.

3.1. General statement

↥ The six defilements are the mental consciousness and the five forms of mentation discussed above. Earlier, the treatise was tracing how they arise in dependence on their causes, so it described them in sequence from subtle to coarse. Here it also seeks to show the stages of their abandonment, so it proceeds from coarse to subtle.

3.2. Each defilement and its abandonment
3.2.1. Associated with attachment
BDK 31 ↗The defilement united with attachment

“Defilement associated with attachment” is mental consciousness inasmuch as it is nourished by the afflictions of views and craving.ᵀ It is associated with coarse discrimination and grasping.ᵀ When practitioners of the two vehicles reach arhatship, they are entirely free of the afflictions abandoned through seeing and cultivation. Bodhisattvas can become free of them from the ten stages of understanding onward.

Defilement associated with attachment · 執相應染 zhí xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement united with attachment [to atman]
associated · 相應 xiāng yìng · Skt. saṃprayukta · BDK p. 32 united
BDK 31 ↗The stage of establishment of faith

Here, “the stage corresponding to faith” refers to the ten stages of understanding. The faculty of faith is fully developed and can no longer be lost.ᵀ That is why the stage is called “corresponding to faith.” As the Sūtra for Humane Kings says, “Thirty persons are in the noble womb of the acceptance that subdues [afflictions] — the ten minds of faith, the ten of stability, and the ten of firmness.” Here “firmness” designates the ten dedications of merit, “stability” the ten practices, and “faith” the ten stages of faithful understanding. Upon entering this stage, one has already realized the emptiness of the person. The afflictions abandoned through seeing and cultivation can no longer become active. Hence the expression “free of them.” Throughout this treatise, counteracting and abandoning [defilements] are discussed with reference to their manifest activity.

stage corresponding to faith · 信相應地 xìn xiāng yìng dì · BDK p. 31 stage of establishment of faith
3.2.2. Associated with noninterruption
BDK 31 ↗The defilement united with the continuing mind

“Defilement associated with noninterruption” is continuing consciousness among the five forms of mentation.ᵀ It arises in succession in association with grasping at dharmas. “Noninterruption” is another name for continuity.ᵀ From the ten stages of understanding, one cultivates contemplation of consciousness-only and the preparatory practice of investigation. Upon realizing the three modes of absence of intrinsic nature on the first ground, discrimination that grasps at dharmas can no longer become active. Hence “one is completely free of it upon attaining the ground of pure mind.”ᵀ

Defilement associated with noninterruption · 不斷相應染 bù duàn xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement united with the “continuing mind”
association · 相應 xiāng yìng · Skt. saṃprayukta · BDK p. 32 united
ground of pure mind · 淨心地 jìng xīn dì · BDK p. 31 stage of pure-heartedness
3.2.3. Associated with discriminating cognition
BDK 31 ↗The defilement united with the discriminating analytical mind

“Defilement associated with discriminating cognition” is the fourth of the five forms of mentation, discriminating consciousness.ᵀ Up to the seventh ground, whenever the two kinds of wisdom arise, it cannot become active. On emerging from contemplation and attending to particular things, when the mind operates spontaneously, it can become active again. Hence “gradually becomes free.” From the seventh ground onward one abides in contemplation for extended periods, so this manas ceases entirely to become active. Hence “wholly free on the ground of the practice of signlessness.”ᵀ On the seventh ground, contemplation of signlessness still involves deliberate application and effort. Hence the name “ground of the practice of signlessness.”

Defilement associated with discriminating cognition · 分別智相應染 fēn bié zhì xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement united with the discriminating “analytical mind”
ground of the practice of signlessness · 無相方便地 wú xiàng fāng biàn dì · BDK p. 31 stage of expedient means without any trace
3.2.4. Unassociated defilement manifesting form
BDK 31 ↗The defilement disunited from the represented world of objects

“Unassociated defilement manifesting form” is the third of the five forms of mentation, manifesting consciousness.ᵀ As visible images appear in a bright mirror, so forms appear here. Hence “unassociated defilement manifesting form.”

The “ground of mastery over form” is the eighth ground. One has gained mastery over pure lands.ᵀ The coarse forms of impure lands can no longer appear, so one is said to be free of this defilement.

ground of mastery over form · 色自在地 sè zì zài dì · BDK p. 31 stage of freedom from the world of objects
3.2.5. Unassociated defilement of perceiving mind
BDK 31 ↗The defilement disunited from the mind that perceives

“Unassociated defilement of perceiving mind” is the second of the five forms of mentation, evolving consciousness.ᵀ The capacity to perceive is constituted in dependence on the mind in motion.

The “ground of mastery over mind” is the ninth ground. Here one has attained the four unobstructed knowledges.ᵀ An obstructed apprehending cognition can no longer arise, so one is said to be free of this defilement.

ground of mastery over mind · 心自在地 xīn zì zài dì · BDK p. 31–32 stage of freedom from the [evolving] mind

“Unassociated defilement of root activity” is the first of the five forms of mentation, activating consciousness.ᵀ Through the power of ignorance, mind stirs in nonawakening.

Unassociated defilement of root activity · 根本業不相應染 gēn běn yè bù xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 32 defilement disunited from the basic “activating mind”
BDK 32 ↗Those bodhisattvas who have passed the final stage

The “bodhisattva's final ground” is the tenth, since the stainless ground is included in this ground.⁕ᵀ Strictly speaking, subtle characteristics of evolving and manifesting are still present on the tenth ground. The account of gradual freedom simply follows the characteristic assigned to each ground. As a later passage says, from “depending on activating consciousness” through “what is seen by the mind of a bodhisattva on the final ground is called the recompense body [saṃbhogakāya].” If one were free of activating consciousness, no aspect of perceiving would remain. Thus, as long as activating consciousness has yet to be exhausted, the capacity to perceive and the capacity to manifest have yet to be exhausted as well.

bodhisattva's final ground · 菩薩盡地 pú sà jìn dì · BDK p. 32 final stage

1. The defilements and the stages of their abandonment

2. Causes and conditions of arising and ceasing › 2. The nature and characteristics of the causes and conditions › 2. The conditioning factors and their distinctions › 1. The defilements and the stages of their abandonment

1.2. The six defiled minds
BDK 31 ↗Six kinds of defiled states of mind

“Defilement” here comprises mental consciousness and the five modes into which manas was divided above. Since they are abandoned from coarse to subtle, the order of exposition is now reversed.

1.2.1. Defilement associated with grasping
BDK 31 ↗The defilement united with attachment

The first, “defilement associated with grasping,” consists of the afflictions, abandoned through seeing or cultivation, that the mental consciousness mentioned above produces.ᵀ As the text said above, “It conceives self and mine and grasps falsely in various ways,” down to “this consciousness grows through the afflictions of views and craving.”

defilement associated with grasping · 執相應染 zhí xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement united with attachment [to atman]
BDK 31 ↗The stage of establishment of faith

“Can leave it behind at the stage associated with faith” refers to the ten understandings among the three sets of worthy stages.ᵀ The Sūtra for Humane Kings speaks of “the thirty persons in the noble embryo of the patience of subduing,” the minds of faith and the other worthy stages.⁕ Upon entry into this stage, the coarse delusions abandoned through seeing and cultivation can no longer become active. Hence “leave behind.” Throughout this treatise counteraction and abandonment concern what currently arises in activity. Residual seeds are outside its discussion. Its account of the stages of abandonment can therefore diverge considerably from that of other scriptures. This need cause no surprise.⁕

stage associated with faith · 信相應地 xìn xiāng yìng dì · BDK p. 31 stage of establishment of faith
1.2.2. Defilement associated with continuity
BDK 31 ↗The defilement united with the continuing mind

The second, “defilement associated with uninterrupted continuity,” is continuing consciousness, the fifth of the five modes of manas.ᵀ It associates uninterruptedly with grasping at a self in dharmas. One leaves it behind completely on entering contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas on the first ground.

defilement associated with uninterrupted continuity · 不斷相應染 bù duàn xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement united with the “continuing mind”
1.2.3. Defilement associated with discriminating discernment
BDK 31 ↗The defilement united with the discriminating analytical mind

The third, “defilement associated with discriminating discernment,” is discerning consciousness, the fourth mode of manas.ᵀ Through the seventh ground, when insight into the two emptinesses arises this defilement is inactive. When one emerges from contemplation, attends to conventional things, and the mind operates spontaneously, it can still become active. Hence “gradually leaves behind.” From the seventh ground onward it ceases for good and no longer arises. This is “leaving behind completely.” The Sūtra Unraveling the Intent explains this point: “As for their seeds, it is only with vajra-like mind that they are cut off all at once.” The Compendium of Abhidharma explains the matter at length.⁕

defilement associated with discriminating discernment · 分別智相應染 fēn bié zhì xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement united with the discriminating “analytical mind”
Why the first three defilements are associated

↥ These first three defilements operate coarsely and possess the three kinds of equality. They are accordingly called “associated.”ᵀ

associated · 相應 xiāng yìng · Skt. saṃprayukta · BDK p. 32 united
1.2.4. Unassociated defilement of manifesting visible form
BDK 31 ↗The defilement disunited from the represented world of objects

The fourth, “unassociated defilement of manifesting visible form,” is manifesting consciousness, the third mode of manas. It displays visible images like a bright mirror.ᵀ

unassociated defilement of manifesting visible form · 現色不相應染 xiàn sè bù xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement disunited from the represented world of objects
BDK 31 ↗The stage of freedom from the world of objects

“The ground of mastery over form” is the eighth ground.ᵀ

ground of mastery over form · 色自在地 sè zì zài dì · BDK p. 31 stage of freedom from the world of objects
1.2.5. Unassociated defilement of the seeing mind
BDK 31 ↗The defilement disunited from the mind that perceives

The fifth, “unassociated defilement of the seeing mind,” is evolving consciousness, the second of the five, because “the power of seeing depends upon mind in motion.”ᵀ

unassociated defilement of the seeing mind · 能見心不相應染 néng jiàn xīn bù xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 31 defilement disunited from the “[evolving] mind that perceives”
BDK 31–32 ↗The stage of freedom from the evolving mind

“The ground of mastery over mind” is the ninth ground.ᵀ

ground of mastery over mind · 心自在地 xīn zì zài dì · BDK p. 31–32 stage of freedom from the [evolving] mind
1.2.6. Unassociated defilement of fundamental activity
BDK 32 ↗The defilement disunited from the basic activating mind

The sixth, “unassociated defilement of fundamental activity,” is activating consciousness, the first of the five. Through the force of ignorance, thought stirs without awakening.ᵀ

unassociated defilement of fundamental activity · 根本業不相應染 gēn běn yè bù xiāng yìng rǎn · BDK p. 32 defilement disunited from the basic “activating mind”
BDK 32 ↗The final stage of bodhisattvahood

“The bodhisattva’s final ground” groups together the tenth ground and the stainless ground as a single stage.ᵀ

bodhisattva’s final ground · 菩薩盡地 pú sà jìn dì · BDK p. 32 final stage
What is abandoned on the higher grounds

↥ Strictly speaking, subtle appearances still manifest from the eighth ground onward. But at that ground one has attained mastery over pure lands, and coarse forms never again appear. This is the sense in which they are left behind. From the ninth ground onward subtle seeing also persists. But one has gained mastery over mind and the seeing aspect grows subtler. This is the sense in which it is left behind. How do we know? The text below says, “Dependent on activating consciousness,” down to “what is seen by bodhisattvas at the final ground is called the recompense body (saṃbhogakāya).” “Apart from activating consciousness there is no aspect of seeing.” Thus as long as activating consciousness has not been exhausted, the seeing aspect, too, remains inseparable from it.

BDK pp. 32–33

Association and the two hindrances

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 32 On [the expression] “the one world of reality is yet to realized.” From this state those [bodhisattvas] who have advanced from the “stage of the establishment of faith” to the “stage of pure-heartedness,” after having completed and severed [their deluded thoughts], will be more and more liberated as they advance, and when they reach the “stage of Tathāgatahood,” they will be completely liberated.

On “united.” By the word “united” [appearing in the first three defilements] is meant that though difference (i.e., duality) exists between the mind (subject) and the datum of the mind (object), there is a simultaneous relation between them in that when the subject is defiled the object is also defiled, and when the subject is purified the object is also purified.⁕

On “disunited.” By the word “disunited” is meant that [the second three subtle and fundamental defilements are the aspects of] nonenlightenment on the part of the mind existing prior to the differentiation [into the subject-and-object relationship]; therefore, a simultaneous relation between the subject and object is not as yet established.

On the “defiled state of mind.” p. 32–33 It is called “the hindrance originating from defilements,” for it obstructs any fundamental insight into suchness.

On “ignorance.” Ignorance is called the “hindrance originating from misconceptions of objects,” for it obstructs the wisdom that functions spontaneously in the world.

Because of the defiled [state of] mind, there emerges the subject that perceives [incorrectly] ( i.e., the evolving mind) and that which reproduces [the reproducing mind], and thus one erroneously predicates the world of objects and causes oneself to deviate from the undifferentiated state [of suchness]. Though all things are always in quiescence and devoid of any marks of rising, because of the nonenlightenment due to ignorance, one erroneously strays from the Dharma (i.e., suchness); thus one fails to obtain the wisdom that functions spontaneously by adapting oneself to all circumstances in the world.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

4. Counteracting and abandoning ignorance
BDK 32 ↗The one world of reality is yet to be realized

From “failing to understand” onward comes the fourth part, on counteracting and abandoning ignorance. The abiding ground of ignorance can be considered in two senses.

  1. As an acquired abiding ground, it can gradually be cut off from the first bodhisattva ground onward.

  2. As an innate abiding ground, it can be cut off only by the wisdom of a buddha's awakening.

↥ The treatise groups the innate and the acquired together under the common name of ignorance. Hence the passage from “upon entering the ground of pure mind one becomes free in part” through “on the tathāgata ground one can become entirely free.”ᵀ

tathāgata ground · 如來地 rú lái dì · Skt. tathāgata-bhūmi · BDK p. 32 stage of Tathāgatahood
5. Association and nonassociation
BDK 32 ↗The meanings of united and disunited

The fifth part explains association and nonassociation.ᵀ Of the six defilements, the first three are associated. The last three, together with ignorance, are unassociated.ᵀ

nonassociation · 不相應 bù xiāng yìng · Skt. viprayukta · BDK p. 32 disunited
unassociated · 不相應 bù xiāng yìng · Skt. viprayukta · BDK p. 32 disunited
5.1. Association

↥ In the discussion of association, “mind and thought-dharmas are distinct” names mind and its mental factors.ᵀ Kātyāyana's treatise calls them “mind and the dharmas thought by mind.”⁕ “According to distinctions of defilement and purity” refers to discriminating among defiled and pure dharmas and to the distinctions among views, conceit, craving, and so forth. “The same cognitive aspect” means sameness in that which cognizes. “The same object-aspect” means sameness in the object cognized.

mind and thought-dharmas are distinct · 心念法異 xīn niàn fǎ yì · BDK p. 32 difference (i.e., duality) exists between the mind (subject) and the datum of the mind (object)
The three equalities

↥ Association is explained here in terms of three equalities.

  1. “Mind and thought-dharmas are distinct” expresses equality in individual substance. Each afflictive mental factor occurs as one instance, with no second instance of it [at that moment].

  2. Sameness of cognitive aspect is equality in cognition.

  3. Sameness of object-aspect is equality in object.

↥ The first three defilements exhibit these three equalities and are present together [with mind]. They are therefore called “associated.”

How can the cognitive aspect be the same?

↥ Question. The Yogācārabhūmi says, “Mind and its mental factors have the same object but differ in their mode of apprehension. Present together at one time, each operates individually.” Here the treatise says that their cognitive aspect is also the same. How can this apparent contradiction be reconciled?

↥ Answer. Both points hold, so they are compatible. How so? In self-view the activity is that of viewing. In self-love the activity is that of loving. It is because their activities differ in this way that the mode of apprehension is said to differ. But both the view and the love construe their object as “I.” In this sense the cognitive aspect is the same. The two statements are therefore compatible.

5.2. Nonassociation
BDK 32 ↗On “disunited

In the discussion of nonassociation, “it is mind itself in nonawakening, with no distinction at any time” means that equality in individual substance does not apply here. There are no distinct mental factors apart from mind. Given the absence of that first equality and of anything else apart from mind, what basis could the remaining two equalities have? Sameness of cognition and sameness of object therefore have no application. Hence “no sameness of cognitive aspect and object-aspect.”ᵀ The negation here signifies absence.

no sameness of cognitive aspect and object-aspect · 不同知相緣相 bù tóng zhī xiàng yuán xiàng · BDK p. 32 a simultaneous relation between the subject and object is not as yet established Wŏnhyo distinguishes the knowing and the object taken by mind and mental factors. Hakeda presents the relation in terms of subject and object.
How can ālayavijñāna be associated with five mental factors?

↥ Question. The Yogācārabhūmi says, “The ālayavijñāna is associated with five mental factors and takes two kinds of object.” This is precisely what the present treatise calls “unassociated defilement manifesting form.” Why does it speak of nonassociation here?

↥ Answer. Here the term “association” is used with reference to the distinct operations of the afflictive mental factors. There are no afflictive mental factors in manifesting consciousness. It is in this sense called unassociated. The newer treatise speaks with reference to the universal mental factors, and hence calls it associated. For this reason these two accounts are compatible as well.

6. The two obstacles
BDK 32 ↗The two hindrances

The sixth part explains the two obstacles. In the explicit exposition they are called the “two hindrances.” In the implicit exposition they are called the “two obstacles.” I explain this at length in my Treatise on the Two Hindrances. The present passage follows the implicit exposition, in two parts.

  1. It first distinguishes the two obstacles. ↓

  2. From “what does this mean?” onward it explains the reasons for the distinction. ↓

6.1. Distinguishing the obstacles
The obstacle of the afflictions

↥ In the first part, “the defiled mind” refers to the six forms of defiled mind. “Fundamental wisdom” is the discernment that illuminates quiescence.ᵀ The defiled mind runs counter to quiescence and is therefore called the “obstacle of the afflictions.”

Fundamental wisdom · 根本智 gēn běn zhì · BDK p. 33 fundamental insight
The obstacle to wisdom
BDK 33 ↗On ignorance

“Ignorance” refers to root ignorance. “Wisdom that acts in the world” is subsequently acquired wisdom. Ignorance is so benighted that it can distinguish nothing. Hence it runs counter to the wisdom that makes distinctions in the world. This is the sense in which it is called the “obstacle to wisdom.”

6.2. Why each is an obstacle
BDK 33 ↗Because of the defiled state of mind

The explanation of the reasons makes this point explicit.

Defiled mind and fundamental wisdom

↥ “Because the defiled mind perceives, manifests, and delusively grasps objects” refers in brief to evolving consciousness, manifesting consciousness, and discriminating consciousness. “Runs counter to the nature of equality” means it runs counter to the equality of subject and object in fundamental wisdom.ᵀ This explains the obstacle of the afflictions.

nature of equality · 平等性 píng děng xìng · Skt. samatā · BDK p. 33 undifferentiated state [of suchness]
Ignorance and subsequently acquired wisdom
BDK 33 ↗Though all things are always in quiescence

“All dharmas are ever quiescent and exhibit no characteristic of arising” identifies the dharma-nature about which ignorance is deluded.ᵀ “Through ignorance and nonawakening one delusively runs counter to the Dharma” shows how ignorance is deluded about dharma-nature. Hence the passage from “one cannot attain” through “[knowledge of every] kind” directly explains how ignorance runs counter to wisdom concerning the world.

characteristic of arising · 起相 qǐ xiàng · BDK p. 33 marks of rising

2. Association and nonassociation
BDK 32 ↗On “united” and “disunited

The second section now explains association and nonassociation.ᵀ The first three defilements are called associated. The last three, together with ignorance, are unassociated.ᵀ As the text said above, “Unassociated with mind, a thought suddenly arises. This is called ignorance.”

association · 相應 xiāng yìng · Skt. saṃprayukta · BDK p. 32 united
nonassociation · 不相應 bù xiāng yìng · Skt. viprayukta · BDK p. 32 disunited
unassociated · 不相應 bù xiāng yìng · Skt. viprayukta · BDK p. 32 disunited
Association
BDK 32 ↗Though difference exists between the mind and the datum of the mind

“Mind and the mental dharmas differ” means that the individual afflictive mental factors have distinct characteristics.ᵀ For example, in defilement associated with discriminating discernment, self-view, self-love, and self-conceit differ in their activity.⁕ The Kātyāyana text speaks of “mind and the dharmas thought by mind.” Here “mental dharmas” is that same expression, “dharmas thought by mind.” Both are alternative terms for mental factors.

Mind and the mental dharmas differ · 心念法異 xīn niàn fǎ yì · BDK p. 32 difference (i.e., duality) exists between the mind (subject) and the datum of the mind (object)
BDK 32 ↗When the subject is defiled, the object is also defiled

“According to the distinction between defilement and purity” concerns differentiating defiled and pure dharmas, conceiving the distinction of self and mine, and the like.

↥ “The same characteristic of knowing” means sameness on the side of that which knows.

↥ “The same characteristic of the object” means sameness on the side of what is cognized. Here association is named on the basis of three equalities. ↓

1. Equality in number of instances
BDK 32 ↗Association: the three equalities

“Mind and mental dharmas differ” points to equality in number of instances: each afflictive factor has one instance of its own, with no second instance [of that factor].ᵀ

Mind and mental dharmas differ · 心念法異 xīn niàn fǎ yì · BDK p. 32 difference (i.e., duality) exists between the mind (subject) and the datum of the mind (object)
2. Equality in cognition

↥ “The same characteristic of knowing” points to equality in cognition.

3. Equality in object

↥ “The same characteristic of the object” points to equality in object. Possession of these three is the reason for the name “association.”

Shared cognition and differing modes of operation
BDK 32 ↗How mind and mental factors can share the same knowing

Question. The Yogācārabhūmi says, “Mind and mental factors share a single object. They differ in their mode of operation. They coexist at one time, each carrying on its own activity.” Yet here even the characteristic of knowing is said to be the same. How can these contrary statements be reconciled?

↥ Answer. Both meanings hold, so there is no contradiction. How so? Self-view operates as a view. Self-love operates as love. In these respects their operations differ. But view, love, and the others all take their object as self. In this respect they share the characteristic of knowing. Thus both statements hold without interfering with each other.

Nonassociation
BDK 32 ↗On “disunited

“Mind itself is unawakened, with no differentiation at any time” explains the absence of the first equality. Apart from mind there are no distinct afflictive mental factors here. Hence “mind itself is unawakened, with no differentiation at any time.” In the absence of equality in number of instances, on what would the other two equalities depend? There is accordingly no equality of knowing or of object. Hence “the characteristic of knowing and the characteristic of the object are not shared.”ᵀ

the characteristic of knowing and the characteristic of the object are not shared · 不同知相緣相 bù tóng zhī xiàng yuán xiàng · BDK p. 32 a simultaneous relation between the subject and object is not as yet established Wŏnhyo distinguishes the knowing and the object taken by mind and mental factors. Hakeda presents the relation in terms of subject and object.
Why the five universal factors do not make this defilement associated
BDK 32 ↗Why the seeing mind is called disunited

Question. The Yogācārabhūmi says, “The ālayavijñāna associates with five mental factors.” This is precisely what our text calls the defilement of the seeing mind. Why does it call it unassociated?

↥ Answer. The treatise uses “associated” for the distinct operations of afflictive mental factors. The defilement of the seeing mind has no such afflictive factors and is called unassociated. There is therefore no conflict. Even though the five subtle, universally present mental factors are there, mind and its factors cognize together. Since they grasp at characteristics where there are none, this is a general grasping at dharmas.⁕ There is no distinct investigating view belonging to the factor of discernment, and therefore no specific grasping at a self in dharmas here.

↥ How do we know that ālayavijñāna, too, involves grasping at dharmas? The Sūtra Unraveling the Intent says, “At and beyond the eighth ground, no afflictions become active. Only the cognitive obstruction remains as support.” At this stage none of the delusions of the other seven consciousnesses is active. Only the ālayavijñāna is manifest [among the states in question]. Thus we know that this consciousness constitutes the cognitive obstruction. If the sūtra were speaking of the presence of seeds, the seeds of the afflictive obstruction would likewise still be unexhausted. Thus we know that its statement concerns the cognitive obstruction in its active manifestation.

3. The two hindrances
BDK 32–33 ↗The hindrance from defilements and the hindrance from misconceptions of objects

Beginning “further, the meaning of defiled mind,” the third section gathers these matters under two hindrances. There are, in brief, two ways of understanding them.

3.1. The account in other scriptures and treatises

↥ The first approach identifies an obstruction common to the two vehicles.⁕

  1. The afflictions of the ten latent tendencies keep one revolving in saṃsāra and obstruct the fruit of nirvāṇa. They are called the afflictive obstruction.

    1. Grasping at dharmas and similar delusions are a hindrance particular to bodhisattvas. They obscure what is to be known and obstruct the fruit of awakening. They are called the cognitive obstruction. This is the approach taught in other scriptures and treatises.

3.2. The account in the Awakening of Faith

↥ The second approach distinguishes the two as follows.

  1. Any mind that stirs in thought, grasps at characteristics, and so on runs counter to the quiescent nature of wisdom that knows reality as it is. This is called the afflictive hindrance.ᵀ

    afflictive hindrance · 煩惱礙 fán nǎo ài · BDK p. 32–33 hindrance originating from defilements

    1. Fundamental ignorance, dark, deluded, and unawakened, runs counter to the discerning activity of wisdom that knows phenomena in their full extent. This is called the hindrance to wisdom.ᵀ

      hindrance to wisdom · 智礙 zhì ài · BDK p. 33 hindrance originating from misconceptions of objects

↥ The present treatise adopts the second of these approaches.⁕ It therefore calls the six kinds of defiled mind the afflictive hindrance, and the underlying ground of ignorance the hindrance to wisdom. Yet if one matched them directly, one would expect ignorance to obstruct wisdom regarding reality, and defiled mind to obstruct wisdom regarding phenomena in their full extent. Why should it be otherwise? Because the match need not always hold. The treatise itself explains why it need not hold.

The base text is Yoshito S. Hakeda’s translation from the Chinese attributed to Paramārtha, in The Awakening of Faith, BDK English Tripiṭaka 63-IV, Numata Center, 2005 (original English edition © 1967 Columbia University Press). Page references give the printed pagination. English numbered headings and Hakeda’s explanatory essays are editorial material. The interleaved text covers his translation of the treatise, including the first item that crosses onto p. 34. The PDF’s line-break hyphenation and legacy font encodings have been normalized. Source PDF · Chinese treatise, T1666

Both English commentaries are new translations from the Chinese. The popups preserve the wording of each work, including quotations that differ from the received treatise. Their citations use Taishō volume, text, page, column, and line. Mandarin readings use syllable-spaced citation tones. Hakeda sometimes rearranges clauses or incorporates a Chinese question into a following assertion, so the Chinese can run in a different order when read through his English.

Sanskrit in the terminology notes gives a conventional Buddhist equivalent where identifiable. Parentheses indicate when the Sanskrit applies to one part of a Chinese expression, comes from a quoted sūtra, or is a proposed reconstruction. For the five modes of mind, Suzuki marks karmavijñāna for 業識 as tentative. Hakeda uses pravṛtti-vijñāna for 轉識. The mirror passage Wŏnhyo quotes provides Sanskrit parallels for 現識 and 分別事識. The headings are editorial. They follow Wŏnhyo’s announced divisions through the paragraphs in which he develops them. Within each BDK passage, the commentary follows its Chinese order. Where a division continues across a BDK break, its heading and parent divisions identify the resumed discussion. The commentary paragraph on p. 33 follows Wŏnhyo into his gloss on the first, coarse characteristic and stops there.
